Target What runs there Strongest evidence ESP32-S3 hearth_sink, a Sendspin sink (setup guide); i2s_player, which loops a fixed test stream Two boards in a Wi-Fi group for ten minutes without an underrun; all decode fixtures run in real time on a board; the sink pairs and plays under QEMU in CI ESP32-P4 The AC-3 and E-AC-3 decoder, and hearth_sink built for boards of silicon revision v1.x, which reach Wi-Fi through the board's onboard ESP32-C6 (firmware image); AC-4 decode in a build with CONFIG_ICLFORGE_AC4 (off in the published images; AC-4 on the P4) All AC-3 and E-AC-3 decode fixtures run in real time on a board at 360 MHz; CI builds the sink firmware ESP32-C3 The same decoder, in the fixed-point tier Correct under qemu-riscv32 emulation. No board has run it ESP32-C6 Fixed-point decoder; hearth_sink's Sendspin player, stereo only All decode fixtures run on a board; a stereo Sendspin group with an ESP32-S3 played ten minutes with no underruns on either board (setup guide). CI builds the Sendspin player for this part, for the 4 MB and the 16 MB flash layouts, and does not run it: ESP-IDF's RISC-V QEMU emulates the ESP32-C3 and no other part ESPHome An external component wrapping the ESP32-S3 decoder Config-checked in CI against the manifest; not yet a media_player or speaker source Windows, Linux and macOS hearth (the desktop window, Qt 6.8+) with its engine and Network page; hearth-testsink, hearth-testserver and hearth-render development tools Engine and Sendspin interoperability tests run in CI, and the window builds there on all three platforms; each committed AC-4 test stream that the decoder accepts plays through the engine sample for sample as the library decodes it Android TV Hearth for Android, a Sendspin sink that passes AC-3 and E-AC-3 to the receiver on its HDMI output One recorded run on an NVIDIA Shield TV (2019) into an Onkyo TX-RZ740: AC-3 5.1 and E-AC-3 5.1 for two minutes each with no underrun, sent by the test server. CI builds a debug APK and runs its tests on an emulator

The desktop player's passthrough uses the same path as forge play. That command has played the AC-3, E-AC-3 and signed Atmos stream shapes listed there to a receiver through a Raspberry Pi 4B without an underrun (Raspberry Pi passthrough). The window's own use of it is tested against a stand-in link (Passthrough to a receiver).

docs.title: Hearth for Android
docs.text: Hearth for Android is a Sendspin sink for Android TV. It pairs with the desktop player, passes the AC-3 or E-AC-3 stream it is sent to the AV receiver on the box's HDMI output, and shows a karaoke item's lyrics in time. It is built from source; no release carries it, and it does not decode on the device, so a stream that reaches it as PCM is not heard. Hearth for Android has the build, the pairing, the screens and what has been run.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• Send AC-4 as it is to an ESP32-C6 running a published firmware image. That image has no AC-4 decoder, so such a sink gets PCM decoded here; the P4 and S3 images take the stream themselves. ESP32 sinks has the detail.
  • Play every track of a container. An MP4, Matroska or MPEG-TS file plays its first AC-3, E-AC-3 or AC-4 track; the others are not offered, and a Matroska file's codec delay is not trimmed.
  • Fetch lyrics, or time them from the recording. Hearth reads .lrc files beside a stream, and times the words of one by hand (Timing the lyrics); it does not find or download them, or work the times out from the sound.
  • List AC-4 objects on the Play page. The Objects card shows the positions of E-AC-3 objects. An AC-4 item's objects are rendered into the speaker layout, and the Media page says an A-JOC stream carries object metadata without listing it.
  • Remove an item from the queue. The window has no control for it.
  • Trim the AC-4 decoder's delay at the start of an item (see above).
  • Play to a group before the network is found. The output chosen in the picker is kept across starts, and a group is one of the choices; but the network starts after the window opens, so the group is not ready for the first moments, and playback is refused with that reason until it is rather than played on this computer.
  • Send a receiver anything but AC-3 and E-AC-3 as a bitstream. An AC-4 item is decoded for it (Passthrough to a receiver).
  • Notice by itself that a receiver was switched on. What each output takes is read when playback first starts and again each time the output picker opens, so a receiver switched on while the window is open is taken up when the picker is next opened. The output Hearth is playing to is not read while it is in use: a receiver switched on in the middle of a decode to its own output is sent a bitstream once playback has been stopped and started.

docs.title: Hearth for Android
docs.text:
Hearth for Android is a Sendspin sink for Android TV. It is advertised on the network, pairs with the desktop player, and hands the AC-3 or E-AC-3 stream Hearth sends it to the AV receiver on the box's HDMI output, as the bitstream it is. When the item is a karaoke stream with a lyrics file, it shows the words in time on the TV.

Status as of 2026-10-13: built from source; no release carries it

The app pairs, passes AC-3 and E-AC-3 to a receiver and draws the lyric screen. It does not decode anything itself yet, so a stream that reaches it as PCM, FLAC or Opus is accepted and not heard, and it does not list AC-4 or TrueHD. CI builds a debug APK and runs its tests on an emulator; no release publishes one, and it is not in an app store. The plan and what is left are in planning/hearth-android.md.

The pictures on this page are the app's own drawing at 1080p, written by its tests. They are not photographs of a television.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• An Android TV box wired by HDMI to an AV receiver that decodes Dolby Digital and Dolby Digital Plus. The app plays nothing through a TV's own speakers. It has been run on an NVIDIA Shield TV (2019, Android 11) into an Onkyo TX-RZ740.
  • A computer running Hearth on the same network, to pair with it and send it a stream.
  • To build it: a vcpkg checkout, the Android SDK with NDK 26.1 and CMake 3.31.6, and adb.

docs.title: Build and install
docs.text:
export VCPKG_ROOT=/path/to/vcpkg
cd apps/hearth/android
./gradlew :app:assembleDebug
adb install -r app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk

The first build compiles the native libraries' dependencies, which takes about 25 minutes; vcpkg's cache keeps them for the next. The app's README has the build's details and its tests.

docs.title: Pair and play
docs.text:
The idle screen with the code a server asked for.

  1. Start the app on the box. The screen shows the sink's name, Hearth on <the box's name>, with its address and port, and says it is not paired yet.
  2. Pair it from Hearth. On the desktop player's Network page, select the sink and press Pair with this computer. The TV shows a six-digit code; type it into Hearth. A server that asks for the code as a QR is shown one beside the name.
  3. Put it in a group. A paired sink is not played to until it is in a group, and the idle screen says so until its first stream: on the Network page, create a group with this sink in it. A group of one plays to a single sink.
  4. Play. Choose the group in Hearth's output picker and play a file.

A paired sink before its first stream.

The pairing code as a QR.

docs.title: What it plays
docs.text:
Hearth sends What happens AC-3 or E-AC-3 Passed to the receiver as IEC 61937 bursts, each in the time slot it is due in. The receiver decodes it, and its display names the format PCM, FLAC or Opus Accepted and dropped: nothing is heard. Hearth sends these to a sink that cannot take a stream as it is AC-4 Not listed by the sink, so Hearth decodes it and sends PCM, which the sink drops

While a stream plays, the foot of the screen names its format and how it leaves the sink, for example "Dolby Digital 5.1 · Passing through".

Because the receiver gets the coded stream, what it plays is the receiver's decode. For a karaoke stream that means every vocal the stream carries, whatever is chosen on Hearth's Karaoke page.

docs.title: The lyric screen
docs.text:
A line being sung.

When Hearth plays a karaoke item that has a lyrics file, it sends the sink the words and where the sound is in them, and the sink follows them on its own clock. The screen shows the line before, the line being sung with the colour running through it word by word, and the lines to come. A duet's lines carry each singer's name, an instrumental break counts in with four dots, and a line in Hebrew, Yiddish or Arabic runs right to left. A file timed by line and not by word is shown a line at a time, and a file with no times is shown as text to scroll.

An item with no lyrics is named in the header by what Hearth says is playing, with its position and length.

A duet.

docs.title: The controls
docs.text:
The controls sheet, opened with the remote's centre button.

The remote's centre button opens a sheet over the foot of the screen. The four directions move the focus, the centre presses, Back closes it, and it closes itself after eight seconds.

  • Lyric delay: shows the words later or sooner, in steps of 50 ms up to a second either way. With the sheet closed, left and right nudge it.
  • Vocals: Both, V1, V2 or None. This asks Hearth for that choice. It changes what Hearth's own page shows and what the decoding members of the group play; this TV plays the stream as coded, and the sheet says so.
  • Text size: S, M or L.

The delay and the text size are kept.

docs.title: When something needs attention
docs.text:
Screen When What it says Starting The sink is not up, the box has no network address, or the HDMI route takes neither format The name, what it is waiting for, and what to check Idle Nothing is playing The name, the address, who it is paired with, a pairing code when a server has asked for one, and the formats the route passes through Attention The sink did not start, the receiver would not take a stream, or the HDMI link dropped and did not come back within 20 seconds One sentence of what happened and what to do; over a lyric it is a banner at the foot

An attention banner over a lyric.

After two minutes with nothing changing on the screen, it dims and moves slowly, to spare an OLED panel. Any key brings it back.

docs.title: What has been run
docs.text:
On 2026-10-12 an NVIDIA Shield TV (2019) on an Onkyo TX-RZ740 played two programmes sent by hearth-testserver, the development server, with the receiver queried for what it was decoding:

Programme The receiver said Bursts played Underruns AC-3 5.1, 448 kbit/s, 121 s Dolby Audio - DD, 48 kHz, 5.1 ch 3,790 of 3,792 0 E-AC-3 5.1, 256 kbit/s, 121 s Dolby Audio - DD+, 48 kHz, 5.1 ch 3,792 of 3,792 0

Not run: the desktop window playing to the box (the runs used the test server), an Atmos stream, another receiver, and a phone scanning the QR. The app's README has the runs in full, with what a dropped HDMI link costs.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• Decode on the device. It passes the stream through, so it needs a receiver, and the karaoke choice does not change what the TV plays.
  • Play PCM, FLAC or Opus. A stream of those is accepted and dropped.
  • AC-4. No receiver here has decoded AC-4 over this route, so the sink does not list it.
  • Take a microphone. The microphone and the pitch score are in the desktop player.
  • Come as a package. It is built from source and installed with adb.

Decoding on the device and playing as an ordinary Sendspin player are phases 4 and 5 of the plan.

docs.title: Using the desktop player
docs.text:
hearth is the desktop player: a window that plays AC-3, E-AC-3, E-AC-3 with Atmos objects, AC-4, TrueHD and MLP files through this computer's speakers or to a group of network sinks. It decodes TrueHD and MLP and does not pass them through (Hearth says what that means). This page walks through the window page by page. Hearth is the reference for what each feature does and does not do, and Karaoke covers the Karaoke page.

The pictures are of a build of main on Windows, playing three files made for the purpose: an E-AC-3 stream with six Atmos objects, a 5.1 AC-4 stream and the karaoke example.

docs.title: First run
docs.text:
The first-run dialog over an empty Play page.

The first time it starts, Hearth says three things before it plays anything:

  1. It plays to this computer's default output. The strip at the top of the window names the output, and clicking it opens the list of the others.
  2. Speakers are set per output. The Speakers page holds each output's routing, levels, delays and bass management. Nothing in the operating system's own sound settings changes.
  3. Network sinks need a group to play. Hearth lists the Sendspin players it finds on the network. Pair one, then add it to a group on the Network page; a group of one plays to a single sink.

Open Speakers goes to the Speakers page, and Not now closes the dialog. It does not come back.

docs.title: The window
docs.text:
Every page has the same frame. The header holds the output strip, the seven page buttons (Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+7) and ?, which opens the keyboard reference. The transport bar along the bottom has previous, play or pause, stop and next, the position with a scrubber, the item's length, the Gapless toggle and the volume.

Hearth opens where you left it. The window's size, its position and whether it was maximised are kept with the other settings (window/geometry and window/maximised) and restored on the next start. The window is never smaller than 960×620, and a remembered position that is on no connected screen any more, such as a monitor that has been unplugged, is ignored: the window opens at its remembered size where the system puts it. The first start opens at 1280×800. The lyrics in full screen are not remembered as the window's state; leaving them returns the window as it was.

docs.title: Play
docs.text:
The Play page 9 seconds into an E-AC-3 stream with objects, on a stereo output.

Queue. Add files… and Add folder… add to the queue, and so does dropping files or a folder on the page. A folder lists its .ac3, .ec3, .ac4, .mp4, .mkv and .ts files. Each row has the codec (A3, E3 or A4), the channel count, the sample rate, the bit rate and the length, and the row that is playing shows how far through it is. A file Hearth cannot read is marked not playable, with the reason, when the queue reaches it. The window has no control that removes an item.

A file can also be opened from outside the window: hearth song.ac3 on a command line, or a double-click on an .ac3 or .ec3 file on Windows once the installer has run. If Hearth is already running, the file joins its queue and starts (Command line).

Now playing names the item and what it is: the codec, the coded layout, the objects, the rate, the container, and what follows it in the queue and whether the join is gapless.

Levels · at play time has a meter for each output of the device, in dBFS, with the output's number and name and a CLIP light. The meters, the loudness and the frame's metadata are of the sound leaving the speakers now, not of what the decoder has read ahead.

Loudness · BS.1770-4 gives the momentary, short-term and integrated loudness, the loudness range and the true peak. The integrated figure starts again with each item.

This frame shows the metadata of the access unit being heard: dialnorm, the heavy compression and dynamic range words, whether it has short blocks, and its bit rate.

Objects draws the room from above, with the speakers of the layout and each object of an E-AC-3 stream where its metadata puts it; a raised object is drawn hollow. An AC-4 item's objects are not listed here.

Signal path is the path from the file to the speakers in three steps: what decodes the stream and in which dynamic range mode, what the renderer folds or places it onto, and the output it is heard on. Choose… opens the output picker.

A karaoke item adds a Lyrics card with the words in time and a Full screen button (Karaoke).

docs.title: Where it plays
docs.text:
The output picker on a computer with one stereo output, no receiver and no sinks paired.

The strip in the header says where the sound goes and why, in a sentence. Clicking it opens the output picker, which has three sections:

  • This computer · PCM. Each output of the computer, with its channels and the sample rates it takes. Hearth decodes the stream and sends it PCM. The one in use says playing here.
  • Passthrough · the receiver decodes. The outputs that say they accept AC-3 and E-AC-3 as a bitstream, each with a mark for the formats it takes. Choose one to play to it as a receiver: an AC-3 or E-AC-3 item it takes is sent to it untouched, as IEC 61937 bursts, and the receiver decodes it. Anything else is decoded here and played to the same output as PCM: an AC-4 item, a karaoke stream with a reproduction chosen, a programme other than a stream's first. The row in use says playing here while a bitstream goes out.
  • Network · Sendspin. The groups made on the Network page.

Choose a row and press Play here, and playback moves there. The choice is kept: the window plays there again the next time it is opened, before anything plays. Until you choose one the window decodes to the computer's default output.

An output or group that is not there when the window opens does not change what is kept, and it is not played to:

  • A passthrough row whose output the computer does not list now, such as a receiver that is switched off or unplugged, starts as a decode to the default output. Nothing is sent as a bitstream to some other output that takes one. The receiver is played to again at the next start it is listed for, unless another row is chosen first.
  • A This computer · PCM row whose output is not there starts as a decode to the default output.
  • A network group is played to once it is ready. The network is found after the window opens, so for the first moments the group is not ready, and the header says so instead of playing the item on this computer; a group that has been removed is refused the same way until another row is chosen.

While a bitstream goes out, the receiver decodes it with its own settings and plays it on its own speakers. The signal path says sent as it is and Not rendered here, the Decoder page says its controls reach only the meters, the Speakers page says its setup is not applied, and the volume in the transport bar is closed: the receiver's volume is the one that acts. The levels and the loudness on the Play page are of a decode made here beside the stream. Sending a bitstream holds the output, so other programs on the computer are silent through it meanwhile. Passthrough to a receiver has the rest.

docs.title: Media
docs.text:
The Media page for the stream with objects.

The Media page shows what the decoder reads from a file, without playing it. Showing chooses any item in the queue. Copy puts the text on the clipboard, and Export JSON… saves it as JSON.

  • Stream: the codec, the sample rate, the measured bit rate, the length, the objects and the container.
  • Container, for an MP4, Matroska or MPEG-TS file: its format, the track played and, for MP4, the edit list.
  • Bitstream information, for AC-3 and E-AC-3: the service, the dialogue level, the surround mode, the downmix levels and the copyright bits.
  • Objects · OAMD, for a stream with objects: how many there are, and each object's position, gain and whether it is active.
  • Probe summary: whether the stream carries dynamic range control and heavy compression, how many blocks switch to short transforms, the CRC count and the EMDF payloads.

An AC-4 item has cards for its table of contents and presentations instead (AC-4).

docs.title: Speakers
docs.text:
The top of the Speakers page for a stereo output.

The Speakers page describes the speakers on the output in use. The settings are kept for that output and come back on the next start.

  • Speaker layout. Pick a layout from 2.0 to 7.1.4, or List to write one as text: a name such as 7.1.4, or one token for each output of the device (a location, an angle such as 30/0, or a dash for an output with no speaker). Heights says whether the height speakers are on the wall, in the ceiling or up-firing. The plan draws the layout.
  • Routing · speaker to device output. A grid with a row for each speaker and a column for each output of the device; a click sends a speaker to an output, and the arrow keys move around the grid. Use the device's order puts it back, and Clear empties it.
  • Levels and delays. For each speaker: large or small, a trim in dB, a delay, and a button that plays the identify noise on it.
  • Bass management. One crossover frequency, from 40 to 250 Hz. A speaker marked small sends what is below it to the LFE output.
  • Identify. Pink noise on one output at a time, at -30, -20 or -12 dB, to hear which speaker is wired to it.

A change applies to what is playing. Hearth renders to the layout given here and does no room measurement or equalisation.

docs.title: Decoder
docs.text:
The AC-3 and E-AC-3 tab.

The Decoder page has a tab for AC-3 and E-AC-3 and a tab for AC-4, and opens on the one for the item that is playing. A change reaches that item at its next access unit or frame.

On the AC-3 and E-AC-3 tab:

  • Dynamic range: Line mode, RF mode, or Custom with the cut and the boost scaled apart, heavy compression, dialogue normalisation, and the level RF mode holds the output under.
  • Stereo and mono, used when the layout is 2.0: a Lo/Ro or an Lt/Rt downmix, the phase shift of the surround sum, and whether the LFE is mixed in.
  • This stream: what the playing stream carries of each of those.
  • Programme: which independent programme of an E-AC-3 stream plays, and for a 1+1 stream, channel 1, channel 2 or both.
  • Objects: whether the object layer is reconstructed (Auto does so when the layout has heights), and in which domain.
  • Errors and transform: what plays in place of a frame that will not decode (stop, repeat and fade, or mute), and the fast inverse transform.

The AC-4 tab, with a 5.1 AC-4 item playing.

On the AC-4 tab:

  • Presentation: which presentation of the stream plays. Automatic takes the first one in your language.
  • Dialogue: dialogue enhancement, the level of the dialogue against the music and effects where a presentation carries them apart, and audio description with its level.
  • Dynamic range: which device's compression curve applies, the output level, and dialogue normalisation.
  • Stereo and mono: the downmix, whether the stream's preferred downmix is followed, and whether the LFE is mixed in.
  • Errors: what plays in place of a frame that will not decode.
  • Immersive and objects: the layout an immersive stream is folded to, and core decoding, a lighter reconstruction of the immersive element and its objects.

The Karaoke page button at the top right goes to the karaoke choice, which belongs to the decoder and has a page of its own.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
The Network page with nothing found. The pictures here were taken with network discovery off.

The Network page lists the Sendspin players Hearth finds on the network. A Hearth sink takes the coded stream itself; any other Sendspin player takes PCM that Hearth has decoded.

  1. Find. Sinks appear by themselves; Look again asks the network once more. A sink can be an ESP32 board running hearth_sink, an Android TV box running Hearth for Android, or any other Sendspin player.
  2. Pair. Select a sink and press Pair with this computer. The sink shows a six-digit code, new for each attempt, on its own web page and on its serial console; type it in. Pairing makes a key that both keep, and after it the sink takes streams from Hearth without a code.
  3. Group. New group…, or Create a group straight after pairing. A group of one plays to a single sink. The group editor shows what each member will be sent (the coded stream, PCM at its own layout, or Opus) and why, and holds the group's volume and mute.
  4. Play. Choose the group in the output picker.

A paired Hearth sink has a settings view with three tabs: Speakers, for the sink's own layout and trims; Decoder, for its decoder settings and for whether audio decoded here reaches it as PCM or as Opus; and Firmware, which shows the image it is running and updates it over the network. The sink guides have the detail: ESP32-S3, ESP32-C6, ESP32-P4 and sink firmware.

A sink another server holds, such as one Music Assistant holds, shows as in use by another server, with a Take it back button.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The Settings page.

  • Playback: gapless joins between items, whether the queue and the position come back on the next start, whether a file that fails is skipped or stops the queue, and the lyric delay.
  • Network: the name sinks and players show for this computer, whether Hearth looks for Sendspin players, and the pairing records, each with Forget.
  • Appearance: the theme, the palette, the text size and motion. Motion is System, Reduced or Full: System follows the desktop's own request to cut back animation, and Reduced draws the waiting mark as three still squares instead of a turning spinner (Motion says how each platform's setting is read).
  • Language: English, German, Spanish, French, Arabic, Hebrew or Yiddish. Every page is translated; the translations are machine-made and no speaker has read them (Languages).
  • Diagnostics: a text file of what Hearth has done (the outputs opened, the streams played, the sinks found and paired, and every error), saved, copied or viewed live. Pairing keys, codes and file paths are left out of it.
  • About: About Hearth… opens the version and the build it came from, the licence, the repository, and Licences…, which lists what this build carries from others with each licence. The keyboard reference's About… (below) opens the same window; Forge and Crucible reach theirs from their Settings too.

docs.title: Keyboard
docs.text:
The keyboard reference, opened with F1 or the ? button.

Key What it does Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+7 Play, Media, Speakers, Decoder, Network, Settings, Karaoke F1 Opens the keyboard reference F11 The lyrics in full screen; Esc leaves it Space In the singer view: pause or play Left, Right In the singer view: back or forward five seconds Q In the singer view: show or hide the queue

Tab reaches each control in turn, and Space or Return activates the one with focus. The reference's About… button opens the version and the licences, as the About card on Settings does.

docs.title: How the pictures were taken
docs.text: hearth --smoke-shot <png> --page <name> saves a page to a file with network discovery off and a scratch settings store (Command line). These were taken on Windows with QT_QPA_PLATFORM=windows:darkmode=0, which draws the light theme whatever the desktop is set to, and QSG_DISTANCEFIELD_ANTIALIASING=gray, which keeps coloured subpixel edges out of the text, with the three files named by --open and a position by --seek.

docs.title: Hearth Player for Windows
docs.text:
hearth-player is a Sendspin player that plays through the computer's speakers. A server that lists it (Music Assistant, Hearth's own server, hearth-testserver) sends it AC-3 and E-AC-3 streams undecoded, Dolby Atmos objects included, over _iclforge_player@v1, and the player decodes them, renders the objects, folds everything to stereo and plays it. PCM, FLAC and Opus arrive over player@v1 and play as well.

It is the same sink the test sink uses (libs/sink: the pairing, the stores, the decoder), with a device for its output instead of a WAV file. hearth-testsink stays as it was.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
hearth-player --list-devices
hearth-player --device null --address 127.0.0.1 --port 0 --no-mdns
hearth-player

With no options it advertises _sendspin._tcp on port 8928 as hearth-pc-<computer name>, plays to the default output endpoint, and prints its client_id, a pairing token and, when a server asks to pair, the dynamic code. --device ID takes an id from --list-devices; --device null plays to nowhere in real time, which is what the tests use. --pair static --static-code DIGITS offers a fixed code instead (window on standard input opens it), and --pair none --unpaired-access takes any server. --help lists the rest.

The identity and the long-term pairing key are kept in %LOCALAPPDATA%\hearth-player (--state chooses another place), so a server that has paired once reaches the player again without a code. Nothing is kept in the repository.

docs.title: What it lists
docs.text:
Role Formats _iclforge_player@v1 ac3, eac3 (objects reconstructed and rendered; output layout 2.0) player@v1 pcm, flac, opus, stereo, 48 kHz 16-bit (PCM and FLAC also 44.1 kHz and 24-bit)

AC-4 is not listed. The extension role states the layout as 2.0 and the number of outputs as 2, so a server that renders for a sink knows nothing taller than stereo is wanted.

docs.title: How it keeps time
docs.text:
Every burst carries the time, on the player's clock, it is due. The player holds decoded frames until they are within 150 ms of that time, then queues them on the device. When a burst is due it asks the device when the frame would be heard (the device's queue and the delay the platform adds) and compares: the difference is the sync error. The first burst of a stream sets its alignment, with silence if it is early. After that the device's clock, which is not the player's, is followed a frame or a few at a time: the error is smoothed over about sixteen bursts, and when the smoothed error is above a millisecond, bursts drop or gain frames (trimmed), so a sound card that runs 300 ppm slow stays within a few milliseconds, not drifting for minutes. An error beyond 25 ms, which is a period and a half of WASAPI's shared mode and so more than the platform's own position can be trusted to, is corrected at once, by dropping frames if it is late and by playing silence if it is early, and counted (corrected). stream/clear drops what is waiting and flushes the device.

The console status line, printed every two seconds while a stream plays and when the state changes, shows the state, codec, channel count, objects (and whether they were placed: they are folded into the stereo mix, so not-placed is right for this player), frames waiting, underruns, invalid chunks, the newest sync error, the worst, and the corrections made.

docs.title: The firewall
docs.text: A server reaches the player at TCP port 8928, and finds it by mDNS (UDP 5353). Windows asks about both the first time a program listens on a real interface. hearth-player uses libs/sendspin's firewall helper for this: when it is first started on a non-loopback address it relaunches itself elevated, once, to add an inbound rule for its own executable, and the User Account Control prompt is the question. Declining leaves everything working on this computer and unreachable from others. --address 127.0.0.1 never asks. Nothing else changes Windows' settings.

docs.title: How Music Assistant sees it
docs.text: As a Sendspin player named hearth-pc-<computer name>, with player@v1 and _iclforge_player@v1 listed, and a state object stating layout: "2.0", two outputs, ac3 and eac3. A server that wants Atmos sends it the coded stream and nothing to decode. A server that does not know the extension role sends it PCM as for any player.

docs.title: An ESP32-C6 sink
docs.text:
hearth_sink runs on the ESP32-C6 as a stereo Sendspin player. It plays AC-3 and E-AC-3 streams of up to two coded channels. A wider stream is refused before a decoder opens for it, and the console says why once per stream.

The limit is memory, not decode speed. The C6 has no PSRAM, so the player's buffers and WiFi's receive buffers share the internal RAM. On a board on 2026-09-22, AC-3 and E-AC-3 5.1 each stopped within about 12 seconds when the decoder could not allocate its working memory. The part does decode 5.1 in real time with WiFi running: see the ESP32-C6 platform page. The E-AC-3 decoder has used less memory since (its 5.1 peak in the fixed tier is 109,806 bytes now, from 164,066), and the sink has not been run again on a board to see whether the limit has moved.

docs.title: Karaoke streams
docs.text:
A karaoke stream (bsmod 7 above 1/0) of AC-3 or E-AC-3 has five coded channels and an LFE at 3/2, wider than the two this board decodes, so Hearth decodes it and applies the reproduction there, and the C6 plays the stereo PCM it is sent as a plain Sendspin player. That is the same for both codecs, and the board lists eac3 among its karaoke codecs without that changing it: the channel limit applies regardless. On a C6 on 2026-10-12 Hearth said "This sink decodes AC-3 up to 2 channels, and this stream has 6, so it is decoded here and folded to 2.0 PCM" (and the same for E-AC-3), and the board reported itself as a player@v1 and no levels of its own. Hearth's live karaoke cases compare a board's own outputs with the host's decode, so they skip a board like this one and say why. The reproduction a listener hears from a C6 is the desktop's, and it is the same one every other member of a group plays (Karaoke).

The C6 build does not decode AC-4. CONFIG_ICLFORGE_AC4 builds the decoder for this part in the fixed-point tier, and the decoder does not fit beside WiFi: 2.0 peaks at 286,365 bytes, where the part has about 236,000 free with WiFi up, and 117 KB with the sink and its player up (ESP32-C6). A play of an AC-4 stream on the board is refused (why: "memory") and the board runs on. A C6 sink takes AC-4 programmes from Hearth as PCM. An ESP32-P4 or an ESP32-S3 built with sdkconfig.ac4 decodes AC-4 a Sendspin group sends it (ESP32-P4).

A stereo group of a C6 and an S3 has played ten minutes with no underrun on either board (example README). idf.py qemu does not support the C6, so CI builds its image but only a board runs it.

Pairing, groups and firmware updates work the same as on the S3; see An ESP32-S3 sink and Sink firmware. This page covers what differs on the C6.

docs.title: Which image
docs.text:
CI builds two C6 images, and a release carries both:

Image For hearth-sink-esp32c6 A C6 module with 4 MB of flash, the least any C6 module has hearth-sink-esp32c6-16mb A C6 module with 16 MB of flash

Sink firmware — Which image explains how to check a board's flash size and install from a release.

docs.title: Build and flash
docs.text:
From firmware/hearth-sink in an ESP-IDF terminal:

idf.py set-target esp32c6
idf.py "-DSDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS=sdkconfig.defaults;sdkconfig.hw;sdkconfig.sendspin;sdkconfig.c6;sdkconfig.sendspin-c6" build
idf.py -p PORT flash monitor

For a module with 16 MB of flash, add ;sdkconfig.flash16mb at the end of the list so the build uses the larger partition table.

sdkconfig.c6 and sdkconfig.sendspin-c6 record why each setting has the value it has, from measurements on a board: the ring size, the DMA queue and WiFi's code kept in flash. The example's README covers running it on a C6.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• ESP32-C6 platform — decode timing and memory, with and without WiFi
  • ESP-IDF component README

docs.title: An ESP32-P4 sink
docs.text:
hearth_sink runs on the ESP32-P4 as the best of the sink family: the part with the room to decode E-AC-3 7.1.4 with its tools on, and AC-4 to 5.1, in real time. It has one I2S controller whose TDM frame holds 512 bits, which reaches sixteen 32-bit channels into both DACs of the planned pair from one line, and, on a board with a panel, it draws the words of a karaoke song as they are sung.

Status as of 2026-10-20: the v1.x board plays; the v3.x kit shows the screen, takes a tap, plays through 16 TDM slots, plays a karaoke song with its words and decodes AC-4 5.1; the clocks on the pins are not measured, and the glass costs the heaviest stream a tenth

The sink runs on a DFRobot FireBeetle 2 (chip revision v1.3), stereo, over Wi-Fi hosted on its onboard ESP32-C6. The v3.x kit arrived on 2026-10-20 and the v3.x image ran on it the same day: it boots on a v3.2 chip at 400 MHz, joins Wi-Fi, is found by Music Assistant, draws the idle and the lyric screens on the panel, answers a tap on every button of the controls sheet, and plays a 5.1 stream through the full sixteen 32-bit TDM slots in real time with no underrun. A karaoke song with word-timed lyrics then played for 99 s with no underrun or late chunk, the words following it on the glass, and the owner, who watched and used the Adjust sheet, said it appeared and looked fine. The glass takes decode time: its scan-out costs the decoder 1.3% (AC-3), 6% (E-AC-3) and about 10% (AC-4 5.1), and with the song filling the screen the light streams' decode time moves by 5 to 12% (under 1% of a frame). The glitches the first measurement put on the glass are not its: about one play in five reaches the kit with its first chunk 300 to 600 ms late, with the glass, without it and at 40 Hz, over Wi-Fi and (more often) over wired, and those plays lose the start of their first second: lwIP's six-entry TCP receive mailbox refused the first segments; PR #1610 makes it 32, and none of 40 plays had a late first chunk (the trace). Not checked on the kit: the TDM clocks on the pins (it needs a scope) and tearing beyond the owner's look. The board suite is played on it, with a baseline. Its RJ45 port works beside the Wi-Fi (wired): the sink answers on it, plays Sendspin through it, takes an update over it, falls back to Wi-Fi when the Ethernet cable is pulled and returns to wired when it is put back, so the kit can run on a PoE splitter; the splitter itself is not yet tried. planning/karaoke-p4x-panel.md has the plan, the first run and the list of what it runs next.

Pairing, groups and firmware updates work the same as on the S3; see An ESP32-S3 sink and Sink firmware. This page covers what differs on the P4.

docs.title: Two chips, two images
docs.text:
The P4 has had two silicon generations, and their firmware images are not interchangeable (Espressif's v3.x user guide, section 1.1): an image for one refuses to start on the other. A release carries one for each.

Chip revision v1.x Chip revision v3.x ("P4X", v3.1 and newer) Image hearth-sink-esp32p4-rev1 hearth-sink-esp32p4-rev3 Example board DFRobot FireBeetle 2 (v1.3) ESP32-P4X-Function-EV-Board, 7-inch panel CPU 360 MHz (400 MHz asserts in its boot) 400 MHz I2S clock source APLL, 125 MHz at most: no TDM above two channels the 160 MHz PLL: TDM at the full 16 × 32 bits Screen none the 7-inch 1024 by 600 panel, with touch Verified on a board on a board (a v3.2 kit, 2026-10-20): screen, touch, 16-slot TDM in real time, a karaoke play with lyrics, AC-4 5.1 (scratch build); the clocks on the TDM pins not yet measured

GET /hardware tells which a board is, and ota.py chooses the image from it, so a board updated over its network gets the right one (Sink firmware).

docs.title: Build and flash
docs.text:
From firmware/hearth-sink, in an ESP-IDF v6.1 terminal. A P4 is not built with set-target and plain defaults: say the target and the overlays.

Chip revision v1.x (the FireBeetle 2, stereo, no screen):

idf.py -DIDF_TARGET=esp32p4 "-DSDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS=sdkconfig.defaults;sdkconfig.hw;sdkconfig.p4;sdkconfig.sendspin;sdkconfig.ac4" build
idf.py -p PORT flash monitor

Chip revision v3.x with the 7-inch panel (the image CI publishes as hearth-sink-esp32p4-rev3):

idf.py -DIDF_TARGET=esp32p4 "-DSDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS=sdkconfig.defaults;sdkconfig.hw;sdkconfig.p4;sdkconfig.p4-rev3;sdkconfig.sendspin;sdkconfig.ac4;sdkconfig.panel;sdkconfig.panel-dsi" build

A board with no panel, to see the screen (any P4; the picture is read back over HTTP, below):

idf.py -DIDF_TARGET=esp32p4 "-DSDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS=sdkconfig.defaults;sdkconfig.hw;sdkconfig.p4;sdkconfig.sendspin;sdkconfig.panel;sdkconfig.panel-null" build
File What it sets sdkconfig.p4 The P4 itself: the wide I2S sink, PSRAM, the code run from PSRAM, the Wi-Fi buffers and the DMA queue, with the reasons for each. Written for v1.x silicon sdkconfig.p4-rev3 After sdkconfig.p4: chip revisions v3.1 to v3.99, 400 MHz, and the bootloader at the Warn log level (a v3.x bootloader is 25,152 bytes at Info against the 24,576-byte window; 22,448 at Warn) sdkconfig.panel LVGL's heap in PSRAM, TrueType fonts, right-to-left text sdkconfig.panel-null / sdkconfig.panel-dsi The frame buffer with no panel, or the 7-inch MIPI DSI panel

AC-4 is sdkconfig.ac4, in both release profiles: since the fold of p4-rev1-ac4 into p4-rev1 and, on 2026-10-29, into p4-rev3, an image of either revision decodes AC-3, E-AC-3 and AC-4. The v3.x image keeps the decode task's stack of an HTTP play in PSRAM (sdkconfig.p4-rev3): the screen leaves it 74 KB of internal RAM at the start of a play, and an AC-4 5.1 play leaves 8 to 10 KB of it at its tightest (planning/ac4-in-release-images.md; ESP32-P4 platform page).

docs.title: On the v1.x board
docs.text: It plays AC-3 and E-AC-3 onto 2.0 in a paired Sendspin session, and decodes AC-4 to 5.1 in real time (ESP32-P4). TDM does not open above two channels on this silicon: the controller has no PLL clock source before v3, and the audio PLL it falls back to tops out at 125 MHz, short of the ~147 MHz a 512-bit frame needs at 48 kHz. That is a limit of the chip, and GET /hardware says so on such a board.

docs.title: Karaoke on the v1.x board
docs.text:
The board reproduces AC-3 and E-AC-3 karaoke itself at its 2.0 layout, which is the only one it can open. Hearth's live karaoke cases at ICLFORGE_HEARTH_LIVE_KARAOKE_LAYOUT=2.0, on a v1.3 board booted from its first slot on 2026-10-13, found the board's output levels within 0.2 dB of the host's decode for AC-3 and within 0.7 dB for E-AC-3, for as coded, aware, and capable with a vocal, with none, and with the melody and a vocal moved, with the layout, routing, trim, delay and crossover settings pushed as well. At 2.0 the aware reproduction is the Lo/Ro fold as coded already is, so the two read alike. The 3.0 layout the case uses by default needs three slots and cannot open here; it is not measured on a v3.x chip.

One earlier run on the same image, started from the board's second slot straight after an update restart, played nothing and logged burst player: a stream control message did not fit the ring (the player's ring was not draining). It did not repeat in eight runs after a clean start from the first slot, and its cause is not known.

docs.title: On the v3.x kit
docs.text:
Run on a v3.2 chip and a panel; the pins' clocks are not measured

What follows was built from ESP-IDF's headers, the v3.x user guide and the vendor drivers' own values, and the first run on the kit (2026-10-20) corrected it in four places: a crash in the DSI code, the touch controller's address (0x14), its axes (turned half a turn from the display's) and how often it must be read, all fixed. A line below that says what the kit did was seen on it; one that says what the chip should do was not.

docs.title: What changes for the audio
docs.text:
• 400 MHz, and PSRAM at 200 MHz by ESP-IDF's default for this chip. The decoders do not scale with the clock: on the kit, with no panel, the decoder alone takes 10% less time than on the v1.3 board for AC-3 and 17% less for AC-4 (11% more clock), and a Sendspin burst at the same layout (2.0) takes 3 to 6% less. A burst used to cost about 176 µs for each output of the layout (the renderer, the patch, the trims, the meters and the playout's copy) whether or not the stream filled it, and the kit's player starts at 9.1.6, sixteen outputs, where the v1.3 board's sink has two: the kit's first Sendspin figures were 13% to 100% above the v1.3 board's for that reason. The player now does that work for the outputs that carry audio only, and hands the DAC zeros for the rest: an AC-3 2.0 stream takes 2.4 ms a burst at 2.0, 5.1 and 9.1.6 alike (2.6, 3.3 and 5.2 ms before), and an AC-4 5.1 stream 29.9 ms at 9.1.6 (33.4 before). The kit's figures are in Memory and time.
  • TDM opens: the i2s_wide sink takes the 160 MHz PLL (I2S_CLK_SRC_PLL_160M) as the clock source on this silicon, which the 16 × 32-bit frame needs (a 147 MHz source at least). The source is chosen when the image is built, because the two revisions are two images. On the kit, a 5.1 stream rendered onto the layout 9.1.6 opened sixteen 32-bit slots and played for 30 s in real time with no underrun, 30,336 ms of audio in 30,185 ms of wall clock, the six coded channels in their slots and the other ten at zero. Whether the clocks leave the pins at 24.576 MHz (BCLK) and 48 kHz (WS) is not measured: it needs a scope or a logic analyser.
  • The DACs are not wired and no firmware programs an ES9080 over I2C: the board plays to a frame whose unused slots are zero, which is what the ES9080 contract is (sink tiers).

docs.title: The screen
docs.text:
The board shows the lyrics of the item playing, against the sound the board is playing: the server sends the document and where in it the sound is, and the board follows on its own clock, which knows its own output delay. The same lyric file and the same karaoke stream Hearth plays on a desktop (Karaoke).

One colour for a word sung, one fill for the word being sung, and one for a word not yet sung, as on the desktop, with one cue that is not colour (the underline), so that no one has to tell the colours apart. The picture above and the others on this page are drawn by the firmware's own screen code (firmware/hearth-sink/main/panel/lvgl/lyric_screen.cpp) and rendered by a tool on a computer (below).

Screen When Nothing is playing. The board's name, its address and network, and what it waits for; the pairing code while an attempt shows one The song is held and has not started. The first lines, so a singer sees what is coming A duet. The first singer's lines at the left, the second's indented, each tagged with its name from the file An instrumental break of four seconds or more: four dots that go out one a second, so the line's start is seen coming A file with line times only. The whole line, emphasised; no word is invented Hebrew or Yiddish. Right-aligned, the words flow right to left and the fill runs from a word's right edge Cyrillic or Greek. Drawn as Latin is, in Noto Sans behind Archivo, with the same fill A script the fonts cannot draw (Arabic here). One sentence in the line's place; the title in it is left out; a music note is dropped A file with no times. The text, scrolled by touch, not followed Playing, and no lyrics are held (below). The speakers of the layout in force, each glowing with its own level Playing, no lyrics, and the server has said what is playing (the title card, below). The title, the artist, the album and year, and the song's time with a progress line Playing, no lyrics, and the clock chosen (below). The time, the date and the line over them; nothing until a time server has answered The same with that screen turned off. The sentence this screen had before Adjust. The lyric delay in 50 ms steps and the text size, and nothing else; put away after eight seconds untouched Preferences. What is chosen once and left, grouped and scrollable (below): the screen for a song with no lyrics and when it dims; a choice the board cannot make is greyed, with the reason

Controls. Touch changes only what the board owns: its lyric delay (±1,000 ms) and its text size (Smaller, Normal or Larger, which the sheet says beside its buttons) in Adjust, and what it shows while a song has no lyrics, when that dims and the rest of what is chosen once in Preferences (below). Which vocals sound and the reproduction are the server's settings and are shown, not changed, until the role has a way to carry a request back.

docs.title: Adjust and Preferences
docs.text:
The footer has two buttons, Preferences and Adjust (Adjust is where it always was, at the right). One is for what a person does while a song is on, the other for what they choose once and leave.

Adjust keeps the two tweaks of the lyric screen: the lyric delay (50 ms steps, up to 1,000 ms either way) and the text size (Smaller, Normal or Larger). It is 250 px tall on the kit's panel (it was 352 when it also held the screen for a song with no lyrics and its dim time) and puts itself away after eight seconds untouched.

Preferences is a full-screen, scrollable list of everything that is chosen once and left, grouped Display, Sound, Network, Time, Updates and System (a group with nothing in it is not drawn), with Close at the top right. It keeps the screen lit while it is open, puts itself away after a minute untouched, and is built when it opens and deleted when it closes, so the lyric screen is as it was with it shut. It holds what the screen shows while a song has no lyrics and when it dims (the two settings that were in Adjust), the screen's brightness, how the clock view writes the time, the night schedule and the time zone, then the Sound group (the test tone through each speaker, and the level and distance of each speaker on the Speakers sheet), then the Network and System groups: wired or Wi-Fi, the player's name, About, the paired servers, Restart, Reset preferences and Factory reset (On the screen). The technical settings (slot width, the second I2S line, the time server) stay in the developer view and the routes.

The brightness is a stepper (every tenth from 10% to 100%), the clock's hours and seconds are a choice and a switch, and the night schedule is a switch, a button that opens an editor for its two times, and a switch for whether it darkens the idle screen too. A value that is chosen in a list or a pair of times is a button that opens an editor over the sheet, with a Done of its own:

Each time steps a quarter of an hour round the clock (22:00 up is 22:15, and 00:00 down is 23:45); a button held keeps stepping, ten times a second, and after eight steps moves an hour at a time. The pair is written half a second after the last step, so that a held button is one write and not forty. The editor says what the two mean (Dark from 22:00 until 07:00, through midnight, by the board's own time. A touch lights the screen for 30 seconds.), that the schedule is switched off when it is, and, for the same time twice, that the screen is never dark.

The time zone is the same picker as the web page's: the regions of the zone table (Africa to Pacific, and No zone (UTC) above them), then the places in one, opening at the region of the zone already chosen with that place in view, so a person who wants the city next to the board's own does not scroll for it. A tap on a place chooses it at once; the editor says Now: Melbourne (Australia), and Regions (a chevron on a narrow bar) goes back up.

One product base, many boards. What a board can do is data, not an #ifdef and not "is this the P4X". iclforge::BoardCaps (libs/device/include/iclforge/board_caps.hpp) describes it: the display (how it is attached, its size, whether it has touch and a backlight), the sink (the bits in a TDM frame, whether a second line is possible, whether the chip can open a TDM frame at all, and the slot width and second line in force), the networks, whether the board keeps the time, the object cap, and the chip's own facts (HardwareFacts, which GET /hardware reports). The firmware fills it from the build and the hardware (main/board_caps.cpp), and board_variants.hpp has every board the product knows and a few it does not (an ESP32-S3 with a 320 by 240 SPI panel, an ESP32-C3 with a panel that has no touch) for the host tests to walk.

The preference registry (libs/device/include/iclforge/preferences.hpp) is the list the screen, GET /preferences and the web page all draw from. An entry has an id, a group, a label, a kind (choice, stepper, toggle, text, action, info, list or sheet: a row that says what is set and opens an editor of its own), whether a change applies live, at the next play or after a restart, the route that sets the same value, its choices, what Reset preferences does with it (on_reset: put back to its default word, or keep; an entry that says neither fails a host test), and availability(caps), once for the entry and once for each choice: whether this board can do it and, if not, why. The values are read and set through a typed Backend that the firmware implements once over the settings_* functions (main/preferences.cpp), so the screen, the routes and the host tests go through the same code.

A preference the board cannot support is shown, greyed, with the reason, and never hidden. On a board whose screen has no touch, the Dark view (which a touch lights) and the dim time (which a touch wakes) are greyed, and the sheet says why:

A tap on a greyed control does nothing, and prefs::set_value() refuses it before the board is asked. The host tests (libs/device/tests/test_preferences.cpp) check every entry against every known board: a reason wherever something is greyed, and a default that is never a choice the board cannot make.

Preference Id Route Available when Screen without lyrics: speakers, title, clock, meters, dark, off now-view /now-playing the board has a screen; clock needs a clock, meters a screen of at least 240 x 240 and the Sendspin player, dark needs touch Dim after: 1, 5, 15, 30 minutes, 1, 2, 4 hours, never dim-after /dim-after the board has a screen with touch Speakers style: glow, pulse speakers-style /speakers-style the board has a screen (it is greyed, with the reason, while the screen is set to the clock or off, which draw no speakers) Brightness: 10% to 100% in tens brightness /brightness the board has a screen whose backlight it controls Clock hours: 24 or 12 clock-hours /clock-format the board has a screen and keeps the time Clock seconds: on or off clock-seconds /clock-format the board has a screen and keeps the time Night schedule: on or off night-schedule /night-schedule a screen with touch, and a clock Night from and to: a pair of times (editor) night-times /night-schedule the same Night covers idle screen: on or off night-idle /night-idle the same Time zone: a place by region (editor) time-zone /timezone the board keeps the time Wired or Wi-Fi: automatic, wired, Wi-Fi network-preference /network-preference the board has both a wired network and Wi-Fi Name of this player name /name always About about /hardware always Paired servers paired-servers /pairing the board runs the Sendspin player Restart restart /restart not while an update is under way, nor while the new image is on trial Reset preferences reset-preferences /reset-preferences not while an update is under way Factory reset factory-reset /factory-reset as Restart Identify speakers: a button, Identify, that opens the Speakers sheet and plays the tone through every speaker in turn identify-speakers /identify the build has a Sendspin player; a song playing says so under the row Speaker levels and distances: a sheet (kind sheet), the same Speakers sheet, with the room, a level and a distance for each speaker speaker-trim /trim the build has a Sendspin player; the distance needs delay lines (PSRAM) Late night: standard or late night; from the next stream, and put back by Reset preferences (Late night) late-night /dynamic-range the build has a Sendspin player: it decodes the Dolby streams

GET /preferences lists every entry as this board sees it, on every board (one with no screen lists the Display entries greyed with This board has no screen.): its id, group, label, kind, how a change applies, the route, the value, whether it is available and why not, and each choice the same way. It is read-only; a change goes through the entry's own route.

{"profile":"p4-rev3","display":"dsi","preferences":[{"id":"now-view","group":"Display","label":"Screen without lyrics","kind":"choice","apply":"live","route":"/now-playing","value":"speakers","available":true,"reason":"","choices":[{"id":"speakers","label":"Speakers","available":true,"reason":""}]}]}

Any size of screen. The sizes are the display's, not 1024 by 600's. libs/device/include/iclforge/screen_metrics.hpp derives the margins, the gaps, the type and the height of a button from the display's shorter side (host tested for every size), and the footer and both sheets are laid out from them, so the kit's own sizes are as they were:

Display Margin Type Button (Adjust / list) Adjust sheet 1024 by 600 32 24 72 / 64 250 px 800 by 480 24 22 64 / 56 222 px 480 by 320 16 18 56 / 52 194 px 320 by 240 10 16 48 / 48 170 px

The fingertip. A control that is touched is at least 48 px on both sides, with at least 6 px to the next one: 48 px is 7.2 mm on the kit's 7-inch 1024 by 600 panel (about 6.7 px a millimetre) and 7.4 mm on a 2.4-inch 320 by 240 module, over the 7 mm that Apple and Google give as the least a finger hits reliably (44 pt, 48 dp). The preview tool (below) draws Adjust and Preferences at the four sizes above and fails the run if text is cut off, a control sticks out of what holds it or off the screen, a touch target is under 48 px or closer than 6 px to another, a tap does not do what it says, a greyed choice answers a tap, or a list longer than the glass does not scroll. A display backend for a chip other than the P4 is not written (no such panel is on the bench): panel/lvgl/display.hpp is the seam one would fill, and everything above it takes its size from the display.

Adding a preference is a registry entry (id, group, label, choices and their availability rules), a getter and a setter in Backend (a pure virtual, so a firmware that forgot the setter does not build), the same pair in the host tests' fake, and the firmware's implementation; only a control that is not one of the five kinds needs an editor, and it names one (Pref::editor: a pair of times, a place in a list) which panel/lvgl/prefs_editors.cpp draws. There are no bespoke buttons in lyric_screen.cpp.

A tap's setter runs on the panel's own task, which holds the panel's lock (a std::mutex, not recursive) for the frame that reads the tap, so no panel_set_* may take that lock or touch the glass: a tap on Brightness - or + once hung the screen for good (the first run on the kit, 2026-10-26) because the brightness setter did both. What the screen follows is iclforge::panelfollow::PanelFollow (libs/device/include/iclforge/panel_follow.hpp): atomics only, the brightness only marks the backlight stale, and the panel's loop gives the glass the level in its next cycle (within a tenth of a second). test_panel_follow.cpp holds a lock across every setter, and reads panel.cpp to fail if a panel_set_* mentions a lock, a wait or the glass.

docs.title: A song with no lyrics
docs.text:
Most of what is played has none. While a stream plays and the board holds no lyrics, the panel shows the speakers: the room the layout in force describes, seen from above with the front at the top. Ear-level speakers are circles, height speakers rounded squares, the LFE a wide box along the bottom, and each speaker glows with its own level, from the board's own measure of the last 100 ms. A speaker with nothing on it is a hollow outline, so a dead output can be seen. The line above says what arrives and what it is played on (Dolby Digital Plus 5.1 to 7.1.4, PCM to 2.0).

It is meant to be left on for hours in a dim room: the glow moves in a few steps, and is never brighter than the accent at 55%. After five minutes with nothing touched (the time is a Preference, or PUT /dim-after: never, or whole minutes from 1 to 240) the backlight goes to 4% and a black screen with one line is over everything; any tap brings the speakers back, and the tap does not also press what is under it. Only this screen dims: the lyric screens and the idle screen do not.

How the speakers follow the sound (the plan is planning/p4x-speakers-options.md). The screen reads the level of every 100 ms window the player measures (a lock and two short arrays, BurstPlayer::levels(); the heading and the title are still read five times a second), where it once read every other one. A level is judged against the loudest the room has lately been (it rises at once and falls 2 dB a second, and is never lower than -48 dB of full scale), so that the same music shows the same at any volume: the player's volume is applied before the meter, and against full scale the glow would shrink with the knob. The core of a speaker is six steps over 30 dB (6 dB a step) and the halo, from the peak, two. The level rises at once and falls at 60 dB a second, so a hit is a step down in the window after the next, and a step changes only when the level is 0.4 of a step past its edge (0.7 for the halo), so that a level on a boundary does not flicker. A speaker with nothing on it is still a hollow outline. These are the constants of libs/render/include/iclforge/render/room_plan.hpp, chosen over a synthetic groove in 2.0, 5.1 and 7.1.4 (firmware/hearth-sink/preview/speakers_options/tune.cpp): 72% of the onsets of 5 dB or more showed as a step up in the same window (the 5 Hz glow before it: 3 to 26%), 3 to 5% of steady windows moved a step, and the view flushed 18 000 pixels a second at 2.0, 56 000 at 5.1, 82 000 at 7.1.4 and 101 000 at 9.1.6 (the lyric screen's song filling: 192 000). The pixels are what the view costs; what they cost a stream on the kit (the first design, at about 45 000 a second at 5.1, cost a burst 0.4%, below) is still to be measured for these constants.

The speakers' style. glow (the default) is the above. pulse makes the filled circle of each speaker grow and shrink with its level, a little: eight sizes between 88% and 112% of the plan's, moved by at most three in a window, held until the level is a quarter size past an edge, and a speaker 18 dB or more under the room's loudest (or silent) stays at its smallest and does not move. The halo is not resized, so a size change redraws the circle's rectangle and nothing else. It needs no meter and no seam the glow does not have. It is set in Preferences (Display) or with PUT /speakers-style; the value is kept on the board as np_style (0 glow, 1 pulse; never renumbered).

Both styles stay: the owner, 2026-10-25, saw the glow, as it was and as it became, beside the pulse at plus and minus 12% (the bound is kPulseReach), and kept both as a choice, with the glow the default.

Which screen shows is the owner's: speakers (the default), title, clock (below), dark, or off, which is the old sentence. The plan, with how each was chosen and built, is (planning/p4x-now-playing.md).

The title card. The board lists metadata@v1 in its hello, which a board with a screen does and one without does not, so a server that has the role tells it what is playing: the title, the artist, the album and its year, and where in the song it is. The card is those, and nothing the server did not say: the title in 72 down to 34 px by its length (the lyric line's rule, and the same Smaller and Larger steps), in two rows at most with three dots after them; the artist under it in 36 px, the album and year in 24 px muted; the song's time at the top right and a progress line under the header, as the lyric screens have them, where the server gave a progress and the board's clock has converged.

The Meters view. A choice of the screen without lyrics (meters, stored as np_view 5, never renumbered; Preferences, Display, Screen without lyrics, or PUT /now-playing): an instrument rather than a picture of the room. The top of the screen is a third-octave spectrum of the main mix (31 bands from 20 Hz to 20 kHz, 0 dB a full-scale sine, 60 dB of range) with a dB scale, a peak tick that holds one second and then falls, and the colours of a level meter: green, then amber from -30 dB and red from -15 dB. Under it are the room's channels, drawn the way the size of the screen and the number of outputs ask for (iclforge/meters_view.hpp, representation_for):

Screen width A 2.0 room More than two outputs under 400 px the pair, L and R, with a peak tick each the pair (the stereo downmix of the room) 400 to 799 px the pair one meter for each of L, C, R, LFE, Ls, Rs (the surround sum) 800 px and wider the pair every output, in groups: Front, Surround, Rear, Height, LFE

The bars are green, amber from -18 dB and red from -6 dB, with a peak tick that holds 1.5 s. The spectrum has one bar a band on the wide screen, two bands a bar on the middle one and three (an octave) on the small one. The Meters view needs a screen of at least 240 by 240 and the Sendspin player, because the player is where the sound is: on a board without either, the choice is shown greyed with the reason and PUT /now-playing answers 409. While Meters shows, Speakers style does nothing (the glow and pulse are the speakers' view) and is greyed too.

What it draws comes from the player, not the glass: after the output stage has set its gain, BurstPlayer hands each block of the frames about to be played to a BlockTap (iclforge/block_tap.hpp), one pointer read when nothing is listening. MeterTap (iclforge/meters_tap.hpp) keeps a mono mix of the outputs in a ring of 340 ms and, for each output, the largest sample in each 50 ms; the screen takes the mix, analyses it (iclforge/dsp/spectrum.hpp: a 2048-point transform of the signal at 12 kHz for the 17 bands up to 800 Hz and a 1024-point one at 48 kHz above it, so that a low band is not smeared over a fifth of a second and a high one is not slow), averages the power over 80 ms, and lets the bars fall at 30 dB a second (meters 24). It does this twenty times a second whatever the frame rate. The spectrum, the channel bars and the pair of meters are each one canvas, redrawn only where a bar or a tick moved, in a few rectangles (one for each run of neighbouring bars that move alike), so an update is a handful of invalid areas and not a hundred (a rectangle for each part of each bar, which the kit measured at 80 to 290 ms a refresh). When the screen is dimmed or another view is chosen the tap is removed, so a board that is not showing meters pays nothing for them. Everything the view draws, and the analysis's tables (about 63 KB with the transform's work buffers, in PSRAM), exist only in an image with a panel; the C6 and S3 images have the tap's interface and nothing else. How fast it runs on the kit, and the protocol that measures it, are in (planning/p4x-meters-view.md).

What the Meters view costs, and the rate it holds. GET /panel-stats (port 80, on a board with a screen) says what the panel costs: LVGL's refreshes (the start of one to its end, the flush to the glass included), the panel task's stack never-free minimum, the PSRAM and internal heap now and at their lowest, and, once the view has been opened, the Meters view's own figures since it opened: the rate it holds, how long an update's analysis, widgets and render take (last, mean, largest), the updates that were late or missed, and what the player's tap costs the audio path for a burst of 1,536 frames. The developer view shows the same in its PERFORMANCE section. The view runs at twenty updates a second when the panel's task can keep up and ten when it cannot (iclforge/meters_governor.hpp): over the last 20 updates, an average cost above 70 % of the 50 ms step, or 4 updates started more than 15 ms later than the loop could have started them, drops it to ten; it returns to twenty only after 10 s at ten with the cost under 60 % and nothing late, so that it does not flip; the first two seconds of a view are not judged (its first draw and the cold code are not what it costs). The target is 20 Hz if possible, else a steady 10 Hz (no more than 1 % of the steps without an update, an update under half of its step), and the kit protocol says which room holds which. The audio comes first: while the decoder is busy (a mean burst of 14 ms or more of its 32: a 7.1.4 object stream, AC-4; not a 5.1 E-AC-3 room) the view is held at ten, since the drawing and the analysis beside the decoder cost it 1.5 to 2 ms a burst in those rooms (ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_PANEL_YIELD, default 1; 2 also keeps the panel's task on the decode core, and 0 turns it off). How each room holds up on the kit, and the protocol that measures it, are in (planning/p4x-meters-view.md).

The stream, in the footer. While the speakers or the card show, the footer says what the stream is and who sends it, in the most that fits: Decoded on this board - 768 kb/s - from Music Assistant, then Decoded here - 768 kb/s - from Music Assistant, then the same without the server, then the figure alone. With Preferences and Adjust both in the footer there are 386 px for it on the kit's panel (it was 558 with Adjust alone), which holds Decoded on this board - 768 kb/s and not the server's name: the developer view has that. A coded stream (E-AC-3, AC-3, AC-4) is sent undecoded and decoded on the board, which the wording says; a PCM one was decoded by the server, and the footer says PCM from Music Assistant. The bitrate is what was played: the coded bytes of the chunks played over the time they took, over windows of a second and smoothed, not a figure from a header (it is absent until the first second has played). The server is the name in /status server without the id in brackets (Music Assistant (d5369777-music-assistant) is Music Assistant); the developer view keeps the whole string.

A layout for a server that sends none. A board's layout is the image's (CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_LAYOUT, 2.0 on the kit) until a server's settings replace it for the stream: Hearth sends one, Music Assistant does not, so a 5.1 or 7.1.4 stream to a 2.0 board shows two speakers. PUT /layout now keeps what it is given in NVS, so it survives a restart, and the board starts with it (a stored layout this sink cannot carry is said on the console and the image's stands):

curl -X PUT -d 7.1.4 http://<board address>/layout

The role's own settings message still wins for the stream and is not stored.

Until a title has come, there is no card. With title chosen and nothing said (a server that does not send the role, or has not yet), or with a title in a script the fonts cannot draw, the speakers show in its place, and nothing but a title makes a card. Once a title is known the speakers' own header says it too: Title - Artist at the left, the time at the right and the progress line under it, in place of what arrives and what it is played on (which the dark screen still says).

The card dims as the speakers do, and its dark screen names the song (Playing - Blue in Green - Miles Davis). What the store keeps is small and fixed (a title of 256 bytes, an artist or an album of 160, cut at a character and not in the middle of one), in strings that keep their capacity, so a server's update and the panel's five reads a second allocate nothing from the internal heap an AC-4 decoder leaves little of. Two servers say it differently, and the board reads each as it means it (planning/hearth-sendspin-extension.md, C36): the specification's object is the whole state, so what it leaves out is gone (and aiosendspin 10, which Music Assistant runs now, sends it so); aiosendspin 9.1.1's carried only what changed, a field it cleared given as null, so that a pause (a progress and nothing else) leaves the title alone and a track with no artist does not keep the last one's. A state stamped in the future (a scheduled change, which aiosendspin can send up to 20 s ahead and Music Assistant does not) takes effect when it arrives.

Dark is for a listener who wants no light at all while music plays. With it chosen, the backlight is off from the moment a song with no lyrics begins, however long ago anything last touched the panel, and the screen says nothing. A tap lights the speakers for 30 seconds from the last touch (another tap moves that on), and then it is dark again. The tap that lights it does not also press what is under it; the developer view and Preferences keep the screen lit while they are open (the Adjust sheet puts itself away after eight seconds, inside the 30). Preferences' dim row, which has no meaning here, is greyed and says "Not used by the Dark view: a touch lights it for 30 seconds, then it is dark again." Only this screen goes dark: a lyric screen and the idle screen are lit as they always were.

Route Takes Default GET and PUT /now-playing speakers, title, clock, meters, off or dark speakers GET and PUT /dim-after never, or minutes from 1 to 240 5 GET and PUT /speakers-style glow or pulse glow GET and PUT /brightness a whole number, 10 to 100: the percent the backlight is at while the screen is lit 80 GET and PUT /clock-format 24, 12, 24 seconds or 12 seconds 24 GET and PUT /night-schedule two times and a state: 22:00-07:00 on; PUT also takes just the times (and switches it on), or on, or off 22:00-07:00 off GET and PUT /night-idle on or off off

All six are stored on the board and take effect at once, with no restart; a board with no panel answers 404. The brightness is the lit level, and the dim floor stays under it: the dimmed screen is at 4%, or at the brightness if that is lower, and the dark view is off whatever it is. A screen whose backlight cannot be dimmed (the frame buffer a board with no panel runs) refuses it with a 409. GET :8081/panel says which view is chosen, whether the screen is dimmed (a black cover is up, dimmed or dark) and the backlight in percent: 80 lit (or the brightness set), 4 dimmed, 0 dark; whether Preferences is open (prefs_view), how many times it was built and the longest a build took (prefs_builds, prefs_build_us_max); and the time of day's state.

docs.title: The clock
docs.text:
The time of day, for a room where the sound is the thing and the panel is a glance: the time at 200 px, the date under it, and nothing else, in the muted tone (the time at about 80% of it and the date at about 60%, so that neither is the brightest thing in a dim room). By default it is in 24 hours and shows no seconds, so what the screen redraws is the time's rectangle once a minute (the preview counts 224,000 pixels, against none for a second that passes), and the line over it still says what the stream is (Dolby Digital Plus 5.1 to 5.1).

A person can have 12 hours (9:47, with a small PM beside it; midnight is 12:05 AM) and the seconds (small beside the digits, :12), in any combination: PUT /clock-format takes 24, 12, 24 seconds or 12 seconds. The small text is a label of its own, so a second that passes redraws about 9,600 pixels and not the digits' 300,000, and with the seconds off a second redraws nothing.

The time is the board's own, kept with a time server, which every board does. Until the first answer the view draws the heading and nothing else, never a time it made up (and an answer from before 2026 is a server with a wrong clock, and is not taken for the time either).

With no time zone set the clock says UTC, and says so:

A dim leaves the clock on the glass. Dimming lowers the backlight to its floor, as for the speakers, but the clock is what a dark room has the screen for, so no black cover goes over it: a clear one catches the tap that wakes the screen, and the time goes on changing under it.

docs.title: The night schedule
docs.text:
Go dark between two times, by the board's own time (the time of day, in its zone). It is off until a person switches it on, and then it is 22:00 to 07:00 until they change the times. While it is in force the no-lyrics screen behaves as the dark view does: dark from the moment it begins to show (a song that starts at 23:00 is dark at once; one already playing at 22:00 goes dark once nothing has touched the glass for 30 seconds), a tap lights it for 30 seconds from the last touch, and the tap that lights it does not also press what is under it. A window that ends before it starts crosses midnight; the same time twice is an empty window (never dark: a whole day is the Dark view's job); a board that has not heard the time yet is lit, never dark by accident; and a zone with daylight saving moves the window with the clock (the night the clocks go forward is eight real hours of dark, the night they go back ten). With the Dark view chosen, or the screen without lyrics Off, the rows say the schedule is not used (The Dark view is dark already: a touch lights it for 30 seconds, as at night.).

The idle screen is a switch of its own (night-idle, Night covers idle screen), off. Whether the night should darken the screen between two songs as well is the owner's to say; with it on, the idle screen counts as showing while the night is in force and is dark from the moment the night begins, with the same touch. It is not used while the schedule is off, and the row says so.

Kept as one number. NVS night holds the two times and both switches (from in bits 0 to 10, to in bits 11 to 21, bit 22 on, bit 23 the idle screen), so a power cut cannot leave half a schedule; a number no build wrote is dropped with a line on the console and the Kconfig default (ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_NIGHT_SCHEDULE, 22:00-07:00 off, and ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_NIGHT_IDLE) stands. Reset preferences returns it; the time zone it is read in stays. The panel is handed the schedule and the board's local minute of the day (read only while the schedule is on, and nothing until the clock has converged) and lyric_screen.cpp passes both to dim_state(): that is the whole of what the screen does for it. The rule, its words and its changeover cases are host-tested (test_now_view.cpp), and the preview tool drives it on the screen: lit at noon, dark at 23:00, a touch lights it for 30 s, lit at 07:00 and with no time known, and the idle screen dark only when told.

On the kit, the title card (2026-10-21): hearth-testserver said a song over Sendspin (--title, --artist, --album, --year, --track-seconds, and --then-after for a second song with no artist) and the panel's read-back was the card above, then the second song alone with nothing kept from the first, and the speakers again when the play ended; a play that said nothing, with the card chosen, showed the speakers; a 119-character title ended in three dots after two rows, and 0:08 / 24:45 fitted. A 5.1 E-AC-3 programme at layout 5.1 took 5,325 µs a burst with the view off, 5,341 with the speakers (their header the song) and 5,333 with the card (three plays each, none late, no underrun or resynchronisation); at 2.0 with a stereo programme 2,614, 2,628 and 2,633; at 7.1.4 6,475, 6,478 and 6,491. The role itself cost nothing that showed: the image without it took 5,364 µs for the same play. The panel redraws about 5.7 times a second for the song's time and line. The owner's Music Assistant had not reconnected to the kit by then, so what it sends this role is from aiosendspin's source (the whole state each time, as the specification has it) and not yet seen on the board.

On the kit, the speakers (2026-10-21): over Sendspin, a 5.1 E-AC-3 test programme with no lyrics drew exactly this picture; with the speakers showing, a burst took 4,573 µs against 4,555 µs with the view off (three 60 s plays each, no late burst, underrun or resynchronisation, and the same least free heap), and at 2.0 with a stereo music programme 2,099 against 2,114 µs. With dim-after at one minute the screen went dark 60.4 s after the speakers began to show, and a tap woke it. The glass's brightness at 4% and a finger's tap in place of an injected one were not looked at; the scan-out is the same whatever is drawn, and dimming leaves it alone. The dark view, run the same way (the same programme for 190 s, injected taps, the read-back sampled twice a second): dark as soon as the song showed, on a panel nobody had touched; a tap on Adjust lit it within 0.8 s and did not open the sheet; dark again 30.1 s after that tap; two taps 20 s apart kept it lit and it was dark 30.2 s after the second. A real finger, and the glass with its backlight off, were not looked at.
