docs.title: An ESP32-S3 sink
docs.text:
hearth_sink turns an ESP32-S3 board into a network audio player. It uses Sendspin to receive synchronised audio from a compatible server. The board can play stereo PCM, or decode AC-3 and E-AC-3 (including Atmos objects) for its configured speakers.

This guide covers building, flashing, network setup, pairing, and group playback. The example README and the ESP-IDF component overview contain implementation details and measurements. For the stereo ESP32-C6 player, see An ESP32-C6 sink.

Status as of 2026-10-13: Hearth plays to sinks; a board built with the AC-4 decoder takes AC-4 in a group

The desktop app discovers sinks, pairs, plays to groups and updates firmware over the network (Hearth index). These boards play AC-3 and E-AC-3 in a group, and the release image lists ac3 and eac3, not ac4, as the streams its Sendspin role takes. Built with CONFIG_ICLFORGE_AC4 and the 64 KB data cache an ESP32-S3 lists ac4 too, at 2 channels and 25 frames a second, and decodes 2.0 AC-4 from a group in real time (ESP32-S3); an ESP32-C6 does not fit it beside Wi-Fi and refuses the play; an ESP32-P4 decodes it to 5.1 in real time (ESP32-P4). For development without Hearth, hearth-testserver still plays E-AC-3 to boards (Play AC-3 and E-AC-3).

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• An ESP32-S3 board with 8 MB of octal PSRAM. The ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1-N16R8 is the board this was built on and measured with. Wi-Fi and the E-AC-3 decoder do not fit the part's internal RAM together, so the network build needs PSRAM (Memory). A board with quad PSRAM needs CONFIG_SPIRAM_MODE_QUAD in place of sdkconfig.psram's octal mode; no such board has run it.
  • A USB cable to the S3's own USB connector (the one marked USB on a DevKitC-1). It carries the flashing, the console and the network setup.
  • ESP-IDF v6.1, installed as Espressif's guide describes, and a checkout of this repository.
  • A 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network that passes mDNS between the board and the server. The S3 has no 5 GHz radio.
  • For sound, a DAC on the I2S pins (Wiring). A board with nothing wired still plays and reports its levels.

docs.title: Build and flash
docs.text:
Without building: a release publishes this board's image, hearth-sink-esp32s3, and the browser installer writes it over the USB cable, then gives the board its network. Sink firmware covers the same with esptool, and updating the board over its network afterwards. Then continue at The page.

To build it yourself, in an ESP-IDF v6.1 terminal, from firmware/hearth-sink:

export SDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS="sdkconfig.defaults;sdkconfig.hw;sdkconfig.psram;sdkconfig.psram-4k;sdkconfig.sendspin;sdkconfig.ac4;sdkconfig.s3-fast;sdkconfig.s3-dcache"
idf.py set-target esp32s3
idf.py build
idf.py -p PORT flash monitor

In PowerShell, set the first line as $env:SDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS = "...". PORT is the board's serial port, such as COM5 or /dev/ttyACM0. The files over the defaults do this:

File What it sets sdkconfig.hw The console on the S3's own USB connector, so one cable does everything sdkconfig.psram Octal PSRAM for the decoder's large allocations and the player's ring, a deeper I2S queue, and a 32 KB instruction cache sdkconfig.sendspin The Sendspin player on Wi-Fi, the page and the REST routes on port 80, nothing played at boot, and lwIP's task on core 0 beside the network sdkconfig.psram-4k PSRAM tried first for every allocation of 4 KB and more, so that an E-AC-3 stream leaves the board 44 KB of internal RAM at its least where 16 KB left it a few hundred bytes sdkconfig.ac4 The AC-4 decoder, both decode stacks at 40,960 bytes (in PSRAM on this part), a frame's per-channel stages on both cores sdkconfig.s3-fast The flash read four bits a clock (QIO), 64-byte lines in the data cache, and the firmware's code and constants run from PSRAM sdkconfig.s3-dcache A 64 KB data cache, which is 32 KB of the heap

The QIO mode is the second stage bootloader's, so a board takes it with one USB flash that includes its bootloader (idf.py flash does); a network update leaves the mode the board has, and a bootloader that cannot set the flash chip's quad-enable bit stays in DIO.

Since 2026-10-29 the published image has all of them: one image decodes AC-3, E-AC-3 and AC-4. The 64 KB data cache costs 32 KB of the heap (the board boots with 75 KB of internal RAM free in place of 110) and the allocation limit stays at 4 KB, so an E-AC-3 stream leaves 44 KB and an E-AC-3 JOC 7.1.4, 9.1.6 or 5.1.4 play 60 KB at the end of its lap; an AC-4 play takes 512 for itself. With all of them the part decodes 2.0 in real time (SIMPLE mode at 0.40 of a frame's duration, A-SPX at 0.50, with the decoder's second core), the frame-rate converter at every rate (0.67 to 0.87) and E-AC-3 7.1.4 (0.75), and 5.1 in SIMPLE mode at 0.99; the rest of 5.1 takes 1.25 to 1.44 and 5.1.4 2.28 to 2.69. The ESP32-S3 page has what each file bought.

idf.py set-target writes a fresh sdkconfig from those files. After that, idf.py menuconfig changes one build: the pins, the slot width and the layout are under iclforge hearth sink, and the player's buffers under Sendspin player. If you build more than one shape, give each its own -B <build directory> and -DSDKCONFIG=<build directory>/sdkconfig, or the second inherits the first's settings.

After flashing over the S3's own USB connector, the chip can stay in its download mode, with boot:0x0 (DOWNLOAD) on the console. Press RESET. The port disappears and comes back at every reset, so idf.py monitor --no-reset is the way back to the console after one.

idf.py flash leaves the NVS partition alone, so a board keeps its network, its name, its keys and its pairings when you flash a new build. idf.py -p PORT erase-flash clears all of them.

docs.title: Join a network
docs.text:
A board that has no network to join listens for Improv Wi-Fi on its console port. A freshly flashed board has none, since a build names a network only if you set one under iclforge hearth sink in idf.py menuconfig (for boards flashed from one image), so it listens at once:

  1. Close the serial monitor (Ctrl+]), so the port is free.
  2. Open improv-wifi.com in a browser with Web Serial (Chrome or Edge on a computer) and connect to the board's serial port.
  3. The board says it is a Hearth sink and gives its name. It does not scan for networks, so type the network's name, then its passphrase.
  4. The board stores both and joins, then advertises itself and starts its player. Improv offers a link to the board's page, http://<address>/. If the join fails, Improv says the board could not connect, and you can send the network again. A network that accepts the board but gives it no address within 30 s counts as a failed join.

A board is called hearth- followed by the last six hex digits of its MAC address until you name it. It advertises _sendspin._tcp over mDNS under its name, which is how a server finds it, and answers as <name>.local.

To move a board to another network, use the page's Wi-Fi network field, or PUT /network with the SSID and passphrase on two lines. The board joins that network at its next restart. A board that cannot join its stored network when it starts listens for Improv again, so give it the new network the same way.

docs.title: The page
docs.text:
http://<name>.local/, or the board's address, shows:

  • Sendspin: the server connected to the board, its clock, the stream's timing, underruns, a meter for each output over the last 100 ms, and how many servers are paired. While a pairing runs, its six-digit code is shown at the top. A board keeps a pairing for each server it has paired with, and one server plays to it at a time.
  • Now: the board's own player, which plays a location sent to POST /play: its state, and the stream's path from source through decode to the output.
  • Settings: the wiring, the slot width and the output layout under Speakers; the network the board is on, its name and the network to join under Network; and under Time the time the board keeps, whether it asks a time server (on by default), its time zone and the server to ask (the time of day). A choice is sent as it is made; a name, a layout typed in full, a network, a zone or a server is sent with its button.
  • Levels and distances: a level and a distance for each speaker of the layout, and a test tone out of each (Speaker levels, distances and the test tone).
  • Real time, Hardware and Counters: how long each frame takes, what the board is - chip, memory, the sink's ceiling and the firmware - and the player's counters.

The same routes answer without the page (GET /api lists them): GET /status for a script, and PUT /name, /layout, /slot-width, /wiring and /network to change what the board is, and GET and PUT /trim and POST /identify for the speakers' levels and the test tone. A new name is advertised at once (Name, restart and reset). The page and the routes have no password (Security).

docs.title: Name, restart and reset
docs.text:
The name. A board is called hearth- and the last six hex digits of its MAC address until you name it, with the page's Name field or PUT /name. A name is 1 to 32 bytes of text (a letter with an accent is two) with no control character in it and no space at either end; the board answers 409 to anything else, and keeps the name it had. A rename takes effect at once, with no restart:

What What a rename does mDNS The host name (<name>.local: lower case, a hyphen between words, a Latin letter with an accent as the letter it is spelt with, so "Café" is cafe), the instance name and the _sendspin._tcp record all change. The servers The name in the player's hello changes. An idle board tells its servers to dial again and they list it under the new name; a board that is playing waits until the stream has ended, so that a rename never cuts the music. The page, the screen's footer, Improv Their next draw or request reads it. The pairings Nothing. A pairing is the server's key and the board's own key, not the name, so every server stays paired. The router's list of clients The name the board gave DHCP changes at its next boot; an address already leased keeps the old name until then.

A name that a person gave the player on the server (Music Assistant keeps its own) is not changed.

Restart. POST /restart restarts the board into the image that runs now, after telling its servers it is going. It is refused (409) while an update is under way, and while the running image is still on trial, when a restart would go back to the image before it. On the ESP32-P4 it resets the whole system, which a Wi-Fi link behind the companion chip needs (An ESP32-P4 sink).

Reset preferences. POST /reset-preferences puts the choices a person made once back to their defaults, at once and with no restart: every entry of the board's preferences that says it is reset (what the screen shows without lyrics, when it dims, the brightness, the clock's hours and seconds and the night schedule; an entry added later says for itself), each through its own setter, so the screen and the clock follow as they follow a change. It keeps the name, the Wi-Fi network and the choice between wired and Wi-Fi, the DAC wiring, the speaker layout and the time zone (the room's, not a matter of taste), the time server and whether the board asks it, and the pairings. On a board with a screen the same thing is Reset preferences on the sheet (An ESP32-P4 sink).

Factory reset. POST /factory-reset with the body erase everything erases the paired servers (the board gets a new identity, so each server has to pair with it again, and has to remove it from its list first), then every setting (the name, the network and its passphrase, the wiring, the layout and the preferences), then the Wi-Fi driver's own copy of the network, and restarts the board as a new one. It is taken only for a request that names the board by its own address or name, as the firmware routes are.

A board on Wi-Fi alone has no network after a factory reset. It cannot be reached to be told one. Connect it to a computer with a USB cable and give it a network over Improv, as Join a network says. A board with a wired network (the ESP32-P4X kit) stays on it and asks the router for an address again. An image built with a Wi-Fi network of its own (a development build; no published image has one) joins that network again.

curl -X POST http://hearth-1a2b3c.local/reset-preferences
curl -X POST -d "erase everything" http://hearth-1a2b3c.local/factory-reset

docs.title: Pair a server
docs.text:
Every connection to the player is encrypted with Noise, and a server plays to the board only once the two are paired. There are two ways to pair.

By the token. The console prints the board's pairing token at every start, and again when you type pair token:

sendspin: pairing token SP:0AO4BQKDC3YEKAULMZ4UMZFDRQGZSLVY9...

A server given the token pairs straight away. Whoever has it can pair, so it is printed nowhere else.

By a code. A server that pairs by code makes the board show six digits, on the console as sendspin: PAIRING CODE 482-913 and at the top of the page's Sendspin section, for as long as the pairing runs. Type them into the server. After twenty wrong codes the board refuses to pair until you type pair reset or choose Allow pairing again on the page.

The board keeps eight pairings, each with the name the server gave, and lists them the most recently used first: on the page's Sendspin section, and for pair list. A ninth pairing replaces the one used least recently, never one a server is connected on. A pairing made before the board kept names shows without one until its server next takes the board. Lines typed on the console are commands:

Command What it does pair list Prints the pairings: each server's ID (the first eight characters), its name, and whether it is connected pair token Prints the pairing token again pair reset Allows pairing again after twenty wrong codes pair cancel Ends the pairing that is running pair forget ID Removes one server's pairing, by the ID pair list prints, and closes its connection. The board keeps its other pairings and its identity; that server has to pair again. Forget beside a server on the page does the same pair forget Removes every pairing and gives the board a new identity and token; Forget every server on the page does the same sendspin Prints the player's state: the server, the role, the clock, and the stream's counters

docs.title: Music Assistant compatibility
docs.text:
CI validates the sink against a scripted aiosendspin 9.1.1 server, the library version used by Music Assistant. Music Assistant itself has not been tested with a board. The validated server finds the board over mDNS, pairs with it, and plays stereo PCM at 48 kHz, 16 or 24 bits, through the player@v1 role. The board renders left and right onto the layout's front speakers; other speakers stay silent. A one-speaker layout mixes the two channels. The sink does not offer FLAC or Opus.

A board plays for one server at a time. As the Sendspin specification sets out, a server that asks to play takes the board from one that is only connected or is already playing. A pairing in progress is not interrupted.

docs.title: Play AC-3 and E-AC-3
docs.text:
AC-3 and E-AC-3, with any Atmos objects, go to the board undecoded through Hearth's own role, _iclforge_player@v1. The board decodes the stream, renders it onto its layout, and applies the server's settings: the layout, routing, trims, delays and decoder settings.

hearth, the desktop app, sends it: its Network page pairs with the board and makes groups, and the output picker plays to a group (Hearth). hearth-testserver plays one file to one or more boards as a group. It is a developer tool, built from this repository with the hearth feature:

cmake --preset config-linux-gcc -DVCPKG_MANIFEST_FEATURES=hearth -DICLFORGE_BUILD_HEARTH=ON -DICLFORGE_BUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF
cmake --build --preset build-linux-gcc --target hearth-testserver

Then, with the board's address and the token from its console:

build/config-linux-gcc/bin/hearth-testserver --play programme.ec3 \
  --player ws://192.168.1.40:8928/sendspin --token SP:0... --layout 5.1 \
  --status http://192.168.1.40/status

The server pairs with the board, gives it the layout, plays the file, and prints what the board reported. --code-log FILE pairs by code instead: it reads the code from a file the board's console is being written to. --help lists the rest.

docs.title: Karaoke
docs.text: A karaoke stream, AC-3 or E-AC-3 flagged bsmod 7 above 1/0, goes to the board undecoded, and the board reproduces it itself under Hearth's karaoke setting: as coded, aware, or capable with the listener's vocals and the three part levels (Karaoke). The board says which codecs it does this for (karaoke_codecs), and this one lists AC-3 and E-AC-3. Checked on an S3 over Wi-Fi on 2026-10-12 with Hearth's live karaoke cases, which play a 3/2 stream with a tone in each channel to the board at a 3.0 layout once per reproduction and compare the levels the board reports at its outputs with the same stream decoded on the host: they followed it within 0.25 dB for as coded, aware, and capable with a vocal, with none, and with the melody and a vocal moved. One E-AC-3 run of three missed the part-level case and is not explained. Run it with ICLFORGE_HEARTH_LIVE_KARAOKE_SINK=<the board's mDNS name> and the tests named network sinks live: ... karaoke stream is reproduced by the board that decodes it.

docs.title: Late night
docs.text:
A film's loud passages and its quiet ones can be a long way apart, and at night the neighbours hear the first and you cannot hear the second. The streams the board decodes carry the mixer's own instructions for closing that distance, and the board has a setting that uses them: GET and PUT /dynamic-range, standard or late-night.

  • standard is what the board always did, and the default: AC-3 and E-AC-3 as the build's operating mode (line, so dialogue is brought to the -31 dBFS reference and the stream's dynrng words are applied), AC-4 as coded, and whatever a server sends for the decoder.
  • late-night applies the stream's heavy compression (the compr words of AC-3 and E-AC-3, the speaker DRC modes of AC-4) at the same level dialogue was heard at, so that switching it on moves no stream by its dialnorm. It is not RF mode, which would be 11 dB louder. It is the listener's choice at the board, and it wins over a server's decoder mode and compression settings for as long as it is on.

It changes the next stream, not the one that is playing, and it is kept over a restart. It can only be as strong as the stream's own words: a stream that carries no compr word decodes exactly as it does in standard, and PCM from Music Assistant has no such words at all. On a stream with them, the loud-to-quiet distance of the test stream fell from 31.3 dB to 23.9 dB (AC-3 and E-AC-3) and from 26.0 dB to 17.6 dB (AC-4). A board with a screen offers the choice as Late night under Preferences, in the Sound group, greyed with the reason where the build has no player; Reset preferences puts it back on standard. Every board with a Sendspin player answers the route; a board with no AC-4 decoder (the C6) is sent PCM for AC-4 and so has nothing to compress there. What was measured, and what was not, is in planning/hearth-late-night.md.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
A group is every player a server plays one programme to. Each board decodes and renders the programme onto its own layout, and plays each sample when the server's clock says, so boards with different layouts stay together. Each board follows the server's clock with Sendspin's time filter. On a home Wi-Fi network, two boards' reported play times stayed within 549 µs of each other over ten minutes. Those are the times the software scheduled: nobody has measured two DAC outputs together.

With the test server, give a --player and its options for each board:

hearth-testserver --play programme.ec3 \
  --player ws://192.168.1.40:8928/sendspin --token SP:0... --layout 2.0 \
  --player ws://192.168.1.41:8928/sendspin --token SP:0... --layout 5.1

Music Assistant group playback has not been tested.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Signal Default GPIO Kconfig Bit clock (BCLK) 5 CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_I2S_BCLK_GPIO Word select (WS, LRCK) 6 CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_I2S_WS_GPIO Data out (DOUT) 7 CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_I2S_DOUT_GPIO Second line's data out 8 CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_I2S_DOUT2_GPIO

The defaults avoid the S3's strapping pins, its USB pair and the console UART; any free GPIO will do. The signals are 3.3 V. The board sends no MCLK, so a DAC that needs one needs it added.

  • A stereo I2S DAC, such as a PCM5102 or MAX98357A, plays a 2.0 or 1.0 layout: one or two channels open standard I2S.
  • A TDM DAC plays three or more channels, which open TDM. A TDM DAC set up for one frame shape over I2C, such as an ESS ES9080, needs CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_I2S_FIXED_FRAME=1, which opens the full TDM frame for every layout, stereo included. The firmware does not set the DAC up over I2C: whatever does has to match the slot width below.
  • A second line carries a second DAC. Wire its data pin, and tick A second I2S line is wired to a DAC on the page (or PUT /wiring with 1). It shares the first line's bit clock and word select. Whether the two lines stay sample-aligned with DACs on both has not been checked.
  • A DSP that supplies the clocks, such as an ADAU1452, needs CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_I2S_SLAVE=1. This has not been tried.

docs.title: Slot widths
docs.text:
An S3 I2S line carries at most 128 bits a frame, so the slot width decides how many channels a line takes:

Slot width Samples Channels on one line With a second line 32 bits (the default) 24-bit, left-justified 4 8 16 bits 16-bit 8 16

So a 5.1 or 7.1 layout needs 16-bit slots, or 32-bit slots on two lines. 7.1.4 and 9.1.6 need 16-bit slots on two lines. Set the width to what the DAC is set up for: Slot width on the page, or PUT /slot-width with 16 or 32. It takes effect at the next play, and is refused while one runs. A layout that no longer fits after a change fails at the next play, and the page says why.

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text: The layout is the board's speakers, one per output slot: a name such as 2.0, 5.1, 5.1.4 or 7.1.4, or a list such as L,R,C,LFE,Ls,Rs in the order the DAC's outputs are wired. Set it on the page or with PUT /layout, and it applies from the next chunk the board plays. A server that sends its own settings replaces it. At 2.0 and 1.0 the decoder folds the programme down. On a wider layout each channel plays at its own location, objects are placed by their positions when the layout has height speakers, and nothing is upmixed. The README has the grammar and the rules.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Internal RAM is what this build is short of. Wi-Fi, lwIP, two HTTP servers, the Sendspin session and the decoder share what the part has: about 300 KB free before any of them starts (304,680 bytes in the footprint probe under QEMU), and the decoder's allocations of up to 16 KB go there first. In the ten-minute group run, the least internal RAM free while a stream played was 139 bytes on the 2.0 board and 23 bytes on the 5.1 board. Nothing failed in those runs, but in an earlier one-minute run a 108-byte allocation did, with no effect on the stream. The console's sendspin.progress lines report it as heap_least every four seconds or so.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• The page and its routes have no password. Anyone who can reach the board on the network can play a URL on it, change its settings or the network it joins at its next restart, and forget its pairings. Anyone who can load the page during a pairing can also read the code, and so pair a server of their own. Keep the boards on a network you trust.
  • The token is the credential. It pairs a server with no code, and only the console prints it.
  • Keys are stored unencrypted. The board's identity, its pairing token, its pairings and the Wi-Fi passphrase are in NVS, which these builds do not encrypt: anyone holding the board can read them.

The threat model has the rest.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
• The server does not list the board. The console's mdns: line says whether the board advertised itself. Check that mDNS passes between the board's network and the server's: an access point that isolates its clients, or a second VLAN, stops it. http://<address>/status shows whether the board is up.
  • Improv says the board could not connect. Check the network's name and passphrase, and that it is a 2.4 GHz network, then send them again. The board keeps listening.
  • Pairing fails. Type sendspin on the console to see the player's state. After twenty wrong codes, pair reset. A server that paired before pair forget has to pair again, and so does one forgotten by its ID.
  • Underruns. The page's Sendspin section counts them. The console's closing line for each stream gives them, with the average time a chunk took to decode and render (burst_us). A chunk holds 32 ms of audio, so a burst_us near 32,000 means the board cannot keep up with the programme on its layout. Otherwise, look at the Wi-Fi between the board and the server.
  • A layout is refused. It has more channels than the slot width and wiring allow (Slot widths).
  • The console shows boot:0x0 (DOWNLOAD) after flashing. Press RESET.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• The example's README: every setting, the REST routes, and the measurements.
  • ESP32-S3: the decoder on this part, and its timing and memory.
  • The plan: what Hearth is building, and in what order.

docs.title: Sink firmware: install, update, go back
docs.text:
Every tagged release publishes hearth_sink built for five boards, so a board can be set up and kept up to date without ESP-IDF. CI packages the images whenever its esp lane runs, which is after a merge to main that changes the ESP32 trees or a tree its component ships, and nightly (the lane table); the release workflow attaches them to the GitHub release. This guide is for someone with a board and a release. It covers:

  • which image a board takes, and checking a download;
  • installing a new board, and moving a board that runs an older build;
  • updating over the network, what the board does during an update, and going back;
  • what to do when a board does not come back.

To build the firmware yourself instead, see An ESP32-S3 sink. planning/esp32-ota.md has the design and the reasons for it.

Status as of 2026-09-30: unsigned development images

The images are checked for damage at every step, but not signed: while the boards are in development, anyone on a board's network can update it, as anyone with a USB cable can. Signed images come when the boards leave development. Until the first tagged release that carries sink firmware, build from source (An ESP32-S3 sink) or take the esp32-firmware artifact from a recent CI run; the release workflow and Sink installer are already wired for when that release lands.

docs.title: Which image
docs.text:
Image For hearth-sink-esp32s3 An ESP32-S3 with 16 MB of flash and 8 MB of octal PSRAM, such as the ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1-N16R8 hearth-sink-esp32c6 Any ESP32-C6 module; it uses a 4 MB partition table hearth-sink-esp32c6-16mb An ESP32-C6 with 16 MB of flash hearth-sink-esp32p4-rev1 An ESP32-P4 of silicon revision v1.x, such as the DFRobot FireBeetle 2 hearth-sink-esp32p4-rev3 An ESP32-P4 of silicon revision v3.x with a 7-inch panel, such as the ESP32-P4X-Function-EV-Board (An ESP32-P4 sink)

The two P4 images refuse each other's chips: one for v1.x silicon will not start on v3.x and the other way round, which is why a release carries both. The P4 reaches Wi-Fi through its onboard ESP32-C6, whose own firmware these images do not change.

Telling boards apart. Over USB, esptool chip-id names the chip and its revision, and esptool flash-id gives the flash size. A board already on the network reports both: http://<board>/hardware gives its chip, revision and PSRAM, and http://<board>/firmware its flash size and partition table. ota.py chooses the image for each board from these, so a board updated over the network never needs this table.

Each image is published as four files, with <version> the release's tag:

File What it is for <image>-<version>.bin The app image, for an update over the network <image>-<version>-factory.bin The whole flash from address 0, for a new board. It also erases the board's settings <image>-<version>-parts.zip The same pieces as separate files with a flash_args, for a board already in use. Its settings are kept <image>-<version>-elf.zip The ELF, for reading a crash's backtrace or core dump

hearth-sink-manifest.json describes all five images for the tools.

docs.title: Checking a download
docs.text:
Every release has a SHA512SUMS file. In the directory you downloaded into:

sha512sum --check --ignore-missing SHA512SUMS

Each file also has a build provenance attestation, which says which repository, workflow and commit built it:

gh attestation verify hearth-sink-esp32s3-v0.11.0-factory.bin --repo iainchesworthlabs/iclforge

When a release is GPG-signed, each file has a .asc signature beside it, and the release carries iclforge-signing-key.asc. Releasing says how the signing works.

ota.py push --release and the browser installer check what they download against the release's manifest and SHA512SUMS before they write anything.

docs.title: A new board
docs.text:
In the browser: the installer writes the image over USB from Chrome, Edge or Firefox 151 and later, and then gives the board its network over Improv. Choose to erase a new board.

With esptool: write the factory image at address 0, from any computer with Python:

pip install esptool
esptool --port PORT write-flash 0x0 hearth-sink-esp32s3-v0.11.0-factory.bin

PORT is the board's serial port, such as COM5 or /dev/ttyACM0. Then give the board its network over Improv, as Join a network describes. A new board is called hearth- followed by the last six hex digits of its MAC address.

docs.title: A board running an older build
docs.text:
A board that runs a build from before the two-slot flash layout, or any other build, moves to the release over USB once. Its name, network and pairings are kept, since neither way erases the board's settings (its NVS partition):

  • In the browser: the installer, choosing not to erase;
  • with esptool: unpack the image's -parts.zip and, in that directory, run esptool --port PORT write-flash @flash_args.

After that, updates go over the network.

docs.title: Updating over the network
docs.text:
Any one of these sends a board a new app image. The board checks it and restarts into it on trial (below).

  • ota.py, from this repository's tools/hearth/, is one Python file with nothing to install. It finds the boards on the network, gives each the image that fits it, checks every download against the release's manifest and SHA512SUMS, and waits for each board to accept its image or go back:

    python ota.py push --release latest --all
python ota.py push --release v0.11.0 --host hearth-eb2c64.local
python ota.py status --all

    --all finds boards by mDNS and needs the zeroconf Python package; --host names a board by its address or .local name. Boards are updated one at a time, and a board that goes back stops the rest. - The board's page, http://<board>/: Update firmware… under Firmware, with the image's .bin. The page reads the image's head first and refuses a file for another chip or project. - hearth, the desktop app: the Firmware tab of a paired sink's settings page. - curl: curl -T hearth-sink-esp32s3-v0.11.0.bin http://hearth-eb2c64.local/firmware. This does no checks of its own; the board still makes all of its own.

Name a board by its IP address or its own .local name: the board refuses firmware addressed to any other name.

docs.title: What the board does during an update
docs.text:
1. Flash mode. The board stops what it plays, says goodbye to its Sendspin server and stops answering settings changes. It writes the image into the slot it is not running, and checks what it wrote before it answers.
  2. The trial. It restarts into the new image, which is on trial. The image is accepted once the board has held a network address, its web server and its Sendspin player together for 30 seconds, within 5 minutes of starting.
  3. Or it goes back. If the image does not get there, panics or resets before it is accepted, the board boots the image it ran before, and reports why. A power cut during the trial also brings the previous image back.

ota.py prints each stage. It then says the board was updated, rolled back (with the board's reason), or did not come back (with what to try). An upload that breaks off on the way, or that a restart of the board cuts short, is sent once more, with the board's own account of what happened. A push that fails does not leave the board waiting in flash mode: the tool tells it to go back to what it runs. The page shows the same in its Firmware section, and hearth in its Firmware tab. Every board keeps its recent console output, and the C6 and the P4 also keep a crash's core dump, both readable over the network; the board's README covers them.

docs.title: Going back
docs.text:
• Roll back on the board's page or in hearth, or python ota.py rollback --host <board>. The board restarts into the image in its other slot, which then has a trial of its own.
  • An older release, pushed as any other: python ota.py push --release <tag> --host <board>.

docs.title: When a board does not come back
docs.text:
1. Cycle its power while the new image is on trial. A reset before the image is accepted boots the previous one. Then python ota.py status --host <board> says what it runs.
  2. Failing that, USB: the installer without erasing, or the release's -parts.zip with esptool write-flash @flash_args.
  3. If the board does not answer on USB either, put it into the chip's download mode: hold BOOT, press and release RESET, then release BOOT. That mode is in the chip's ROM, which nothing can overwrite, so it is always there. After flashing, press RESET once.

docs.title: Install a Hearth sink from the browser
docs.text:
This page puts hearth_sink onto an ESP32-S3, ESP32-C6 or ESP32-P4 board over its USB cable, from the newest release, with nothing to install on the computer. It uses ESP Web Tools and the browser's Web Serial, so it needs Chrome or Edge on a computer, or Firefox from version 151, which added Web Serial in May 2026. Safari cannot do it, and neither can anything on iOS.

The site copies the images from the release when it is published, and each release publishes it again. A browser cannot fetch a release's files from another site, so they are served from here. The page also asks GitHub whether a newer release has firmware, and says so if one does.

The sink firmware guide covers the same steps with esptool and without a browser, updating a board over its network afterwards, and what to do when a board does not come back.

Looking for the newest release's firmware…

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Which board you have. The four images, and how to tell boards apart, are in Which image. The installer checks the chip before it writes anything: an image for another chip is refused.
  • A USB cable to the board's serial connector. On an ESP32-S3 DevKitC-1 that is the connector marked USB. A FireBeetle 2 ESP32-P4 has two USB-C connectors on two different USB peripherals and no auto-reset circuit. Its ROM download mode answers on the one marked USB 2.0 OTG, once you hold BOOT, tap RST and release BOOT by hand (step 3 below), and its console is on the other (ESP32-P4).

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
1. Connect the board, press the button for it above, and choose its port.
  2. Erase, or keep the board's settings. The installer asks.
  3. A new board: erase it.
  4. A board that already runs hearth_sink: don't erase it. It keeps its name, its network and its pairings, and moves to the two-slot flash layout that updates over the network need.
  5. If the installer cannot connect, put the chip into its download mode by hand: hold BOOT, press and release RESET, release BOOT, and try again. This mode is in the chip's ROM, which nothing can overwrite, so it works even on a board whose firmware no longer starts.
  6. When the writing is done, press RESET once if the board was put into download mode by hand.
  7. The installer then offers to give the board its Wi-Fi network over Improv, which the firmware answers. The board stores the network and joins it.

From then on the board's page is at http://hearth-XXXXXX.local/, where XXXXXX is the end of its MAC address. Newer releases go onto it over the network: see Updating over the network.

docs.title: Third-party notices
docs.text: The installer is ESP Web Tools 10.4.0, by the ESPHome project, under the Apache License 2.0. The site serves its own copy, with the licence beside it (assets/sink-installer/esp-web-tools/LICENSE), rather than loading it from a CDN.

docs.title: Choosing the speaker layout of a sink
docs.text: A Hearth sink plays onto the speakers its layout names, one per output slot of its DAC: 2.0 for a pair, 5.1, 7.1.4, up to 9.1.6, or a list such as L,R,C,LFE,Ls,Rs for a DAC wired in another order. What a board can carry depends on how its I2S output is set up and on the chip, not on the layout, so the board says which layouts it can take and why it cannot take the others. The same answer is on the screen (Preferences), on the device's web page and in the REST routes.

docs.title: What a board can take
docs.text:
What decides it Where it is set Effect Slot width, 16 or 32 bits The page's Slot width, or PUT /slot-width One TDM line is one frame of 128 bits on an ESP32-S3 or ESP32-C6, so four 32-bit slots or eight 16-bit ones; 512 bits on an ESP32-P4, sixteen or thirty-two A second I2S line The page's Wiring, or PUT /wiring; only on an ESP32-S3 Doubles the slots. A DAC has to be wired to the second data pin The chip Fixed An ESP32-P4 older than revision v3.0 has no clock for TDM: it plays stereo and nothing wider The build Fixed The ESP32-C6 build decodes streams of two channels at most

The slot width and the second line are the DAC's wiring. Both can be changed while nothing plays, and the list below follows them.

docs.title: The list
docs.text:
GET /layout-options lists thirteen layouts (1.0, 2.0, 2.1, 5.0, 5.1, 5.1.2, 7.1, 5.1.4, 7.1.2, 7.1.4, 9.1.2, 9.1.4, 9.1.6), each with one of three verdicts and, unless it is plainly supported, a sentence:

  • supported: the board takes it, and a play this wide has been measured keeping up on this kind of board.
  • with limits: the board takes it, and something sits on it: the build decodes fewer channels than the layout has, it needs the second line (never checked with a DAC on both lines), a stream this wide was measured falling behind, or nobody has measured a play this wide on this kind of board. The last is written "Not verified", and means exactly that, not that it fails.
  • unavailable: the board cannot play it, and the sentence says why: "7.1.4 needs 12 slots; this board's output carries 4 (32-bit slots, one line). 16-bit slots and a second line would carry 16." The fix field says which setting would change that: slot-width, second-line, slot-width-and-second-line, or hardware when no setting does.
curl http://hearth-1a2b3c.local/layout-options

One verdict decides all of it. PUT /layout refuses an unavailable layout with 409 and the same sentence as the body, and takes a layout with a limit with the limit after the ok; the screen's list greys the same layouts with the same sentences; the device page greys the same presets. A layout the list offers is one PUT /layout takes, and one it greys is one PUT /layout refuses.

docs.title: What each board offers
docs.text:
At the setting each board ships with. The verdicts are the project's host tests', which run every board below against the layout parser and the board's own rule.

Board Setting Carries Offered ESP32-S3 N16R8 32-bit slots, one line 4 slots 1.0 and 2.0; 2.1 not verified. 5.0 to 7.1 need 16-bit slots, and 5.1.4 and wider need 16-bit slots and a second line ESP32-S3, 16-bit slots, two lines 16 slots Every layout. 2.0 is the one measured; the rest are not verified, and those past eight slots lean on the second line ESP32-C6 16-bit slots, one line 8 slots 1.0 and 2.0; up to 7.1 with the build's two-channel limit; wider layouts unavailable, and no setting helps ESP32-P4 below v3.0 32-bit slots 2 slots 1.0 and 2.0; every wider layout unavailable because of the chip, and PUT /layout refuses it with that sentence ESP32-P4 v3.x (the P4X kit) 32-bit slots 16 slots All thirteen supported: a 5.1 stream onto 9.1.6, sixteen slots, ran in real time with no underruns

"Measured" here is a play in the board suite with no underruns, not a listening test.

docs.title: On the screen
docs.text:
A board with a screen has Speaker layout in Preferences, under Sound: the layout in force, in words, and a Change button. Change opens one sheet with two ways in to the same choice.

Quick picks are the layouts a home has, in two groups: Around you (1.0 to 9.1) and With heights (5.1.2 to 9.1.6). A layout the board cannot carry is greyed, and touching it says why in the card above the buttons. Build yours is how many speakers are around you, how many subwoofers, how many heights, and how the heights are mounted: high, or in the ceiling. The room the layout makes is drawn beside the buttons and changes as they are pressed; the footer names the layout in words and holds Apply, and Cancel is in the bar, so neither is ever off the screen. Only the buttons scroll.

What the board plays differently is only the ceiling: heights in the ceiling are put straight overhead, and high heights, on the wall or up-firing, are played the same way (the renderer has one upper tier), so the sheet has one button for them. Bass-managed small speakers are not offered here, because the name has no spelling for them; a speaker list still sets them, through the route and the web page.

The same sheet on an ESP32-S3 whose sink carries four slots: what the board carries is said at the head, the layouts it cannot carry are greyed, and a touch on one gives the verdict's sentence.

The sheet is the same code at every size the product is drawn at; on a smaller display the room moves to the end of what scrolls.

While music plays, Apply asks first, because the sink is opened again and the audio breaks up for a moment. With nothing playing the change is made at the touch.

How it was designed, and what the board can honestly tell apart, is in planning/p4x-layout-builder.md.

docs.title: Changing the layout
docs.text: PUT /layout with a name or a list sets it, and the board keeps it over a restart. What it does to a stream that is playing depends on how the stream arrives, and is described, with its open question, in planning/p4x-layout-options.md.

docs.title: Speaker levels, distances and the test tone
docs.text: A sink sets two numbers for each speaker of the room, a level and a distance, and plays a quiet test tone out of any one of them, so that a person setting up the room can hear which speaker an output reaches and can match the speakers to each other. Both work the same on every sink that has a Sendspin player (the S3, the C6 and the P4), and both apply to everything the sink plays: PCM from Music Assistant, AC-3, E-AC-3, AC-4 and objects from Hearth.

docs.title: What the two numbers do
docs.text:
Range Does Level -12 to +12 dB, in steps of 0.5 Turns that speaker up or down against the others. 0 dB is the stream as it comes. Distance 0.1 to 10 metres, to the centimetre How far that speaker is from where you sit. The nearer speakers are delayed so that the sound of all of them arrives at the same moment.

Each is kept against the speaker's role in the layout, not against the output it is wired to. The roles are the ones the layout names (L, C, R, Ls, Rs, Lrs, Rrs, Vhl, Vhr, Lts, Rts, LFE and the rest of the list in Layouts), and S1 to S16 for a slot that a list places by angle. So the left surround keeps its level and distance when the layout changes from 5.1 to 7.1.4, and a speaker the layout does not have is remembered until the layout has it again. Every speaker starts at 0 dB with no distance.

A speaker with no distance counts as being as far away as the farthest speaker that has one, so it is never delayed. Setting one distance changes nothing; setting a second moves the nearer of the two. The farthest speaker is never delayed: the delay a speaker gets is the extra distance the farthest one has over it, at the speed of sound (343 m/s). That also means the time at which the sink plays a frame, the time its server asked for, is the farthest speaker's, and a group of sinks stays together however each room is measured.

A level above 0 dB can clip a loud passage: the sink clips at full scale and does not limit.

docs.title: Setting them
docs.text:
On the sink's own screen, a board with a touch panel (the P4X kit) has them under Preferences, in the group Sound:

Identify speakers and Speaker levels and distances open the same view, the Speakers sheet. Identify opens it and plays the test tone through every speaker in turn, once; Edit opens it as it is.

The sheet draws the room as the layout in force has it, with every speaker's ID on it (L, C, R, Ls, Rs, LFE, and the rest of a larger room's, the height speakers among them), and the speaker the tone is on is lit as each sounds: which one you hear is the one you see. A tap on a speaker chooses it (it is ringed) and plays the tone through it. For the chosen speaker, Level goes up and down half a decibel a tap and Distance a tenth of a metre, or a metre with -1 m and +1 m (the first + on a speaker with no distance starts it at the farthest distance the others have, so that nothing moves until you move it); the line above them says what is in force at it. A 2.0 room is the same sheet with two speakers:

The five buttons are a bar at the foot of the sheet that is always on the screen: Play (the chosen speaker once), Repeat (it over and over, so that a level can be set by ear), Play each (every speaker in turn), Stop and Reset (the chosen speaker back to 0 dB and no distance). Stop ends the tone and leaves the controls; it is not the only thing on the screen. The room and the chosen speaker scroll between that bar and the title's where they are more than the screen holds (a 9.1.6 room, a small display), and the bar does not move. The tone stops when you leave the sheet, and when Preferences put themselves away. On a screen too narrow for a room the speakers are a row of buttons, and a display too narrow for five buttons on a line wraps them onto two with shorter words (Loop and All):

When the board cannot do something the sheet says why under the controls: a song is playing, the board has no memory for delay lines (the distance is greyed, the level is not), or a Sendspin server is setting the levels. A level or a distance the board refuses (the nearest and the farthest speaker too far apart) is said above the controls.

On the sink's web page, the section Levels and distances lists the speakers of the layout in force, with a level field, a distance field, the delay that comes to, and a Play button for the tone. A field is sent when you leave it. Reset levels and distances asks first.

Over the control surface:

curl http://hearth-a1b2c3.local/trim

lists the speakers as JSON, with what is set, what is in force, and what the board can do.

curl -X PUT http://hearth-a1b2c3.local/trim -d 'L level=-1.5 distance=2.4; R level=-1.5 distance=2.4; Ls distance=1.9'

changes them. The body is statements separated by semicolons or line ends; a statement is a role and level=<dB>, distance=<metres> (or distance=none), or reset; reset alone clears every speaker. All of it is taken or none of it: one wrong statement changes nothing and the reply says which kind of mistake it was. A change is in force at the next chunk of a stream that plays, and is kept over a restart.

A change of level while a song plays moves over the next block of 256 frames (5 ms), so it does not click. A change of a distance drops that one speaker for the length of its new delay (20 ms at most), once.

docs.title: The test tone
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://hearth-a1b2c3.local/identify -d all       # each speaker in turn
curl -X POST http://hearth-a1b2c3.local/identify -d Ls        # one speaker, once
curl -X POST http://hearth-a1b2c3.local/identify -d 'Ls loop' # that speaker again and again
curl -X POST http://hearth-a1b2c3.local/identify -d off

The tone is pink noise, which sounds equally present through a tweeter and a woofer; a subwoofer or an LFE feed gets the same noise in the band 30 to 80 Hz. It goes through the same output stage as the music, so a tone out of the left surround proves the whole way from the slot to the DAC channel to the speaker, and it carries the speaker's level, so a level set by ear is heard on the next tone. The sink's volume applies, as it does to music.

The tone is made to be safe in a room, and the limits are in the code, not in what a request says:

  • At most -24 dB of full scale (RMS), and -30 dB unless a caller asks otherwise. A request for more plays at -24.
  • 1.5 seconds a speaker, with a 20 ms fade in and out so that no speaker is clicked, and half a second between two speakers.
  • 60 seconds in all for anything a request starts, a loop included; then it ends by itself.

It is refused (409, with the reason) while a stream is playing, while a play from the control surface or an update has the speakers, and while a server's own tone is on. It stops at once when a stream begins, when the player is held for a play or for an update, and when asked (off, which fades over 20 ms). The sink is left as the tone found it: the player had the sink open already, and a tone opens or closes nothing. The web page asks the sink to stop when it is closed.

docs.title: What a board can do
docs.text:
The delay of a distance needs a delay line for each output, which the sink keeps in PSRAM. A sink that has none still sets levels.

Sink Level Distance ESP32-S3 with PSRAM Yes Yes, with the nearest and the farthest speaker up to 6.86 m apart ESP32-P4 (v1.x board, v3.x kit) Yes Yes, up to 6.86 m apart ESP32-C6, or any build without PSRAM Yes No: the board has no memory for delay lines

GET /trim says which, in its delay object (available, reason, max_span_m), and a request to set a distance on a board that cannot is refused with that reason. Each speaker's distance can be anything from 0.1 to 10 m, but the nearest and the farthest speaker can be no further apart than sound travels in the delay line: 20 ms, which is 6.86 m (CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_SENDSPIN_MAX_DELAY_MS, 20 in the published images). A request that would put them further apart is refused (409) and says how far apart they can be; a span that is already too wide, left by a build with longer lines, can still be made smaller, and a level can be set beside it.

docs.title: When a server sets them
docs.text: A Sendspin server can send a trim and a delay for each output (trim_db and delay_ms in its settings), and what it sends replaces the sink's own for as long as its settings stand, each key on its own: a server that sends trims and no delays leaves the delays to the sink. GET /trim then says server_level or server_delay, the table still shows what the listener set, and the numbers in force are applied_level_db and delay_samples. A server's tone replaces the sink's own, and the sink's is refused while a server's is on.

docs.title: The Hearth plan
docs.text:
This page points to the plan rather than reproducing it. Design proposals live in the repository's planning/ directory and are deliberately not republished onto this site — see planning/README.md for why: a proposal read alongside reference documentation is too easily read as a shipped feature.

Status as of 2026-09-30: built, with the user guide and the hardware exits open

The plan decided on 2026-09-15 is built apart from the items its own status names: a user guide and screenshots of the running app, and the exits that need a DAC wired to a board, a multichannel endpoint or Music Assistant itself. The appliance plan of 2026-09-07, which it replaced, was not built in that form.

docs.title: What's decided
docs.text:
Decided on 2026-09-15. Hearth has two forms that talk to each other:

  • hearth, a desktop reference player for Windows, Linux and macOS. It plays AC-3, E-AC-3 and E-AC-3 JOC media with every decoder setting the library has, renders to a chosen speaker layout, routes each channel to an output with trim, delay and bass management, and shows the per-channel levels and the bitstream information. It plays to a local device, passes the bitstream through to a receiver, or streams to sinks on the network. The plan designed AC-4 in and left its decoder to a later chip (decision 7); the player has since gained it, as What's built records.
  • hearth_sink, firmware for ESP32-S3 (up to sixteen TDM outputs) and ESP32-C6 (up to eight) boards. A sink is a Sendspin player: Music Assistant can play to it, and hearth sends it the undecoded bitstream through an extension role, which the board decodes and renders to its own layout. The ESP32-P4 joined the sink family after the plan was written.

Between them is Sendspin, with hearth as a conformant server and the boards as conformant players, so groups, clock synchronisation, encryption and pairing come from that protocol.

This replaced the plan decided on 2026-09-07 for a headless appliance: a daemon beside a receiver with a web control page, an optional kiosk window, and an HLS client. The name, Hearth's place as the family's fourth member, and its build identity carried over.

docs.title: What's built
docs.text:
Detail: Hearth overview.

  • ESP32 hearth_sink. A Sendspin player with Improv Wi-Fi setup, pairing, groups and updates over the network, on the ESP32-S3, the ESP32-C6 (stereo only) and the ESP32-P4 (silicon revision v1.x, with Wi-Fi through the board's onboard C6). Two S3 boards played one programme as a group, and a C6 and an S3 played a stereo group. No DAC is wired to any board yet. Setup: An ESP32-S3 sink.
  • apps/hearth. The hearth engine and window (Qt Quick, with Play, Media, Speakers, Decoder, Network and Settings pages; it builds and packages on Windows, Linux and macOS when Qt6 6.8+ is found), hearth-testsink, hearth-testserver and hearth-render. The player reads raw .ac3, .ec3 and .ac4 streams and plays to a local device, to a receiver as a bitstream, or to a group of network sinks. CI runs the engine tests and plays to an emulated S3 from the test server.
  • AC-4 in hearth (phases I2 and I5 of planning/ac4.md). The engine plays channel-based, immersive and object AC-4 through the decoder's public API, decoded for every local output, with the Decoder page's AC-4 controls and the Media page's AC-4 information. A network group's members on the extension role that list AC-4 are sent the stream as bursts, and its PCM members get the decoded audio. An ESP32-P4 or ESP32-S3 sink built with the AC-4 decoder lists it (phase I6); the published images do not.
  • libs/sendspin. Shared by the desktop tools and the board.
  • ESP32-C6. Decode probe timed on a board. hearth_sink's Sendspin player runs on this board, stereo only: a ten-minute group run with an ESP32-S3 had no underruns on either board. Setup: README, "On the ESP32-C6". CI builds the Sendspin player for this part, for the 4 MB and the 16 MB flash layouts, and does not run it: ESP-IDF's RISC-V QEMU emulates the ESP32-C3 and no other part.

docs.title: Karaoke
docs.text:
A karaoke stream is an ordinary AC-3 programme whose channels are parts, not speakers: the backing music, a guide melody, and one or two vocals. ETSI TS 102 366 Annex C defines it for AC-3; E-AC-3 carries the same service type and is reproduced the same way (E-AC-3 and AC-4). iclforge handles it end to end, in three places:

You want to Use Play one, choose which vocals you hear, and sing along to its words Hearth Make one from a backing track, a guide melody and one or two vocals The Forge GUI Encode, probe and decode one in a script forge

There is no separate karaoke program: Hearth has a Karaoke page, and the Forge GUI has a Karaoke entry in its Controls switch.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
examples/karaoke/auld-lang-syne/ is a karaoke stream with everything it is made of, so that nothing has to be built first. It is "Auld Lang Syne", one verse, 16.5 s, generated by a script and not recorded:

  • The parts: a stereo backing, a melody guide and two vocals as WAV files, and a Forge GUI project that opens them in the Karaoke flow. Open the project, press through Hear to listen to the stream as coded, aware and capable, change a part or a level, and Save to encode it again.
  • The stream and its words: auld-lang-syne.ac3 and auld-lang-syne.lrc. Open the stream in Hearth and the words follow the singing, syllable by syllable.

The example's own README gives each step, and the forge encode line that writes the same stream.

A second example is built for duets: examples/karaoke/leave-her-johnny/ is a traditional capstan shanty, one verse, 19.2 s, in which the shantyman and the crew sing different lines and each is silent while the other sings, so that "V1 only", "V2 only" and "both" each sound different and leave a different part for you to sing. Its project names the four parts and nothing of how they are laid out; the Karaoke flow and forge project work that out.

docs.title: What a karaoke stream is
docs.text:
It is a main service with bsmod 7 and a coding mode above 1/0. L and R carry the backing; the slot a programme would use for its centre carries a guide melody (M), and the slots it would use for its surrounds carry one or two vocals (V1 and V2):

Mode Parts, in coded order 3/0 L M R 2/1 L R V1 3/1 L M R V1 2/2 L R V1 V2 3/2 L M R V1 V2

A player that knows nothing about karaoke plays the channels where they are coded, so the vocals come out of the rear speakers. Annex C defines two kinds of decoder that do better:

  • A karaoke-aware decoder (Table C.2.2) plays L, C and R: the backing, the melody guide in the centre, and the vocals mixed in at the surround level the stream carries.
  • A karaoke-capable decoder (Table C.2.3) does the same and lets the listener choose which vocals play: none, V1, V2 or both. With none, what is left is the backing and the guide melody, for singing along to. Annex C also leaves it room to move the level of each part, which iclforge's capable decoder offers.

docs.title: E-AC-3 and AC-4
docs.text:
E-AC-3 carries the same service type: its bsmod is in the infomdat group (Annex E, Table E1.2), and Annex G (Table G.2) gives the E-AC-3 descriptor a karaoke service type. Annex E defines no reproduction for it. iclforge reproduces an E-AC-3 stream flagged this way as it does an AC-3 one, by analogy and as Dolby's own decoder does (How it is checked), where the programme is one independent substream with no object layer. A programme with a dependent substream or an object layer is played as coded: Annex C has no vocals for it. The levels the reproduction uses are the stream's Lo/Ro mixing group (lorocmixlev and lorosurmixlev), or -3 dB each where the stream has none, and forge eac3-encode writes the group whenever bsmod is 7 and the layout has a centre or a surround. A player that does not apply the reproduction plays the vocals from the surround speakers, as it does an AC-3 stream.

AC-4 has no karaoke mode: its specification has no bsmod value for it, so there is nothing to reproduce, and forge warns and ignores the choice on an AC-4 stream. The options for carrying karaoke in AC-4 say what its presentations and objects could do; none is built.

docs.title: Play it in Hearth
docs.text:
Open a karaoke stream in Hearth (a raw .ac3 or .ec3, or an MP4, Matroska or MPEG-TS file with an AC-3 or E-AC-3 track) and choose the Karaoke page (Ctrl+7).

The "Auld Lang Syne" example, 1.8 s in and held there: the word being sung is part way through its fill. hearth --smoke-shot karaoke.png --page karaoke --open examples/karaoke/auld-lang-syne/auld-lang-syne.ac3 --seek 1800 (Hearth's command line). The picture is of 2026-10-12, before the page had its Microphone card, which is now the first card of the right-hand column.

Reproduction is the decoder's choice, kept across starts:

Choice What you hear As coded The channels as the stream codes them: the vocals come from the surround speakers. Aware (the default) L, C and R, with the vocals at the stream's own level. On two speakers this is the ordinary Lo/Ro fold, which Annex C says is the same thing. Capable As aware, with Vocals set to None, V1, V2 or Both. A single vocal plays in the centre with the melody; Both is V1 on the left and V2 on the right, so a stream with only V1 plays it on the left. A level for the melody and for each vocal moves it against the table, from 24 dB down (which is off) to 12 dB up.

The levels are the capable decoder's alone, 0 dB each is the table as it stands, and they are kept across starts with the choice. Raising a part far enough lowers the others a little, so that no speaker is driven past full scale. Reset levels puts all three back. A part at the bottom of its control is off, and the page lists it as muted. A level has nothing to act on for a vocal the stream lacks or the Vocals choice leaves out, and its control is closed.

The page says which part each speaker plays under the choice made, and says in words when the choice does not apply:

  • The stream is not karaoke: an ordinary programme, an AC-4 stream, or an E-AC-3 stream flagged karaoke whose programme has a dependent substream or an object layer, which Annex C has no vocals for. The page says which, and that the stream plays as coded.
  • The stream is going to a receiver as a bitstream. That happens only with As coded chosen and a receiver chosen for passthrough in the output picker: the receiver decodes the stream, and unless it is karaoke-capable, V1 and V2 play from its surround speakers. With Aware or Capable chosen Hearth decodes the stream itself and sends the receiver PCM, so the choice is heard. The page's notice, shown while a bitstream goes out, says both, and has a button to choose another output.
  • The output is a network group: a sink that lists the karaoke settings (and, for an E-AC-3 stream, eac3 among the codecs it reproduces karaoke for) and decodes as many channels as the stream has is sent the stream as it is and told your choice, and decodes it itself; one that does not (an ESP32-C6 decodes two channels) is sent PCM that Hearth has decoded with the choice applied. Every member plays one reproduction, at the same levels (see the Hearth page).
  • The stereo fold is Lt/Rt, for which Annex C defines no reproduction. The page has a button to use Lo/Ro, which does.

docs.title: Lyrics
docs.text: Hearth shows the words of the stream playing from a .lrc file with the same name in the same folder: Auld Lang Syne.ac3 is read with Auld Lang Syne.lrc (the extension in any case). Where there is no .lrc, a SubRip .srt of that name is read the same way (see below), and failing that an Advanced SubStation Alpha .ass (see below), and then a MIDI karaoke .kar (see below).

docs.title: The file
docs.text:
LRC is an informal format; what Hearth reads is:

[ti:Auld Lang Syne]
[ar:Traditional]
[offset:0]
[00:12.00]<00:12.00>Should <00:12.60>auld <00:13.10>acquaintance <00:14.20>be <00:14.60>forgot,
[00:16.00]And never brought to mind?
Part Meaning [mm:ss.xx] A line, shown from that time. .xx is hundredths, .x tenths and .xxx milliseconds. Several tags give one text at several times (a repeated chorus). <mm:ss.xx> before a word The word-timed form: the word starts at that time and runs to the next word's tag, and a line's last word runs to the next line. [offset:+/-ms] Shifts every time. A positive value makes the lyrics appear sooner. [ti:] [ar:] [al:] [by:] [length:mm:ss] Kept for display. V1: V2: V1+V2: at the start of a line A duet: which vocal sings the line (see below). Not shown as text. [v1:name] [v2:name] What the file calls the two singers.

The text is UTF-8, with or without a byte-order mark. A file in another encoding is not shown, and the page says so; playback is not affected.

docs.title: A duet
docs.text:
A karaoke stream has two vocals, and a duet's lines can say which sings each:

[v1:Shantyman]
[v2:Crew]
[00:12.00]V1: Oh, the times are hard and the wages low
[00:16.00]V2: Leave her, Johnny, leave her
[00:20.00]V1+V2: It's time for us to leave her

The marker is the first thing after the time (before any <mm:ss.xx> word tag), in either case, with spaces allowed round the + and after the colon. A line with no marker is for nobody in particular. A plain file with no times may carry the markers too, so that a duet's text can be marked before it is timed. Hearth's timing window sets each line's singer and the two names as the file is timed, and saves them in the file (see Timing the lyrics).

Where a file marks its lines, the Karaoke page has two name fields. A name typed there is for this run of Hearth only, never kept for a song, and comes before the file's [v1:] and [v2:], which come before "V1" and "V2". Every line then says who sings it, three ways: the name above it, the side (the second singer's lines are indented, the first's are not) and the colour. On a karaoke stream the name also says whose line it is for you: guide when the vocal that is playing sings it, you when it does not, and shared when it is a line for both and only one of the two plays. A sentence under the names says the same for the whole file ("The vocal of Shantyman plays: you sing the lines of Crew."), which is what choosing V1, V2, None or Both under Capable changes.

"Leave Her, Johnny", 6.3 s in: the crew's line, indented and tagged guide because both vocals play. hearth --smoke-shot duet.png --page karaoke --open examples/karaoke/leave-her-johnny/leave-her-johnny.ac3 --seek 6300, of 2026-10-12 as the picture above is.

docs.title: SubRip
docs.text:
A .srt file is read as lyrics too, which is what subtitle tools and ripped karaoke subtitles write:

1
00:00:12,000 --> 00:00:15,500
Should auld acquaintance
be forgot

2
00:00:20,250 --> 00:00:22,000
And never brought to mind?

Each cue is a line, and it ends where its cue ends, so the gap between two cues is a stretch where nothing is being sung (which an LRC file, whose lines end where the next begins, cannot say). The text lines of a cue are joined with a space; styling (<i>, <b>, <font ...>) and {...} override blocks are dropped, and a position after the end time is ignored. The number above a cue is not needed, a . is read for a , in a time, and cues out of order are put in order. There are no words in a SubRip file, so there is no word fill: the whole line is emphasised as it is sung. The encodings are the LRC reader's: UTF-8 with or without a byte-order mark, or UTF-16 with one.

docs.title: Advanced SubStation Alpha
docs.text:
A .ass script is read as lyrics too, which is what subtitle-karaoke tools write, and its karaoke tags are word times:

[Events]
Format: Layer, Start, End, Style, Name, MarginL, MarginR, MarginV, Effect, Text
Dialogue: 0,0:00:12.00,0:00:15.50,Default,,0,0,0,,{\k50}Should {\k30}auld {\k80}acquaint{\k20}ance

Each Dialogue: event is a line from its start to its end. Each {\k50} (and \kf, \K, \ko: the same duration, drawn differently) begins a syllable that lasts that many hundredths of a second after the one before; a syllable is a word of the line, so the fill moves by syllable, as the script's own sweep does. Everything else is dropped: the other override tags ({\an8}, {\pos(...)}), the styles' fonts, colours and positions, and any event that draws ({\p1}) or is a Comment:. \N is a space. The columns are the script's own Format: line, with the v4+ order where it has none, and an event with no karaoke tags is a line with no words.

Two columns are read for what they say and not for how they look:

  • Who sings. Where exactly two different actors (the Name column) are named on the sung lines, the ones with karaoke tags, they are the two singers, the one who appears first being the first vocal, and their names are the file's. Failing that, where exactly two different styles are used on the sung lines, those are the two singers; a style's name is its author's own label, so it is not shown as a name. One, three or none marks nobody, because it is not clear who is who. Hearth's duet view then tells each line's singer, as it does for a V1: or V2: marker in an .lrc.
  • Which line at one time. A line written on two layers, an outline under a fill, is one line. Where lines in different styles share a start and an end, a line that is not sung and is in a style of its own (a translation, a romanisation) is dropped beside the sung one, and where none is sung the style that is commonest in the file is the one read. Lines of one style at one time are all read, and a line that ends at another time than the sung one is a line of its own.
  • A script made with Aegisub's karaoke templater. The templater keeps the timed karaoke it was given as a Comment: event with the Effect karaoke, and writes the effects it makes from it as Dialogue: events with the Effect fx, one for each syllable or decoration. Read as they stand, the effects would be the lyrics and the real lines would be skipped as comments. So where a script has a line whose Effect has karaoke in it, that line is read as sung, comment or not, and the fx lines are not read. The templater's own definitions (a comment whose Effect begins template, code or mixin) are never read. A script with no such line reads as it did.

docs.title: MIDI karaoke
docs.text:
A .kar file (a Standard MIDI File whose syllables are meta events) is read for its words, and only its words: the music in it is not played or read. What is taken:

  • the words from the track called Words, where there is one, else from the file's Lyric events, else from its Text events;
  • the title and the artist from the first and second @T lines; the other @ lines (@K, @L, @I, @V) are not words;
  • a / begins a new line, and a backslash a new verse (a line too, here), and so does a line end in the text;
  • every syllable is a word of the line with its own start, from its tick through the file's tempo map (a tempo change on any track moves every later tick), so the fill moves by syllable. A syllable that begins with a space is the start of the next word: the space is joined to the one before it. A line ends where the next begins;
  • a file whose time is counted in SMPTE frames (a frame rate and the ticks in a frame, where the other files count ticks in a quarter note) has a tick of a fixed length, and its tempo events mean nothing: 24, 25, 29.97 and 30 frames a second are the four rates the format defines, and all four are read.

A file with no words, that is cut short, or that counts SMPTE frames at some other rate says so. A MIDI file carries no word of its encoding, and what is read is UTF-8 unless the program is told the page: Latin-1 and the other code pages are not guessed at, so a Western karaoke file with accented letters saved in Latin-1 (and Hebrew in Windows-1255) is refused with the reason, as an LRC file in a code page is, until forge encode ... lyrics=<file> lyrics-encoding=<page> says which page it is in (lyrics-encoding=). Plain ASCII is UTF-8, and most are. Only the title, the artist and the words are checked (and, when a page is named, read in it): the other @ lines are not shown, so a copyright or key line in a code page does not refuse a file whose words are fine.

docs.title: What is shown
docs.text:
• In a word-timed file, a word that has been sung is in the accent colour, a word not yet sung is muted, and the word being sung is underlined and fills in the accent from left to right as it is sung.
  • In a file that times lines but not words, the whole line is emphasised as it is sung. No word times are invented for it.
  • A file with no times at all is shown whole and is not followed.
  • With no file, the page says which name it looks for.

The words follow the position of what is heard: the output device's own clock less its path's delay, so they stay with the sound on a Bluetooth speaker or a receiver with a long path.

They are on the Karaoke page, full screen (the singer view), and on the Play page: an item with lyrics, or a CD+G picture, gets a Lyrics card there beside the queue (in a window 1,580 pixels wide or more) or at the top of the monitor column (in a narrower one). An item with none gets no card, so the Play page is as it was for every other stream.

The Play page at its default size, 1.8 s into the example. hearth --smoke-shot play.png --page play --open examples/karaoke/auld-lang-syne/auld-lang-syne.ac3 --seek 1800.

docs.title: A CD+G disc
docs.text:
A .cdg file with the same name is the picture of a karaoke disc that was ripped on its own, the other half of an "MP3+G" pair: Song.mp3 and Song.cdg. When there is no lyrics file, Hearth shows that picture where the words would be, with the proportions of the disc's 300 by 216 and as large as fits (in whole steps, so the small type stays crisp), drawn against the position of what is heard and moved by the lyric delay as the words are.

The words of a disc are part of the picture. Nothing is read from it as text, so there is no fill, no line to follow and nothing to translate or copy, and the page says so.

When a lyrics file is beside the stream too, the words are shown, since they are what a word-by-word fill and the delay can follow, and a Show choice (Words or Picture) appears in the Lyrics card, and on the bar of the full-screen singer view, to show the disc instead. The choice is for this run of Hearth: it is not kept for the song, it holds from one song to the next while Hearth is open, and a song with only a lyrics file or only a disc is not changed by it. Choosing the picture takes nothing from the lyrics: the file is still loaded, so the timing window, the duet cues and the lyrics a board is sent are as they were. A .cdg that cannot be read beside a lyrics file is not shown and not reported: the words are.

What is drawn is what the disc's own player draws: the screen preset and the border preset, the tile blocks and their XOR form, the scrolls by a tile (the preset form fills the gap, the copy form brings back what left), the smooth scrolling offsets within a tile (the picture is shown up to 5 pixels left and 11 up of where its memory has it, which is how a disc scrolls a line a pixel at a time), the 12-bit colour table of 16 colours, and the transparent colour (drawn as the backdrop, which is black: there is no video here for it to show). A packet that is not CD+G is skipped and keeps its place in time, and a file that is not a whole number of 24-byte packets, or has no CD+G packet in it, is refused with the reason (playback is not affected). The packets are not checked for parity: a rip has already been through the drive's error correction.

docs.title: Keeping the words in sync
docs.text: Settings, Playback, Lyric delay moves the words later (positive) or sooner (negative) by up to a second in steps of 10 ms, on top of the file's own [offset:]. It is kept across starts. A file's times are rarely right to the frame against a particular output.

docs.title: Timing a file by hand
docs.text:
Time the lyrics… on the Karaoke page's Lyrics card opens a window that gives a file its times as the song plays: Space as each line starts, then as each word starts, with your reaction time taken off each press. A file that already has times opens with them, so the window is also where one wrong line or word is put right: choose it, then stamp it again or move it 10 ms at a time. Save writes the .lrc beside the song and keeps the file that was there once, as .lrc.bak. Timing the lyrics has every step.

The example's own file in the timing window, 5.2 s in: every line has a time already, and its words are drawn solid because the file gives their times. hearth --smoke-shot timing.png --page timing --setting "microphone/takesFolder=C:/Users/you/Documents/Hearth takes" --open examples/karaoke/auld-lang-syne/auld-lang-syne.ac3 --seek 5200.

docs.title: The singer view
docs.text:
F11, or Full screen on the Karaoke page's lyrics or the Play page's, opens the words alone, large, on a dark screen. Esc leaves it, and Space pauses.

The example 5.2 s in, with the duet queued behind it. hearth --smoke-shot singer.png --page singer --open examples/karaoke/auld-lang-syne/auld-lang-syne.ac3 --open examples/karaoke/leave-her-johnny/leave-her-johnny.ac3 --seek 5200: a capture draws the view in the window, where F11 gives it the whole screen.

A position bar, Previous, Play/Pause, Next, Queue and the Vocals chooser stay at the bottom, so a singer can move about in the song, pause, skip, pick the next song or change which vocals play without leaving. Choosing a vocal there chooses the capable reproduction with it.

Moving about. Press the position bar, or drag along it: the words and the clock show the place the bar is held at, and the song moves there when you let go, whether it was playing or paused. Left and Right move it five seconds either way, and stop at the ends.

The queue. The strip at the top names the song that comes next. Queue, or Q, opens the queue beside the words: the song that is playing is marked, and pressing another plays it from its start. Q or the button closes it again.

docs.title: In another player, in Crucible
docs.text: Crucible reads the same .lrc file and shows the line being sung on its Room page, against whichever application it is given the file for: a player with no words of its own, or a browser. A player that publishes where it is in the song to the system's media controls is followed from that, and one that does not is followed from a press of Start, which is how Hearth is followed there. The room has a picture of it and the details.

docs.title: Sing into a microphone
docs.text:
The Karaoke page has a Microphone card. It shows you how close your pitch is to the tune while you sing, and it can keep a take of your voice. It records nothing unless you press Record a take, and nothing leaves your computer.

  • It is off until you turn it on. Choosing an input does not open it, and neither does having used it last time. It closes when you turn it off, when you leave the page, and when the item ends or is changed. While it is on the card shows Microphone on, and the operating system shows its own sign as well.
  • Choose the input from the list, or take the computer's default. Refresh looks again after you plug one in.
  • Say whether you are wearing headphones. Through open speakers the microphone hears the backing as well as you, and a pitch score reads as nearly perfect for no singing at all, so the score is shown only when you have said you are wearing headphones.
  • The level shows what the microphone hears. Too loud means a sample reached full scale. If nothing arrives the card says the microphone may be muted or the wrong input is chosen.

docs.title: What it scores against
docs.text: The card names the part it is scoring you against. A karaoke stream carries its tune in its own channels, so the melody guide (M) is used when the stream has one. If you have taken a vocal away (Capable, with the vocals you chose), the vocal you took away is the one you are replacing, and that is the one used.
