A stream with no clear tune in the part, a stream that is not karaoke, and the other formats, have no melody to score against, and the card says so; it still shows the pitch you are singing and how sharp or flat it is.

docs.title: What the score is
docs.text:
The share of the tune's time during which your pitch was within a semitone of it, in any octave. It hears pitch and nothing else: not the words, not the timing, not the feeling. A singer on pitch and out of time with the words scores well on it. The card also says when you are consistently behind or ahead of the tune, which is usually a delay in the microphone and not in you.

Two things on the card change what "within" means, and the card says when either is in use:

  • How close counts is a semitone unless you choose otherwise: close is half a semitone (50 cents), and loose is a whole tone (200 cents). It is kept, and it applies to the marks and the summary as well as the score so far.
  • Score against my key is for singing a whole song a little sharp or flat of the tune: your own key is taken from your first sung notes (it needs about twenty of them) and allowed for, so that you are judged on the shape of your melody. The card says how far you are from the tune's key while it is in use, and the summary says it was. It is off every time Hearth starts, because a score that has allowed for your key is not the same score.

docs.title: What you see while you sing
docs.text:
• The pitch ribbon, under the pitch line on the card and under the words in the singer view (F11): the tune as a ribbon of notes moving past a mark for now, and your voice as a line over it. Where your voice is within the tolerance of the tune the line is thick and solid; where it is not it is thin and dashed, so the difference does not depend on colour. A voice an octave away is drawn on the tune's octave, as it is scored, so the line is where the notes are. When you are not voiced the ribbon says Listening… and draws no line.
  • A mark under each line you have sung: three dots and a percentage, in the lyrics on the page and in the singer view. Three dots is 75 % or more, two is 45 % or more, one is less. Where the levels fall is presentation and not measurement: the percentage is the figure. A line the tune has no notes in has no mark, which is not a score of zero. A line you were not voiced for (under a fifth of its notes' time) says not sung in words and carries no number, since that is not the same as singing it badly. Without your headphones answer there are no marks at all.
  • A summary on the card when it ends: Last performance gives the pitch score, how much of the tune's time you were voiced for, how sharp or flat you were on average and whether you were behind or ahead, and what it was compared with: the part, the tolerance, octaves ignored, and that lines with no notes were not scored. It stays until you turn the microphone on again or choose another song. It is shown there and kept nowhere: nothing is ranked, named or sent.

The singer view 14.9 s into the example, with the performance going on: the marks under the lines already sung, and the ribbon with the voice on the tune. hearth --smoke-shot singing.png --page singer --open examples/karaoke/auld-lang-syne/auld-lang-syne.ac3 --sing examples/karaoke/auld-lang-syne/parts/vocal-1-lead.wav --seek 14900 (Hearth's command line). There is no singer: the example's own lead vocal is the microphone, sung along to the song as the song is heard, and the song goes to an output that plays to nothing, so the picture is taken with no microphone opened and no sound made.

A song you sang only part of scores low as a whole, because the score is over all of the tune's time. The marks say which lines were the ones.

docs.title: The delay
docs.text: A microphone's sound reaches the program a little after it was sung, and some take a tenth of a second or more (a webcam's microphone measured about 130 ms through the whole path, in the Windows shared mode that Hearth uses). The Microphone delay slider is how long, and Move your timing is for the rest: raise the delay if you are told you are behind the tune and are not.

docs.title: A take
docs.text:
With the microphone on, Record a take keeps your voice. The card shows Recording and how long it has run, which is a second sign beside Microphone on, since having the microphone on is not recording. Stop recording keeps it, and turning the microphone off, leaving the page or the item ending does the same.

  • It is your voice alone, not the backing: the microphone's own sound mixed to one channel, at the microphone's rate, as a lossless FLAC file at 24 bits. It can be placed against any copy of the backing and re-mixed. Through open speakers the backing is in it too, which is the other reason to wear headphones.
  • A small file beside it, Song - 2026-10-12 211500.take.json, says which item it was, where in the item its first sample was sung (taken from where the song was when the sound reached the microphone, less the microphone's delay, plus the timing you moved), and the alignment in force, so that any editor can place it and you can move it if you disagree.
  • Where it goes is shown on the card and changed with Choose…: your documents, in a folder called "Hearth takes", unless you chose another. The folder is not made until the first take. Takes are never put beside the song file.
  • The last take is offered with Show in folder and Delete this take, which removes the file and its description.
  • Your takes lists what is in the folder, newest first: the five newest, and how many more there are. Each has Delete, which asks again (Delete for good, or Keep) before it removes the file and its description, because a take cannot be got back. Only takes Hearth made are listed: a file with no description beside it is not one, and is never offered for removal.

docs.title: Make a karaoke stream with your voice in it
docs.text:
A take is a vocal part, and the Forge's Karaoke flow takes any mono file as Vocal 1 or Vocal 2. A take is a recording of one person at one time, so four things need handling first:

  • It is FLAC, and the Forge reads WAV. Convert it with any tool that reads FLAC; the lines below use ffmpeg.
  • It is at the microphone's rate, often 44.1 kHz. The Forge GUI resamples a part to the backing's rate and says so; forge encode refuses a source at another rate, so convert it.
  • It starts partway into the song. item_start_ms in the .take.json is where, in milliseconds (12340 is 12.34 s), with the microphone's delay and any timing you moved already taken off. null means the take could not be placed, and you place it by ear.
  • It is shorter than the song. The Forge holds a part's last sample past the part's end, which is not silence: end the take on silence and as long as the backing. The command below does.

In the Forge GUI, give the backing and the melody guide as their parts, the take converted to WAV as Vocal 1, set its Start offset to item_start_ms divided by 1000, and save.

From the command line, from a stream you sang to (a 3/2 stream with a melody guide and two vocals: forge probe says the layout) and a take:

forge decode song.ac3 parts.wav
ffmpeg -i "Song - 2026-10-12 211500.flac" -af "adelay=12340,apad=whole_dur=213.5" -ar 48000 -c:a pcm_s24le take.wav
forge encode parts.wav mine.ac3 320 L,C,R,Cs src=take.wav map=0.0:L,0.1:R,0.2:C,0.3:none,0.4:none,1.0:Cs bsmod=voiceover

adelay is in milliseconds (the take's item_start_ms) and apad=whole_dur is the song's length in seconds (forge probe shows it as the duration); together they make the take as long as the backing, silent before and after it. -ar is the backing's rate. In forge encode, parts.wav is source 0: its channels 0, 1 and 2 are L, R and the melody guide, and channels 3 and 4, the stream's own vocals, go to none. The take is source 1 and takes the surround, which one vocal makes a 3/1 stream with (L,C,R,Cs, 320 kbit/s). A stream with one vocal has no channel 4, so leave 0.4:none out.

This decodes the stream and encodes it again, which is a second generation of AC-3 for the backing. If you still have the files it was made from, give those to the Karaoke flow instead. A one-click "save my performance as a karaoke stream" in Hearth is not built: the plan holds it until this has been tried (D12). A take made through open speakers has the backing in it as well as your voice, and is a recording of somebody else's work: keep it for yourself.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It does not play your voice back to you. A microphone through the operating system's own audio path adds a tenth of a second on common equipment, which is too late to sing along with; use your headset's own monitoring if it has one.
  • It does not send your voice to other speakers or other devices.
  • It cannot tell a singer from a loud speaker, which is why the headphones answer matters.

docs.title: Make one in the Forge GUI
docs.text:
Choose Karaoke in the Controls switch. Four steps build the stream from the recordings it is made of. The pictures are of the example's project, opened with Project… in the title strip.

1 · Parts. Give each part its own file: a stereo backing, and optionally a mono melody guide, Vocal 1, Vocal 2 and an LFE. Or give one multichannel file whose WAV speakers are already named. The page shows the coding mode the parts make, why, and what is wrong with anything that cannot be used.

forge-gui --smoke-shot parts.png project=examples/karaoke/auld-lang-syne/auld-lang-syne.forgeproj karaokeStep=parts height=1100

2 · Levels. The centre level (the melody guide in a stereo fold) and the surround level (the vocals), which an aware decoder applies.

forge-gui --smoke-shot levels.png project=examples/karaoke/auld-lang-syne/auld-lang-syne.forgeproj karaokeStep=levels

3 · Hear. The stream is encoded and played back the way a karaoke player decodes it: as coded, aware, or capable with the vocals you choose and a level for each part. It plays the encoded stream, not your source files.

forge-gui --smoke-shot hear.png project=examples/karaoke/auld-lang-syne/auld-lang-syne.forgeproj karaokeStep=hear: the capture waits for the stream to be built, and plays nothing.

4 · Save. The format (AC-3, the default, or E-AC-3), the file type (the raw stream, or Matroska, MP4 or MPEG-TS), the bit rate, the lyrics file that goes beside the stream, the equivalent forge encode (or forge eac3-encode) command, and the encode.

forge-gui --smoke-shot save.png project=examples/karaoke/auld-lang-syne/auld-lang-syne.forgeproj karaokeStep=save

Each coded channel is written into the same draft the other tiers edit, so switching to Expert afterwards shows the same bed, bsmod and assignments. The Forge GUI guide has the details of each step and of what a part may be: Forge GUI, Karaoke.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
Encode: a stereo backing and a melody guide and two vocals as five coded channels, with bsmod set to 7 (the token is voiceover, which at a layout above 1/0 is the karaoke main service). The sources are mapped to bed positions with src= and map=:

forge encode backing.wav out.ac3 384 L,C,R,Ls,Rs src=melody.wav src=lead.wav src=harmony.wav \
      map=0.0:L,0.1:R,1.0:C,2.0:Ls,3.0:Rs bsmod=voiceover

A single multichannel WAV whose speakers are named needs no map=.

E-AC-3 takes the same sources, mapping and bsmod. forge eac3-encode has its coding tools positional (none here) before the layout, and writes the stream's Lo/Ro mixing group, which is where a decoder reads the levels of the reproduction:

forge eac3-encode backing.wav out.ec3 384 none L,C,R,Ls,Rs src=melody.wav src=lead.wav src=harmony.wav \
      map=0.0:L,0.1:R,1.0:C,2.0:Ls,3.0:Rs bsmod=voiceover

Probe:

$ forge probe out.ac3
...
bsmod           7 (karaoke)
layout          3/2 (acmod 7, lfeon 0)
renders         5 channel(s): L C R Ls Rs

Decode, as an aware decoder (karaoke) or a capable one with a choice of vocals (karaoke=none, karaoke=v1, karaoke=v2 or karaoke=v1+v2), to L, C and R:

forge decode out.ac3 aware.wav karaoke
forge decode out.ac3 melody-and-v1.wav karaoke=v1

channels=2 or channels=1 gives the 2/0 or 1/0 reproduction. downmix=ltrt is refused with karaoke, as Annex C defines no Lt/Rt reproduction. A stream that is not karaoke is decoded as coded, and the report says so. An E-AC-3 karaoke stream decodes the same way (forge decode out.ec3 aware.wav karaoke), and the report says the reproduction is applied to E-AC-3 as Dolby's decoder does. The library form is OutputConfig::karaoke and OutputConfig::karaoke_vocals; see Decoding.

forge monitor takes the same choice and plays the reproduction on the output:

forge monitor out.ac3 karaoke=none      # L, C, R: the backing and the melody, for singing along
forge monitor out.ac3 karaoke=v1+v2     # V1 left, V2 right

The capable decoder's levels are karaoke-melody=<dB>, karaoke-v1=<dB> and karaoke-v2=<dB> on both commands: each part against Table C.2.3, 0 dB the table, up to 12 dB louder and -24 or off at the bottom, the span and the defaults of Hearth's sliders.

forge decode out.ac3 sing.wav karaoke=none karaoke-melody=-6
forge monitor out.ac3 karaoke=v1 karaoke-v1=-12 karaoke-melody=3

They move nothing under the aware reproduction, so a level without a choice of vocals (karaoke=none, v1, v2 or v1+v2) is refused.

On an output narrower than the stream, which monitor folds to unasked, the 2/0 reproduction plays. forge play applies the choice where it decodes (its PCM fallback), and forge spdif and forge play's bitstream legs hand the coded stream on: they accept karaoke and say it is not applied, since a receiver reproduces the stream. AC-4 is ignored with a warning by all of them, and forge spatial ignores the choice with its own: it places an E-AC-3 stream's objects and has no karaoke bed.

docs.title: From a program
docs.text:
The reproduction and the lyric reader are in the libraries, so a program of your own can use them:

You are in The reproduction The lyrics C or C++ through the C API iclforge_decoder_create_with_karaoke(), C API iclforge_lyrics_parse() and its cursor, C API Python DecoderConfig(karaoke=...), Python iclforge.lyrics Rust Decoder::with_karaoke, Rust iclforge::lyrics::Lyrics A browser or Node (WebAssembly) FoldOptions.karaoke, the npm package parseLyrics in the demo's module, which the decode demo's Words panel uses C++ OutputConfig::karaoke and its levels, Decoding iclforge::lyrics, libs/lyrics

All of them take the same choices (as coded, aware or capable; the vocals; the three part levels in dB over -24 to +12, where the bottom is off) and the same bytes of a lyrics file, and give the same samples and the same lines as forge decode and Hearth do.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• Aligning words to the sound. Hearth's timing window (Timing the lyrics) takes word times from your presses, and an estimate by the letters of a word is only where a press starts from. A forced aligner is outside software, and Timing a song with a forced aligner runs one and reads its result in.
  • Reading a lyrics file in a code page, in Hearth and Crucible. UTF-8 and UTF-16 are read there; Latin-1, Windows-1255 and the other encodings are named and not guessed at. Forge reads one when it is told the page (lyrics-encoding=, or the Code page list on the Karaoke flow's Lyrics row, which shows how the page chosen reads the first lines) and writes the words beside the stream as UTF-8, which every player reads, so a file in a code page is brought in once, at the encode. A MIDI karaoke file has no way to say its encoding; naming the page is how to read it.
  • Text from a CD+G disc. Its words are pixels, so Hearth shows the picture and cannot follow the words.
  • A screen on a sink that has not been run. A board that decodes for itself is sent the lyrics and where the sound is in them, follows them on its own clock and reports the line. The P4 firmware also draws them, with the colour moving as the song does, on a 7-inch panel (An ESP32-P4 sink): drawn and measured on a board with no panel, not yet run on one, and without a microphone, scoring or recording.
  • Karaoke in AC-4. Its specification has no karaoke mode, so nothing is reproduced for it.
  • Knowing what a receiver does with E-AC-3. Annex E defines no reproduction and no TV or receiver was tried here: Dolby's reference decoder reproduces an E-AC-3 karaoke stream, and a player that does not reproduce it plays the vocals from the surrounds.
  • A microphone on a board or on Android. The microphone, the pitch score and the takes are in Hearth's desktop player and the browser demo (Sing into a microphone). The board's part of the plan is not built.

docs.title: How it is checked
docs.text: Two things stand behind it. The reproduction is held to the annex's own tables, transcribed independently of the code: every mode is encoded with a tone in each part and decoded under each reproduction and each choice of vocals, and the tones on each output are what the table says. And Dolby's reference decoder reproduces karaoke for AC-3 and for E-AC-3, which is the one outside decoder to compare with: tools/checks/verify_karaoke_oracle.py encodes a tone-per-channel stream both ways, decodes it with forge decode and with the Reference Player's dlbac3dec, and compares what each output channel carries as ratios. The player is licensed, so the script runs locally and not in CI, and its measured ratios are constants in the library's tests (libs/ac3/tests/decoder/test_eac3_karaoke.cpp). There is still no karaoke stream from anyone else: Dolby's encoder (DEE) cannot write bsmod 7. See Verification.

docs.title: Timing a song with a forced aligner
docs.text:
Hearth's timing window makes a file's word times from your key presses. A forced aligner makes them from the sound: it takes a recording and the words that are sung in it, and returns a start and an end for each word. This page is a recipe for using one outside iclforge, writing its answer as the enhanced .lrc file the karaoke guide describes, and bringing that file into Hearth to be checked.

iclforge neither ships nor depends on an aligner. The repository holds no model and no script that imports one; the script below is on this page and nowhere in the tree.

What was run, and what was not

The recipe was run on 2026-10-12 on Windows 11 with Python 3.13.14, on the CPU, with WhisperX 3.8.6 (alignment) and Demucs 4.1.0 (vocal separation), on one recording. Every number in What one run produced is from that run. The other tools in the table are described from their own README or package page as read on the same day, and none of them was installed. macOS and Linux were not tried. The result was not listened to: there is no reference timing for the recording, so nothing here says the times are right.

docs.title: What an aligner does, and what it cannot tell you
docs.text:
• It assumes the words are what is sung, in the order given. It spreads them over the audio and returns times whatever the audio holds. A verse sung differently, or a line missing from the text, gets times that look like any other.
  • The models are trained on speech. Singing stretches vowels across notes and holds words, and a music bed under the voice is something the model was not trained to ignore. Both are where an aligner is least reliable.
  • A score is the model's confidence, not the time's accuracy. In the run below, the first word of the run on the whole song scores 0.75 and starts 2.9 seconds before the vocal stem's first word, in a stretch where the stem is quiet.
  • The only check is listening. That is what Hearth's timing window is for.

docs.title: Where the vocal comes from
docs.text:
An aligner does best on the voice alone. Where the voice comes from depends on what you have:

You have What to do A recording of the whole song Separate the vocal with Demucs (step 2) The parts of a karaoke stream you are making in the Forge GUI Give the aligner the Vocal 1 file as it is: there is no bed to remove A karaoke stream, and not its parts Decode the stream as coded and take the V1 channel (below)

For a 3/2 stream (a backing, a melody guide and two vocals), forge decode with no karaoke argument writes five channels in WAV order, L R C Ls Rs, and V1 is the fourth:

forge decode song.ac3 parts.wav
ffmpeg -i parts.wav -af "pan=mono|c0=c3" vocal1.wav

c4 is V2. This was run on the repository's examples/karaoke/auld-lang-syne/auld-lang-syne.ac3, and the levels of the channels it wrote matched what forge decode prints for the centre and the left surround. The other coding modes name their channels as the Forge GUI guide lists (L R S, L R C S, L R Ls Rs) and were not run. The example's vocals are generated tones and not singing, so it was not aligned.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
Tool Licence Install Languages What it writes Run here WhisperX 3.8.6 Code BSD-2-Clause. The alignment model is a separate file with its own licence; the English one is wav2vec 2.0 base, MIT pip; Python 3.10 to 3.13 (3.14 is excluded); ffmpeg on the path; a GPU wants CUDA 12.8 41 with a default model in this version: English, French, German, Spanish and Italian from torchaudio, and 36 from Hugging Face, Hebrew among them and Yiddish not. Any wav2vec 2.0 CTC model by name Python lists of words with a start, an end and a score Yes Demucs 4.1.0 Code MIT. The weights are on Hugging Face and the model page states no licence pip; Python 3.10 or later Not language-bound vocals.wav and no_vocals.wav (or four stems) Yes syncalong 2.0.1 MIT pip install "syncalong[whisper]", and the vocal-separation extra for Demucs Whisper's Line-level .lrc only: its documentation describes [mm:ss.xx] per line and no word tags No Montreal Forced Aligner 3.4.3 MIT; pretrained models separately conda-forge (Miniforge); acoustic models come from mfa model download acoustic <name>, and a pronunciation dictionary is needed too Many; its models are trained on speech corpora Not checked No ctc-forced-aligner Code BSD-2-Clause; the default model is CC-BY-NC 4.0 (not for commercial use) pip from GitHub More than 1,100 (its README's count), the text romanised JSON of words with start and end No stable-ts MIT; the repository was archived on 2026-05-30 pip Whisper's SRT, VTT, ASS, TSV, JSON; no LRC No

Of the pages read, only syncalong's mentions music: its documentation says it turns off conditioning on the previous text to avoid repetition loops on songs with repeated choruses. WhisperX's README lists what it cannot time (words whose characters the model has no label for) and overlapping speech, and does not mention singing or music.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
python -m venv aligner
aligner\Scripts\activate
pip install whisperx==3.8.6 demucs==4.1.0

On macOS and Linux the second line is source aligner/bin/activate.

What happened on the machine used: pip took about 35 minutes, most of it resolving. WhisperX pins huggingface-hub below 1.0, and pip backtracked through the 5.x releases of transformers before settling on 4.57.6; adding transformers<5 to the command was not tried. The environment came to 2.2 GB. PyPI's torch for Windows is the CPU build (2.8.0); the GPU build comes from PyTorch's own index and was not used.

The first run of each tool downloads its data, so a machine with no network cannot run it:

What Size From By wav2vec 2.0 base, fine-tuned on 960 hours of LibriSpeech (wav2vec2_fairseq_base_ls960_asr_ls960.pth) 360 MB download.pytorch.org WhisperX, through torchaudio punkt_tab, NLTK's sentence-splitter data 4.3 MB raw.githubusercontent.com (the nltk_data repository) WhisperX, on its first align htdemucs, the separation weights (955717e8.safetensors) 80 MB huggingface.co, repository adefossez/HTDemucs Demucs

docs.title: 2. Separate the vocal
docs.text:
Skip this if you already have the voice alone. Demucs was given a 44.1 kHz stereo WAV:

ffmpeg -i song.ogg -ar 44100 -ac 2 song.wav
python -m demucs.separate --two-stems=vocals -d cpu -o separated song.wav

It writes separated/htdemucs/song/vocals.wav and no_vocals.wav. On the CPU of the machine used (a 16-core Ryzen 9 shared with other jobs) it took 109 seconds for 87.5 seconds of audio, with the weights' download in that.

docs.title: 3. The words
docs.text: A UTF-8 text file, one lyric line to a line. Blank lines are ignored, so a blank line between verses is fine. The words are split on spaces and kept exactly as written, punctuation included.

docs.title: 4. Align, and write the .lrc
docs.text:
Save this as align_lyrics.py:

"""Align a plain lyrics file to a vocal recording and write an enhanced LRC file.

    python align_lyrics.py vocals.wav lyrics.txt song.lrc [words.json] [language]

vocals.wav  the singing, with as little else in it as possible
lyrics.txt  the words, one lyric line to a line (blank lines are ignored)
song.lrc    what is written: [mm:ss.xx]<mm:ss.xx>word <mm:ss.xx>word ...<mm:ss.xx>
words.json  optional: every word with the start, end and score the aligner gave it
language    a two-letter code, "en" when omitted
"""
import json
import sys

import whisperx

SAMPLE_RATE = 16000  # what whisperx.load_audio returns


def stamp(seconds):
    hundredths = round(seconds * 100)
    return f"{hundredths // 6000:02d}:{hundredths // 100 % 60:02d}.{hundredths % 100:02d}"


def main():
    args = sys.argv[1:]
    if len(args) < 3:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    audio_path, text_path, lrc_path = args[:3]
    words_path = args[3] if len(args) > 3 and args[3].endswith(".json") else None
    language = args[-1] if len(args) > 3 and not args[-1].endswith(".json") else "en"

    with open(text_path, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
        lines = [line.split() for line in f if line.strip()]
    tokens = [word for line in lines for word in line]

    audio = whisperx.load_audio(audio_path)
    seconds = len(audio) / SAMPLE_RATE
    model, metadata = whisperx.load_align_model(language_code=language, device="cpu")
    # One segment holding the whole text over the whole recording: the aligner finds the lines.
    result = whisperx.align(
        [{"text": " ".join(tokens), "start": 0.0, "end": seconds}],
        model, metadata, audio, "cpu",
    )
    # The aligner splits the text into sentences itself, so the words come back as one flat list.
    aligned = result["word_segments"]
    if len(aligned) != len(tokens):
        sys.exit(f"{len(tokens)} words in the lyrics, {len(aligned)} back from the aligner")

    missing = [tokens[i] for i, w in enumerate(aligned) if "start" not in w or "end" not in w]
    if missing:
        sys.exit("the aligner gave no time to: " + ", ".join(missing))
    starts = [w["start"] for w in aligned]
    ends = [w["end"] for w in aligned]

    out = []
    at = 0
    for line in lines:
        first, last = at, at + len(line) - 1
        text = " ".join(f"<{stamp(starts[i])}>{tokens[i]}" for i in range(first, last + 1))
        out.append(f"[{stamp(starts[first])}]{text}<{stamp(ends[last])}>")
        at = last + 1
    with open(lrc_path, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as f:
        f.write("\n".join(out) + "\n")

    if words_path:
        rows = [
            {"word": tokens[i], "start": starts[i], "end": ends[i], "score": aligned[i].get("score")}
            for i in range(len(tokens))
        ]
        with open(words_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            json.dump(rows, f, indent=1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Then:

python align_lyrics.py separated/htdemucs/song/vocals.wav lyrics.txt song.lrc words.json

Each line of the .lrc is the line's first word's time, then a <mm:ss.xx> tag before each word, and a last tag with no text after it that ends the line's last word, which is what an enhanced .lrc uses for the end of a line. The script gives the whole text to the aligner as one segment, so the aligner finds where the lines fall; it does not need line times to begin with.

docs.title: 5. Open it in Hearth
docs.text:
Put the file beside the stream under the stream's name (song.ac3 and song.lrc), open the stream and choose the Karaoke page. The Lyrics card says song.lrc, word-timed, and the words are filled as they are sung.

Time the lyrics... then opens the window with the aligner's word times as they are, drawn as set and not as guesses. It corrects them a line at a time or a word at a time:

  • A line. Choose it to play from it, listen, and press Stamp again at the moment its first word starts, or move it with -10 ms and +10 ms. The line's words move with it.
  • A word. Click the word that is wrong. It is outlined, the item is cued 1.5 s before it, and the window says which word it is and when it starts. Play, and press Space as the word starts (in the Words pass the next Space is for that word, once, with the reaction time taken off), or press Stamp again at that moment, or move it with -10 ms and +10 ms. Nothing else moves: its line and the line's other words keep their times. A word stays between its neighbours, so to put one past the next word, move the next word first. Clicking the line lets the word go, and the buttons are the line's again.
  • The word pass skips a word that already has a time, which is every word of this file, so with no word chosen Space has nothing to press there. Pressing all the words in the window means starting without the aligner's times: move the .lrc away and reopen the stream, and the window asks for a text file. A word can also be corrected by editing its <mm:ss.xx> tag in the file, which is text.
  • Save writes the word starts and keeps the first file as song.lrc.bak. It does not write the tag after a line's last word, so after a save that word runs to the next line.

The window's steps are in Timing the lyrics.

docs.title: What one run produced
docs.text:
The recording. Over The River And Through The Wood, arranged and performed by Grant Raymond Barrett (Wikimedia Commons user Grantyny), February 2006, licensed CC BY 3.0. The poem is Lydia Maria Child's, 1845. It is File:Over The River And Through The Wood.ogg on Wikimedia Commons: Vorbis, 44.1 kHz, 87.5 s, 1,186,146 bytes, SHA-1 ddb6810814ec00ee7bdbb43c2e10f431a12b66fe. The words are the ones on that file's description page: 9 stanzas, 43 lines, 210 words. The recording is not in this repository.

The same lyrics, aligned twice: on the Demucs vocal stem, and on the song as released with its bed in it. The times below are from the aligner's own words file.

On the vocal stem On the song as released First word starts, last word ends 9.58 s, 85.08 s 6.66 s, 82.94 s Score, median (10th percentile) 0.85 (0.65) 0.47 (0.27) Words scoring under 0.30 2 26 A word's length, shortest, median, longest 40 ms, 180 ms, 1,520 ms 60 ms, 200 ms, 2,361 ms Words in a stretch where the stem is more than 30 dB under its median 0 1 (the first word) Time, on the CPU 98 s, with the model and data downloads 40 s

The times are those of a machine that was running other jobs. The stem run repeated afterwards, with nothing left to download, took 141 s and wrote a byte-identical file, so the output is repeatable and the time is not a measure of anything.

The first lines of the file written from the stem:

[00:09.58]<00:09.58>Over <00:09.80>the <00:09.96>river, <00:10.36>and <00:10.50>through <00:10.94>the <00:11.10>wood,<00:11.34>
[00:11.42]<00:11.42>To <00:11.60>grandfather's <00:12.12>house <00:12.52>we <00:12.70>go;<00:13.08>
[00:13.62]<00:13.62>The <00:13.78>horse <00:14.02>knows <00:14.20>the <00:14.34>way<00:14.66>

Where the two runs disagree. Median difference of a word's start is 20 ms and the 90th percentile is 320 ms; 37 words differ by more than 100 ms and 29 by more than 250 ms, in ten stretches of one to six words, 15 earlier on the song and 14 later. The largest are the first word, which the run on the song put 2.92 s early, in a part where the vocal stem is quiet (its score there is 0.75), and the last word, 1.12 s early.

Where the stem run is least sure. Its two lowest scores are in "Through the white and drifted snow." the first time it comes, at 15.8 s: 0.27 for "Through" and 0.00 for "the", a word 60 ms long. The line comes again at 68 s, where "Through" scores 0.45, the fourth lowest of the song. The run on the song puts that line's words 0.4 to 0.8 s later than the stem run the first time and 0.3 to 0.5 s later the second. The four shortest words are all "a", at 40 to 50 ms. The longest are the last two words, at 1.3 and 1.5 s.

What these numbers do not show. They do not show that the stem run's times are right. They show that the aligner was more confident on the stem, that none of its words falls in a stretch where the stem is more than 30 dB under the median level of its words, and that the one word that could be checked against the stem (the first) was far out on the song. Scores are lower on the song as released because the model hears a bed it was not trained on, whether or not the times are worse. No stanza stood out in the scores as sung differently from the text; that was read from the scores and not by ear.

What Hearth read. The .lrc was read with iclforge::lyrics::read_lyrics, the reader Hearth uses, built from the repository's libs/lyrics sources: 43 lines, all word-timed, 210 words, none going backwards or of no length, and find_lyrics_file paired it with a stream of the same name. A round trip through write_lrc, which is what the window's Save calls, kept every word and its start and dropped the tag after each line's last word. The timing window itself was not opened on this file: what it does with a word-timed file is from its controller's code and the test that holds it (a file that is timed opens as given). Correcting one word of such a file is held by tst_karaoke_timing.qml, which opens a three-line enhanced .lrc of that shape (a time for each line and a tag before each word), chooses a word, and checks what a press, a stamp again and a nudge do to it and to nothing else; it runs offscreen and not on a display.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One song, one language, one model. The English model is trained on read speech. Hebrew has a default model in WhisperX 3.8.6 and Yiddish does not; neither was run.
  • A bed costs accuracy. On this song, separating first moved 29 of 210 words by a quarter of a second or more, one by nearly three seconds. Whether separation always helps was not tested. Separation can also remove or smear a vocal, and Demucs's own model page states no licence for its weights.
  • The text has to be what is sung. A repeat the singer takes and the text does not have, or the reverse, moves every word after it. Check the text against the recording before aligning.
  • A held word is one long word. A word sung across a long note takes the whole of it (1.5 s for the last word of this song), and where the voice stops is the aligner's guess.
  • The installation is large and slow to resolve, and a new release of any of its parts can change the result. The versions are the ones stated above.
  • Correction in Hearth is by ear, a line or a word at a time. The window does not re-align a stretch, so a run of wrong words is a press or a nudge for each, or a nudge of the line when the whole line is early or late. See step 5.

docs.title: Using the libraries
docs.text:
iclforge::ac3 is the C++23 codec library used by Forge, Crucible, and Hearth. It encodes and decodes AC-3 and E-AC-3, including E-AC-3 streams with Dolby Atmos objects represented through Joint Object Coding (JOC). It also provides loudness metering, level analysis, and quality measurement. It links five libraries that know no codec: iclforge::base, iclforge::dsp, iclforge::objects, iclforge::render and iclforge::containers::iec61937. AC-4 has libraries of its own beside it, which share no code with it (AC-4). So does TrueHD and MLP (TrueHD and MLP), which links iclforge::base only.

Other targets provide container writing, IAB and ADM/BW64 reading, IAMF reading and writing, object signing, platform audio, and AC-4 decoding and encoding. Build and linkage requirements differ by target. Capabilities lists supported formats and limits; Development status is the compact done / partial / not-started companion. Validation describes how output is checked.

Use this page to link the C++ library. Other interfaces are documented under the C API, Python, Rust, and WebAssembly pages. Packages are listed under Releasing.

Every library has its own header directory, src/<name>/include/iclforge/<name>/, spelled iclforge/<name>/... in an #include; the header map lists what is where. The main codec headers are under libs/ac3/include/iclforge/ac3/, and the AC-4 headers under libs/ac4/include/iclforge/ac4/, by area as AC-3's are: core/ (the table of contents), io/ (the elementary stream and the carriage), decoder/ and encoder/. The TrueHD headers are under libs/truehd/include/iclforge/truehd/, split the same way (core/, io/, decoder/, encoder/).

CMake target Purpose iclforge::ac3 AC-3 and E-AC-3 encoding and decoding, and EMDF object signing (see Object signing); links the four libraries below it iclforge::base, iclforge::dsp Bit I/O, the speaker vocabulary, the CPU probe, and the signing key with SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA-256; the FFT, the QMF bank and the sample-rate converter iclforge::objects, iclforge::render The object-audio model and the Object Audio Metadata payload; layouts, routing and the renderer iclforge::containers The codec-blind carriage, in parts: IEC 61937 burst packing and detection for AC-3, E-AC-3 and AC-4, and TrueHD's MAT (iclforge::containers::iec61937, always built); the Matroska, MP4 and MPEG-TS writers and readers (::matroska, ::mp4, ::mpegts), which carry TrueHD too; IAMF reading and writing, as OBUs, ISO-BMFF and fragments (::iamf, see IAMF) iclforge::iab SMPTE ST 2098-2 IAB reading; see IAB iclforge::adm ADM/BW64 reading and writing, and the mapping between ADM objects and the Atmos encoder or decoder; opt-in with ICLFORGE_BUILD_ADM=ON iclforge::ac4 AC-4 decoding and encoding, the sync frames, table of contents and presentations both work through, and the AC-4 content signature; see AC-4 and Signing iclforge::truehd TrueHD and MLP: the bitstream layer, a lossless decoder and a TrueHD encoder; links iclforge::base only; see TrueHD and MLP

iclforge::adm needs the root dependency manifest's adm feature (-DVCPKG_MANIFEST_FEATURES=adm) when building this repository with vcpkg, and is installed as a shared library. The packaged iclforge port has no adm feature and does not package it. The ADM and ADM bridge pages explain the dependency and linkage details.

The AC-4 library is installed and exported as iclforge::ac4_static and iclforge::ac4_shared; the tables and transforms its decoder and encoder share are inside it, with no headers of their own (AC-4 has the detail).

iclforge::base_headers (header-only) is built in-tree and not installed; iclforge::audio and iclforge::sendspin are not installed either (see the end of this page).

In-tree (this repo add_subdirectory'd into a larger build, or as a git submodule):

target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE iclforge::ac3)

iclforge::ac3 resolves to whichever of the static or shared build the enclosing project's BUILD_SHARED_LIBS asks for.

Installed package, from an iclforge-dev-* package (see docs/releasing.md) or a local cmake --install:

find_package(iclforge REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE iclforge::ac3_static)   # or iclforge::ac3_shared

An installed package has no ambient BUILD_SHARED_LIBS default to resolve against, so it exports both variants explicitly rather than a bare iclforge::ac3 — pick the one you want. The package has nothing for a consumer to find: no find_dependency() calls, no system or third-party library to resolve, static or shared. The codec is not dependency-free, though — iclforge::ac3 and iclforge::containers::mp4 use {fmt} for formatting (cmake/Fmt.cmake, and this repo's own vcpkg.json; it stands in for <format>, which NDK r26's libc++ did not implement). Both compile a private copy of it into their own object files (FMT_HEADER_ONLY, in its own inline namespace fmt::ac3_private, through the iclforge::fmt_private target wrapped in $<BUILD_INTERFACE:...>) and link no {fmt} library, so the export graph names none and the archive and the shared library each hold all of {fmt} that they call. That is what leaves the installed package with nothing to declare. A consumer needs no {fmt} of its own, and one that has its own, of any version, never binds to the private copy. It matters most for the static variants. A shared library takes a linked {fmt} in at its own link step, but an archive is not linked at all: one that had linked {fmt} would leave every consumer an unresolved fmt::v12::vprint, which only the same major version of {fmt} can supply.

iclforge::objects takes in a second header-only library the same way: nlohmann/json (cmake/NlohmannJson.cmake), which tokenises an object scene file. It is linked through $<BUILD_INTERFACE:iclforge::json>, used in one source file and named by no header, so it too leaves the export graph with nothing to declare, and a consumer needs none of its own. Its type carries nlohmann's own ABI tag (json_abi_v3_12_0_dp), so a program that has the library of its own, of any version, cannot meet this copy.

iclforge::base takes in a third the same way: fast_float (cmake/FastFloat.cmake), which iclforge::base::parse_double reads decimal text with. It is linked through $<BUILD_INTERFACE:iclforge::fast_float>, used in one source file and named by no header; its functions are inline templates compiled into that object, so an archive has no undefined symbol for it and a consumer needs nothing of its own.

What a static variant does leave to the consumer's link is the C++ runtime. A CMake project links an installed static iclforge:: target with the C++ driver when it enables the CXX language, so a C program using iclforge::c_static needs project(your_project LANGUAGES C CXX); that driver supplies libm as well. With only C enabled the link goes through the C driver and stops at C++ runtime symbols such as operator new, although the exported target records that it holds C++ objects (IMPORTED_LINK_INTERFACE_LANGUAGES). A build outside CMake gets them from the .pc files (see pkg-config below), or adds them to the link line itself (-lstdc++ -lm with libstdc++, -lc++ -lm with libc++).

iclforge::adm is the exception: it PRIVATE-embeds the third-party libbw64/libadm (Apache-2.0, FetchContent'd — see ADM / BW64 reading), neither of which this project installs or exports in its own right, so the installed package only ever exports its shared variant (iclforge::adm_shared, plus the bare iclforge::adm alias — there is no _static counterpart here, unlike every other module on this page) regardless of ICLFORGE_INSTALL_BOTH_LINKAGES. A self-contained .so absorbs libbw64/libadm at its own build step; a static archive would leave a downstream consumer with unresolved symbols into a library this package doesn't ship. iclforge::adm still needs Boost at build time (see the note above) — that requirement doesn't go away just because the installed artifact is self-contained.

vcpkg. A port lives in this repo at packaging/vcpkg-port/iclforge/ and is pending submission to the curated microsoft/vcpkg registry (see docs/releasing.md) — until that lands, point vcpkg at it directly with --overlay-ports/VCPKG_OVERLAY_PORTS (works from any clone of this repo, no waiting on the upstream PR):

vcpkg install iclforge --overlay-ports=/path/to/iclforge/packaging/vcpkg-port

find_package(iclforge CONFIG REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE iclforge::ac3)

iclforge::ac3 (with the object signer), the libraries it links (base, dsp, objects, render) and iclforge::containers with its IEC 61937 part are what the port installs by default. The containers' other parts and every other library are the port's features, and none is on by default (a curated-registry port's default-features may only cover behaviors, not additional public APIs/targets/binaries, and each of these is exactly that):

Feature Targets matroska iclforge::containers's Matroska part (iclforge::containers::matroska) mp4 iclforge::containers's MP4 part (iclforge::containers::mp4) mpegts iclforge::containers's MPEG-TS part (iclforge::containers::mpegts) capi iclforge::c, the C API (see C API) ac4 iclforge::ac4 (see AC-4) iab iclforge::iab (see IAB) iamf iclforge::containers's IAMF part (iclforge::containers::iamf, see IAMF)

Opt in with vcpkg install iclforge[matroska,mp4,mpegts] for the three container writers, or any subset, such as iclforge[ac4] for AC-4 alone. iclforge::adm has no vcpkg feature — out of scope for this port, even though upstream installs and exports both (shared-only, see the note above). Once merged into microsoft/vcpkg, the same two snippets work with a plain vcpkg install iclforge — no --overlay-ports needed.

Conan. A recipe lives in this repo at packaging/conan/ and is pending submission to ConanCenter (see docs/releasing.md) — until that lands, conan create packaging/conan --version <tag> from a clone of this repo builds it straight into your local Conan cache, after which a consumer's conanfile.txt/conanfile.py requires = "iclforge/<tag>" resolves it the same way a published package would. Same scope as the vcpkg port above, with an option for each of its features: capi, ac4, iab and iamf off by default like the port's (-o "iclforge/*:ac4=True" and the like to opt in), and matroska/mp4/mpegts on by default, where the port has them off (-o "iclforge/*:matroska=False" etc. to drop one). tools/checks/check_packaging_versions.sh holds the two recipes to the same components and the same ICLFORGE_BUILD_<NAME> options. The same two find_package/target_link_libraries snippets apply: the recipe installs iclforge's own CMake package config rather than generating a second one, so a Conan consumer's CMakeLists.txt looks identical to a vcpkg or plain-installed one.

pkg-config. Every installed library also gets its own .pc file, ${libdir}/pkgconfig/iclforge-<name>.pc (iclforge-base, -dsp, -objects, -render, -containers, -ac3, -iab, -adm, -ac4 and -c), for a non-CMake consumer:

pkg-config --cflags --libs iclforge-ac3

Picks whichever linkage was actually installed (the shared name when ICLFORGE_INSTALL_BOTH_LINKAGES/BUILD_SHARED_LIBS selected it, else the _static-suffixed one — matching what is actually on disk), and chains Requires: for a library that PUBLIC- links another (iclforge-ac3 requires iclforge-base, -dsp, -objects, -render and -iec61937; iclforge-ac3 requires iclforge-ac3; iclforge-adm requires iclforge-ac3 and iclforge-adm). The prefix= line resolves relative to wherever the .pc file itself ends up (pkg-config's own ${pcfiledir}), so it works the same whether that's a real system install or an unpacked iclforge-dev-* archive.

A .pc that names a static archive lists what the archive needs in Requires.private and Libs.private, and pkg-config puts those on the link line only when asked for --static. That is the mode for an install that holds only the static libraries, the shape a vcpkg or Conan package has:

cc consumer.c $(pkg-config --static --cflags --libs iclforge-c)

iclforge-c.pc requires iclforge-ac3 privately, because libiclforge_c_static.a calls into libiclforge_ac3_static.a (and iclforge-ac4 where the C API carries AC-4). iclforge-ac3.pc, iclforge-containers.pc, iclforge-containers.pc, iclforge-containers.pc, iclforge-containers.pc, iclforge-iab.pc and iclforge-ac4.pc list the C++ runtime and libm in Libs.private. A C compiler does not link them by itself, and a C++ compiler does. The names are the ones CMake recorded for the compiler that built the archives: -lstdc++ -lm with libstdc++ and -lc++ -lm with libc++ on Linux. iclforge-ac3.pc gets them through iclforge-ac3. A .pc that names a shared library has neither field: the library records what it needs, and libiclforge_c.so holds its own copy of the codec, so it does not pull in libiclforge_ac3.so. An install with both linkages, such as the iclforge-dev-* packages, names the shared libraries, and --static does not switch to the archives, so name them yourself: -liclforge_c_static, then the _static archive of each library its Requires chain names, a library before the ones it uses (iclforge_ac3_static, iclforge_render_static, iclforge_objects_static, iclforge_dsp_static, iclforge_base_static and iclforge_containers_static; a build with AC-4 adds iclforge_ac4_static), and -lstdc++ -lm at the end.

Live audio — capture, monitor playback, IEC 61937 passthrough — is iclforge::audio (libs/audio/), a separate target forge/forge-gui link alongside iclforge::ac3 for their own live-audio commands. It is not part of the distributed package: it isn't installed, isn't exported, and find_package(iclforge) says nothing about it. A consumer wanting live capture on their own platform provides their own audio I/O and feeds the resulting PCM to the codec API below directly — iclforge::audio exists to serve this project's own CLI/GUI, not as something a third party is expected to link.

Nearly every code block in this section is an excerpt from a program in examples/ — see Example programs for the full list. What the build compiles and ctest runs is the programs, not the excerpts: an example cannot stop working silently, but an excerpt is re-synced by hand and can drift. Each page's "Full program" link is the canonical form.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
• Capabilities — what ships, with spec sections and limitations.
  • Development status — at-a-glance status across every codec and bitstream feature.
  • Application coverage — which applications expose each broad capability.
  • Example programs — every examples/ program, what it shows, and which page discusses it.
  • Encoding AC-3 — iclforge::ac3::FrameEncoder and EncoderConfig.
  • Encoding E-AC-3 — iclforge::ac3::eac3::FrameEncoder and wide layouts via iclforge::ac3::eac3::AccessUnitEncoder.
  • Decoding — scanning a stream with iclforge::ac3::io::scan and decoding it.
  • Spatial & Atmos objects — the plain-AC-3 object layer and iclforge::ac3::oba::AtmosEncoder.
  • A worked scene — station broadcast — a complete 115-second authored Atmos scene built on the object APIs.
  • Channel plans & routing — custom channel selections and multi-source assignment.
  • Metadata — loudness, DRC and downmix metadata.
  • Muxing & sinks — iclforge::containers::matroska::mux, iclforge::containers::mp4::mux, fMP4/CMAF + HLS/DASH (iclforge::containers::mp4::fragment, iclforge/containers/mp4/hls.hpp, iclforge/containers/mp4/dash.hpp), metering, the IEC 61937/passthrough/monitor sinks, and capture.
  • File I/O — reading and writing WAV.
  • IAB (SMPTE ST 2098-2) reading — iclforge::iab, a standalone Immersive Audio Bitstream reader, elementary .iab files and MXF Track Files alike (on by default).
  • ADM / BW64 reading — iclforge::adm, a standalone BW64/RF64 + Audio Definition Model parser (opt-in, -DICLFORGE_BUILD_ADM=ON).
  • ADM → Atmos bridging — iclforge::adm, mapping the parsed ADM graph onto iclforge::ac3::oba::AtmosEncoder (same opt-in flag).
  • IAMF — iclforge::containers::iamf, a standalone reader and writer: a decoded 7.1.4 programme re-wrapped as a channel-based IAMF Audio Element, object-based Audio Elements with animated positions, Opus, AAC-LC and FLAC packets carried, scalable channel layers reconstructed, ISO-BMFF, raw OBU streams and fragments (on by default).
  • AC-4 — iclforge::ac4, the decoder, the encoder and the inspector both work through: the decoder's controls, the choice of presentation and what the decoder reports; the encoder's configuration, substreams and presentations; and linking (on by default).
  • Measuring quality — iclforge::ac3::quality, the decoded-domain distortion measure and the tonality/masking model the encoder's decision search is judged on.
  • Object signing — iclforge::ac3::signing, the EMDF protection tag.
  • Header map — the headers a caller normally reaches for, and what lives in each.
  • API stability — the v1.0 freeze plan: header tiers, SemVer and deprecation policy, and what's decided versus still deliberately deferred.
  • C API — iclforge::c, a stable, minimal C-callable surface over encode/decode for bindings and embedding.
  • Rust bindings — iclforge-sys (raw, bindgen-generated) plus the safe iclforge crate, both over the C API.
  • Python bindings — the iclforge PyPI package, pybind11-direct over iclforge::ac3::FrameEncoder/FrameDecoder/Eac3Decoder/oba::AtmosEncoder, eac3::FrameEncoder/AccessUnitEncoder and, in a build from this tree, iclforge::ac4::Decoder and iclforge::ac4::Encoder.
  • WebAssembly — the iclforge-wasm-decoder package, built from this tree and not on the npm registry: a push-frame decode API, an AudioWorklet playback pipeline, and an hls.js/MSE bridge over the decoder compiled to WASM, and wrappers for the AC-4 decoder and encoder.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
These hold across the whole API.

Errors are std::expected. Nothing throws for a stream-level or configuration problem. FrameError covers encoding, DecodeError decoding, ScanError scanning, WavError file I/O, MuxError muxing. All five have a describe() returning a std::string_view. The AC-4 libraries do the same with iclforge::ac4::Error, iclforge::ac4::DecodeError and iclforge::ac4::EncodeError, which are not iclforge::ac3::DecodeError and iclforge::ac3::FrameError under other names (AC-4).

Namespaces follow the libraries. Everything is under iclforge::, and a library's public headers declare into the namespace named for it: iclforge::ac3 for the AC-3, E-AC-3 and Atmos codec, iclforge::ac4 for the AC-4 codec, and iclforge::containers::mp4, iclforge::containers::matroska, iclforge::containers::mpegts, iclforge::containers::iamf, iclforge::iab and iclforge::adm for the containers and the readers, which know nothing about AC-3, E-AC-3 or Atmos: they take frames as opaque bytes. The codec's sub-namespaces keep their names under its own: iclforge::ac3::eac3, iclforge::ac3::oba, iclforge::ac3::io, iclforge::ac3::meta, iclforge::ac3::plan, iclforge::ac3::verify, iclforge::ac3::quality and iclforge::ac3::analysis. The libraries split from it have a namespace of their own, iclforge::base, iclforge::render, iclforge::dsp and iclforge::containers::iec61937, and the objects library declares iclforge::oba and iclforge::emdf. Five names are declared both by another library under iclforge:: and by the codec under iclforge::ac3::: oba, emdf, render, internal and detail. Inside iclforge::ac3 an unqualified oba:: is the codec's, so the objects library's Position is written iclforge::objects::oba::Position there. The directory and the header root say which library a header is in, and so does the namespace; tools/checks/check_namespaces.py holds the headers to it, with three exceptions it lists as debts (BitReader and BitWriter of iclforge/base/, and dft512 of iclforge/dsp/fft.hpp, which are declared in iclforge itself).

Within the AC-3 codec, AC-3 is the base case and lives in iclforge::ac3 itself; E-AC-3 additions and overrides live in iclforge::ac3::eac3, nested rather than parallel. iclforge::ac3::FrameEncoder (AC-3) and iclforge::ac3::eac3::FrameEncoder (E-AC-3) sharing a class name across that boundary is this rule applied consistently — the same split the Python bindings mirror by putting the E-AC-3 encoder in a real eac3 submodule rather than a same-module name that would collide.

Audio is float, nominally in [-1, 1). Internally the transform runs in double in an ordinary build; ICLFORGE_DECODE_SCALAR and ICLFORGE_ENCODE_SCALAR choose float or, for the decoder, fixed point on parts that need it (Building). The AC-4 decoder builds in double or float (a fixed request gives it double), and the AC-4 encoder always in double.

Channels are passed as std::span<const std::span<const float>>. The inner spans must outlive the call. Build the outer vector once and refill the buffers underneath it — a fresh vector of spans per frame is a pure waste.

Channel order is A/52 Table 5.8, not WAV order. That is L, C, R, SL, SR with LFE last, against WAVE_FORMAT_EXTENSIBLE's FL, FR, FC, LFE, BL, BR. iclforge::ac3::io::ac3_layout_for and iclforge::ac3::io::wav_channel_order give you the permutation both ways; use them rather than writing it out again. A WAV that states its speakers (WavData::channel_mask) says more than its width does: iclforge::ac3::plan::wav_mask_locations and plan::route take it from there (File I/O). AC-4 uses neither: iclforge::ac4::Decoder writes L, R, C, LFE, Ls, Rs and then the layout's remaining pairs, each channel named in DecodedFrame::speakers, and iclforge::ac4::Encoder takes the same order.

Encoders are stateful and per-stream. They carry MDCT overlap, the 44.1 kHz rate accumulator, and the DRC and heavy-compression controllers, all of which smooth across frames. One encoder per stream, fed in order. The decoders are stateful the same way (overlap-add and dither state). No encoder or decoder instance is safe for concurrent calls on the same instance — the headers note that per-frame scratch and history members are reused across calls — but separate instances share nothing and are independent.

Each encode_frame call takes exactly one frame of PCM per channel. For AC-3 that is always iclforge::ac3::kSamplesPerFrame (1536); for E-AC-3 it is FrameEncoder::samples_per_frame(), which is 1536 unless FrameConfig::numblkscod shortens the syncframe (256, 512 or 768 — see Encoding E-AC-3). Short-changing it is a programming error, not a runtime one.

Every class with non-trivial state hides it behind a pimpl. struct Impl; std::unique_ptr<Impl> impl_; is the only private member on FrameEncoder (both codecs), FrameDecoder, Eac3Decoder, oba::AtmosEncoder, eac3::AccessUnitEncoder, meta::RangeController/HeavyCompressor, meta::LoudnessMeter, analysis::LevelMeter, iec61937::Eac3BurstPacker, iclforge::ac4::Decoder, iclforge::ac4::Encoder and the three io::Wav* classes that started the pattern — adding a buffer or growing a scratch array changes only Impl, defined in the .cpp, so it is never an ABI break for a caller linking iclforge::ac3_shared. The plain config aggregates (EncoderConfig, DecoderConfig, AtmosConfig, FrameConfig, AccessUnitConfig and the AC-4 encoder's and decoder's own) are the deliberate exception: callers build them with designated initializers, so they stay ordinary value types rather than opaque handles, and that ergonomics is worth more than hiding four or five doubles. Their layout is what SameMajorVersion actually has to promise once 1.0 ships: a config struct's fields are frozen at the release that adopts full-version SOVERSION, and a field added afterward needs either a major version bump or an additive extension point (a reserved trailing field, or a new sibling struct referenced by pointer) rather than an in-place insert, which would silently shift every later field's offset for anyone who has not recompiled. The verify::*Trace*/FrameSyntax* pointers a few of them carry (EncoderConfig::trace, DecoderConfig::trace/eac3_trace/ syntax, FrameConfig::trace) are non-owning observers into internal instrumentation headers, not part of the frozen public surface themselves — adding, removing or retyping one of those pointers is not a promise this convention covers.

docs.title: AC-4 (ETSI TS 103 190): iclforge::ac4
docs.text:
iclforge/ac4/decoder/decoder.hpp and iclforge/ac4/encoder/encoder.hpp, with the table of contents both work through, iclforge/ac4/core/toc.hpp, all in the library iclforge::ac4. An AC-4 decoder and encoder written from ETSI TS 103 190-1 V1.4.1 (channel-based coding) and TS 103 190-2 V1.3.1 (immersive and personalized audio). The library is in namespace iclforge::ac4 and links nothing from iclforge::ac3: AC-4 shares no bitstream syntax with AC-3 or E-AC-3. The encoder is described under Encoding a stream, and the AC-4 concepts page explains the format.

It decodes the mono, stereo, 3.0, 5.X and 7.X channel elements in each of Part 1's codec modes (SIMPLE, ASPX and the three A-CPL modes) at every frame rate; the immersive element of 7.0.4, 7.1.4, 9.0.4 and 9.1.4 in full and core decoding, rendered by Part 2's channel renderer (9.X.4); the 22.2 element in full decoding, as coded, to 24 channels (22.2); object audio, A-JOC in full and core decoding and direct-coded objects, with each object's metadata (Objects); streams of several presentations, the one a system chooses decoded with all of its substreams mixed; the output level and dynamic range control, dialogue enhancement and the downmix; and it conceals a frame that does not decode when asked to. It refuses, per substream and per frame, with DecodeError::kUnsupported and a reason: core decoding of the 22.2 element and its rendering to any layout but as coded, and, in a stream at 96 or 192 kHz, what the HSF text does not give it (96 and 192 kHz). It decodes the speech spectral frontend (Part 1 clause 5.2) for the tracks that select it, from the text alone: no stream here uses it. A presentation in the efficient high frame rate mode (frame_rate_fraction 2 or 4, Part 2 clause 5.1.3) spreads one codec frame over that many raw_ac4_frame()s: the decoder holds the fragments, decode() returns no frame until the unit's last transmission frame arrives, and the frame it then returns is at the audio frame rate of Part 2 Table 18, with the unit's first sequence_counter divided by the fraction as its own. A unit that does not arrive whole is concealed as any frame that does not decode is. Development status has the detail, feature by feature, and Validation says how each part is checked.

docs.title: Decoding a stream
docs.text:
A player's stream arrives in pieces. iclforge::ac4::SyncFrameSplitter hands over each sync frame once all of it has arrived, and iclforge::ac4::Decoder::decode_by_block turns it into PCM for one presentation, in blocks of 256 samples. The settings a television offers go in the configuration:

iclforge::ac4::DecoderConfig config;
config.output.output_level_dbfs = -24.0;     // Lout: the dialogue level the output is taken to
config.output.drc = iclforge::ac4::DrcMode::kDefault;  // the mode that output level selects
config.output.downmix = iclforge::ac4::DownmixTarget::kStereo;
config.output.dialogue_enhancement_db = 6.0;  // up to the stream's cap
config.presentation.language = "en";          // where the stream offers a choice
iclforge::ac4::Decoder decoder(config);

// The splitter owns no memory: this holds the frame being assembled.
std::vector<std::byte> storage(iclforge::ac4::kSplitterRecommendedBuffer);
iclforge::ac4::SyncFrameSplitter splitter{storage};
std::size_t frames = 0;
for (;;) {
    const auto next = splitter.next();
    if (next.status == iclforge::ac4::SyncFrameSplitter::Status::kNeedMoreInput) {
        const std::span<std::byte> space = splitter.writable();
        const std::size_t want = std::min<std::size_t>(space.size(), 4096);
        in.read(reinterpret_cast<char*>(space.data()), static_cast<std::streamsize>(want));
        const auto got = static_cast<std::size_t>(in.gcount());
        if (got == 0) {
            splitter.finish();
        } else {
            splitter.commit(got);
        }
        continue;
    }
    if (next.status != iclforge::ac4::SyncFrameSplitter::Status::kFrame) {
        break;  // kEndOfStream, or kTruncated at a cut-off last frame
    }
    ++frames;
    const auto info = decoder.decode_by_block(next.frame.raw_ac4_frame, sink);
    if (!info) {
        const std::string_view reason = decoder.refusal_reason();
        fmt::printf("frame %zu: %.*s\n", frames, static_cast<int>(reason.size()),
                    reason.data());
        return 1;
    }
}
decoder.flush(sink);  // the samples held back short of a block, as one shorter block

Full program: examples/decode_ac4.cpp — decodes the stream it is given to stereo, then prints the presentations it found and the metadata of the one it decoded. ctest runs it on a committed DEE stream.

sink is any callable taking a const iclforge::ac4::PcmBlock&: one span per channel, the speakers they are for, the sample rate and the block's position in the output. iclforge::ac4::BlockSink refers to it without copying it, so it has to outlive the call, which a lambda named before the loop does. A frame's samples rarely divide into 256 (2 002 at 23.976 fps), so each call hands over the whole blocks it has and holds the rest for the next frame, and flush() hands over what is left at the end. Once the layout is set, decoding this way allocates nothing per frame. decode() returns the same output a frame at a time instead, as an iclforge::ac4::DecodedFrame of planar channels.

A frame that produces no output, such as the frames of a stream joined before its first I-frame, returns nothing rather than an error. A frame that does not decode returns its error, and refusal_reason() says why; with DecoderConfig::concealment set to kRepeatFade or kMute, a concealed frame comes back in its place, marked as one.

docs.title: The controls
docs.text:
OutputConfig holds what the listener sets, and Decoder::set_output() changes it from the next frame while a stream plays. A stage takes a new value as it takes the stream's own from one frame to the next, and a new layout starts its channels' synthesis from silence.

OutputConfig field What it sets Default output_level_dbfs Lout (Part 1 clause 5.7.9.3.3), the level the stream's dialnorm is taken to, cutting or boosting by 2^((Lout − dialnorm) / 6) unset: the coded level, nothing compressed drc Which of Table 161's DRC decoder modes compresses: kDefault takes the one clause 5.7.9.2 gives the output level; kHomeTheatre, kFlatPanelTv, kPortableSpeakers and kPortableHeadphones name one; kOff applies the level alone kDefault headphones Whether kDefault takes portable headphones rather than portable speakers where the level falls in their range, −16 to 0 dBFS false dialogue_enhancement_db G_DE (clause 5.7.8): how far the dialogue is raised, up to the cap the stream sets, 3, 6, 9 or 12 dB 0, the tool bypassed downmix The layout (clause 6.2.17): kAsCoded, k5X (a 7.X element folded to 5.X), kStereo (the method the stream prefers), kLoRo, kLtRt, kMono; and for the immersive element and an intermediate spatial format, k7X4, k7X2, k7X0, k5X4 and k5X2 (Part 2 clauses 5.10.2 and 5.10.3), from a 9.X.4 source too. A 22.2 source is delivered kAsCoded only; no 9.X layout is a target kAsCoded mix_lfe Whether a two-channel or mono downmix takes the LFE at the stream's lfe_mixgain, as Part 1 does true dialogue_gain_db g_dialog (clause 6.2.16.1): a presentation's dialogue against its music and effects, up to the stream's g_dialog_max 0 associated_gain_db g_assoc (clause 6.2.16.2), 0 or less: a presentation's associated audio 0 target_device The category of device the output plays on (Part 2 Table 67: k1D, k2D, k3D, kPortable), by which an alternative presentation's target loudness correction is chosen (clause 4.8.5.4) unset: Table 17's by the layout that comes out, stereo 1D, 5.X and 7.X 2D, height channels 3D; never portable

docs.title: 22.2 channel element
docs.text:
The 22.2 element (Part 2 clause 6.2.4.3) is two LFE tracks and eleven channel pairs, in the SIMPLE and ASPX codec modes, and decodes to 24 channels in the order of Part 2 Table A.27's speaker indices: L, R, C, Ls, Rs, Lb, Rb, Tfl, Tfr, Tbl, Tbr, LFE, Tsl, Tsr, Tfc, Tbc, Tc, LFE2, Bfl, Bfr, Bfc, Cb, Lw, Rw (DecodedFrame::speakers names them). The LFEs are therefore not the fourth channel, as they are in the other layouts. iclforge::ac4::Speaker has an enumerator for each speaker of the table, the 9.X.4 screen pair included.

Part 2 gives no renderer or downmix for a 22.2 input (Tables 35 to 43 have no row for one) and lists the element as full decoding only (Table 8). So the decoder delivers 22.2 as coded, refuses every downmix but kAsCoded and decoding = kCore with kUnsupported and a reason that names 22.2, and dialogue enhancement acts on L, R and C. DRC groups the channels by Part 2 Table 69. No stream of this element and no other decoder is available to check it against; the readings are in libs/ac4/ERRATA.md under "The 22.2 element", and the streams its tests decode are built from the standard's tables (Validation).

docs.title: 9.X.4 channel elements
docs.text:
The 9.0.4 and 9.1.4 channel modes (ch_mode 13 and 14) are the immersive element with b_5fronts (Part 2 clause 6.2.4.1): the 7.X.4 channels and the screen pair, Lscr and Rscr, thirteen tracks in all, in SCPL, ASPX_SCPL, ASPX_ACPL_1, ASPX_ACPL_2 and ASPX_AJCC. They decode in full decoding to 13 or 14 channels in the order of Part 2 Table A.27, the LFE after the tops and the screen pair last: L, R, C, Ls, Rs, Lb, Rb, Tfl, Tfr, Tbl, Tbr, LFE, Lscr, Rscr. Core decoding gives the same 5.X.2 as the 7.X.4 modes' (L, R, C, LFE, Ls, Rs, Tsl, Tsr), without the screen pair.

The renderer rows of Part 2 Tables 38 to 43 for a 9.X input fold the screen pair into L and R, or into C, at the custom downmix gains gain_f1 and gain_f2 (6.2.9.4), and the downmix targets k7X4 to k5X2 take them. Tables 35 to 37 render to a 9.X layout, which no downmix names, so a 9.X layout is never a target. Dialogue enhancement acts on Lscr, Rscr and C in full decoding (Table 15) and, for the A-JCC and A-CPL modes in core decoding, by the extension tools of clauses 5.8.2.1 and 5.8.2.2; b_de_simulcast selects the second de_data() for core decoding. DRC groups Lscr and Rscr with L and R (Table 69). Hearth's engine, which cannot place the screen pair (A/52 Table E2.5 has no location for it), asks the decoder for k7X4 when it is given such a presentation and no layout of the listener's own, and plays that render; the ESP32 player refuses the presentation. No stream of these modes and no other decoder is available to check them against; the readings are in libs/ac4/ERRATA.md under "The 9.X.4 element", and the streams their tests decode are built from the standard's tables.

DecoderConfig holds the rest: output, presentation (below), concealment, level (the md_compat level the decoder claims, 7 by default, unrestricted; presentations above it are not chosen), decoding (full or core decoding, Part 2 clause 4.7, full by default), and syntax, a trace of every syntax element read. syntax is an iclforge::ac4::SyntaxTrace, a std::function the configuration owns, and the decoder keeps a copy of its own, so a lambda written in place, in a class's constructor for instance, stays valid; what it captures by reference has to outlive the decoder. The records are described under Validation.

DecoderConfig::executor lets a caller with a second core spread a frame's per-channel work over two threads: each channel's inverse transform and QMF analysis, A-SPX's elements, A-CPL's slots and decorrelators, each output's QMF synthesis and sample rate converter. An iclforge::ac4::Executor (iclforge/ac4/decoder/executor.hpp) is two functions, lanes() and run(count, task, context), which calls task(context, index, lane) once for each index and returns when all have; the tasks of one run read and write what no other task does, so the PCM is the same bit for bit whichever way they run, and a null executor, the default, runs them in order on the calling thread. The executor is the caller's and must outlive the decoder; only the thread that decodes calls it. The ESP32 player's is a task pinned to the core the decode task is not on (CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_AC4_PARALLEL); the tests' is two threads and a lock (libs/ac4/tests/decoder/test_executor.cpp), which decodes every committed stream through it and compares the bits.

decode(frame, next) and decode_by_block(frame, next, sink) take, as well, the frame the following call will be given, and read its syntax on the executor's second lane while this frame is reconstructed (Executor::run_async() and wait_async(), which an executor with no second lane runs in place). The signal, presentations(), metadata(), refusal_reason() and latency_samples() after each call are what a call without next gives. Nothing is read ahead for a frame with object audio, one that does not continue the stream (a change of source), one of the efficient high frame rate mode, or with a syntax trace set; the frame the following call is given must be next, and any other is taken as a change of source; and a set_presentation() between the calls takes effect one frame later, since the frame was read with the choice that stood. The ESP32 player holds one frame back to give it the next.

forge decode spells each control as an option (output-level=, drcmode=, headphones, dialogue-enhancement=, channels=, downmix=, speakers=, mix-lfe=, dialogue-gain=, associated-gain=, md-compat=, decoding=, conceal=); see Commands.

docs.title: 96 and 192 kHz
docs.text:
A substream whose ac4_substream_info() carries sf_multiplier (Part 1 Table 89) is at 96 or 192 kHz, and its group's ac4_hsf_ext_substream() holds the lines beyond 24 kHz (clause 4.2.4.3). The decoder reads the core's lines and the extension's into transforms two or four times as long (Tables 99 to 105, with Annex B's Tables B.2 to B.7 for the bands), inverse transforms them with Table 186's windows, delays them by clause 5.6, and passes them through the sample rate converter of clause 6.2.15 at the same ratio as at 48 kHz. DecodedFrame::sample_rate_hz is then 96000 or 192000, each frame holds twice or four times the samples Table 83 gives at 48 kHz, and decode_by_block() hands them over in the same blocks of 256 samples at that rate. PresentationInfo::sample_rate_hz gives the rate before a frame is decoded, so that a player can open its output at it.

Clause 5.4 says a stream with high sampling frequency data uses none of the QMF domain tools, and 6.2.5.2 that decoding it needs the SAP tool and the inverse transform alone. So only a SIMPLE codec mode of the mono, stereo, 3.0, 5.X and 7.X elements decodes at these rates, and of the output stages only the output level gain (a scalar on the samples) and the downmix (a matrix on them) apply. A stream at 96 or 192 kHz that needs more is refused per frame with DecodeError::kUnsupported and a reason that names it: the A-SPX and A-CPL codec modes, the speech spectral frontend, the immersive and 22.2 elements, object audio, the mixing of a presentation's substreams, dialogue enhancement where the stream sends it and OutputConfig asks for a gain, and the compression of DRC (DrcMode::kOff keeps the output level). A 96 or 192 kHz substream with no extension substream linked is refused too: the text does not say what rate it is at.

No stream at these rates was available, and no other decoder: the tests decode streams built from the text (testdata/ac4-hsf/ and libs/ac4/tests/decoder/hsf.hpp), each channel a tone above 24 kHz where the base rate has none, and hold the output to its frequency, level and waveform. The readings the text left open are in libs/ac4/ERRATA.md under "96 and 192 kHz".

docs.title: Choosing a presentation
docs.text:
A stream can carry several presentations of its substreams: music and effects with dialogue in one language or another, the main audio with audio description, and so on (Part 2 clause 4.8). PresentationChoice says which one to decode, and Decoder::set_presentation() changes it from the next frame. Every presentation's substreams are read in every frame, so a newly chosen one needs no I-frame; its signal starts from silence.

  • presentation_id: the presentation carrying it, which stays with the presentation as the table of contents changes.
  • index: its position in the table of contents.
  • Otherwise the preferences, in the order clause 4.8.2 lists them: language, a BCP 47 tag, a presentation whose tag matches it whole before one whose primary subtag does; associated, the content classifier of the associated audio wanted (Part 1 Table 91), with associated_type refining it by Table 92; and headphones, whether a presentation rendered for headphones before it was encoded (b_pre_virtualized) comes before one that was not, or after it.

Of the presentations this decoder can decode, the stream has not disabled and whose md_compat is within the decoder's level, the one that meets the choice is decoded, the first in the table of contents among equals. iclforge::ac4::select_presentation(toc, choice, level) makes the same choice from a table of contents alone. Where the text leaves the choice open, libs/ac4/ERRATA.md records the reading taken. forge decode takes the choice as presentation= (the position), presentation-id=, language=, associated= and headphones.

docs.title: What the decoder reports
docs.text:
• presentations(): each presentation of the last frame's table of contents, as iclforge::ac4::PresentationInfo: its presentation_id, version, configuration and md_compat, whether it is enabled, an alternative or pre-virtualized, its name (Part 2 clause 6.3.3.1.4; a name sent in chunks over several frames once the decoder has all of it), its language, the channels it decodes to, the sampling frequency it decodes at (sample_rate_hz, also on each substream), its substreams with the role each plays, and whether this decoder decodes it and may choose it.
  • metadata(): the metadata of the presentation decoded, as the frames read so far have sent it: the loudness values (dialnorm and Part 1 clause 4.3.12.3's further values), the DRC configuration with each decoder mode and the one applied, dialogue enhancement's method, channels and cap, and the downmix gains and preferred method. Values a stream sends only in I-frames are kept until a change of source.
  • parse(): a frame read without decoding, as an iclforge::ac4::FrameReport: every substream of its substream_index_table() in index order, what it turned out to be, how many bits the syntax took of it, and, for one not read to its end, the error and the reason. A substream that no element of the table of contents this decoder reads names, an HSF extension substream that nothing claims among them, is reported as refused and unread. An OAMD substream that sends an oamd_common_data() (Part 2 clause 6.2.8.1) reports it as oamd_common_data. An EMDF payloads substream, and an audio substream whose metadata() carries an emdf_payloads_substream(), report the payloads as emdf_payloads: each emdf_payload_id (Part 1 Table 174) and its bytes, in the order read. The decoder does not interpret them.
  • latency_samples(): the decoder's delay at the output rate, 1 313 samples at frame_rate_index 13 and at the other indices the same at the internal rate plus the sample rate converter's delay. decode_by_block() holds back up to 255 samples more.

forge probe json=1 writes the same reports for a stream: see Commands.

docs.title: Objects
docs.text:
A presentation with object audio (Part 2 clause 4.8.3) decodes to objects, which DecodedFrame::objects hands over for the application to render: each object's PCM, as long as the frame, and the properties its object audio metadata sets, which Part 2 Annex F lists as what a decoder gives an object renderer.

  • DecodedObject: a dynamic object or a bed object (kind), the LFE (lfe), a bed object's loudspeaker (speaker), the samples, the properties in force at the frame's first sample, and the updates within the frame, in order.
  • ObjectProperties: whether the object is active, its gain in dB (−infinity for silence) and priority, its position (X from the left wall to the right, 0 to 1; Y from the front wall to the back, 0 to 1; Z from the floor through the screen's height to the ceiling, −1 to 1), its zone constraint, elevation and snap, its width, screen factor and depth exponent, distance and divergence, and the trim and headphone data of add_per_object_md().
