Address patterns match LITERALLY — no OSC glob (?/*/[]/{}) matching — with <n> the 0-based object index:

Address Type tag Meaning /object/<n>/xyz ,fff Position, the same room-coordinate convention Position/the keyframe grammar use per §4.2.1: x∈[0,1], y∈[0,1], z∈[-1,1]. /object/<n>/gain ,f Linear gain — matches ObjectPlacement::gain, not dB. /object/<n>/lfe ,f Linear LFE send. /object/<n>/release , (no args) Hand to SceneCursor::release(object) instead of apply()/push() — there is no placement to merge, only a request to stop overriding.

apply() is the piece worth understanding before wiring this up, because it encodes a real correctness rule rather than a convenience. SceneCursor::push() replaces a whole ObjectPlacement, so routing a position-only OSC message straight through a default-constructed placement would silently reset that object's gain to 1.0 and drop its lfe_send — destroying whatever gain law the caller already has running for it. apply() merges the wire update onto a base placement instead — typically cursor.scene().evaluate(object, time_s), this object's currently-authored value — so every field the OSC message didn't touch carries through unchanged.

The other half of the rule is about position, and it is easy to get backwards: apply() never reuses base's position as the merged position, even when the incoming update carries none of its own. That is deliberate, not an oversight. ObjectScene::evaluate() has already rotated the position it hands back (the scene's Orientation, applied on the way out of evaluate()), and SceneCursor::sample_into() rotates a pushed placement's position again on the way to the encoder. Push a once-already-rotated position back in and a non-identity Orientation rotates it twice. So a gain- or lfe-only update that arrives before this object has ever had a position pushed has nothing safe to push yet — apply() returns std::nullopt in that case, meaning "nothing ready to push." A caller wiring this up for real is responsible for remembering that update against the object and re-applying it once a position finally arrives.

This header is pure, portable, zero-socket, zero-thread code — no I/O of any kind — and is fuzzed (libs/objects/fuzz/fuzz_osc_parse.cpp) and unit-tested (libs/objects/tests/test_scene_osc.cpp) accordingly. The actual UDP listener, iclforge::audio::LivePositionSource, is a separate, app-serving-only piece and is not part of this installed library, for the same reason the rest of iclforge::audio isn't (see Using the libraries's note on live audio); forge live mode=atmos positions=osc:[<bind>:]<port> is where a reader can see it wired up end to end over a real socket.

docs.title: The serialised form
docs.text:
to_json() / scene_from_json(). JSON, not YAML: {fmt} (linked into this library for text formatting generally) formats a number, it is not a parser for either document format, so whichever this is still has to be read and written by code in this repository, and RFC 8259 is a grammar small enough to implement completely and be sure of where YAML 1.2's is not — a hand-rolled "YAML subset" would accept and reject files no other YAML tool agrees with, which is worse than not offering YAML. Both other front ends already have a JSON reader to hand (Qt's, Python's) if they ever want to read a scene without linking this library.

{
  "iclforge_scene": 1,
  "orientation": { "yaw_rad": 0, "pitch_rad": 0, "roll_rad": 0 },
  "objects": [
    {
      "name": "flyby",
      "bed": [],
      "automation": [
        { "t": 0, "x": 0, "y": 0.5, "z": 0.5, "gain": 0.6, "lfe": 0, "interp": "smooth" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Numbers are written short-round-tripped (the shortest decimal that reads back as the same double), one automation point per line and members in a fixed order, so a scene under version control shows real edits rather than formatting churn, and a save/load cycle is bit-exact. The reader is strict about what it does not recognise — an unknown member is an error, because a hand-authored file's likeliest fault is a misspelled key and silently defaulting "gian" to 1.0 would be wrong in a way nothing reports. Forward compatibility rides on the iclforge_scene version number instead. orientation accepts yaw_deg/pitch_deg/roll_deg in place of the radian spellings (but never both for one axis). bed names TS 103 420 Table 12 channel labels — "lr", "c", "lfe", "ls_rs", "lb_rb", "tfl_tfr", "tsl_tsr", "tbl_tbr", "lw_rw", "lfe2" — and an empty array means a dynamic object.

scene_objects_from_keyframe_text() / to_keyframe_text() read and write the older whitespace-column grammar forge atmos-path has always taken, unchanged including its diagnostics — see CLI → Commands. read_scene() and scene_from_text() take either, told apart by whether the first non-whitespace character is {, so a path argument keeps working whichever form the file is in.

The keyframe form is indexed and sparse — a file may mention objects 0 and 2 and say nothing about 1 — and what object 1 should then be is the caller's policy, not the library's: atmos-path fans it out at room centre under its inverse-root gain law, atmos-encode keeps that channel's existing static placement. That is why read_scene() returns raw SceneContents with the gaps still empty; fill them, then ObjectScene::create. scene_from_text() is the convenience for a caller with no policy of its own.

docs.title: Not in the C API or the Python bindings
docs.text:
Both expose AtmosEncoder, and ObjectScene does not follow it there. Its shape has settled: SceneCursor is the seam a live position source plugs into (OSC, above, is one), and both of those surfaces are candidates for the coming API freeze, where an experimental type would be a lasting commitment. Exposing half of it (say, the serialisation free functions but not the type) would be worse than exposing none: a C caller would get a scene it could load and not evaluate. Load and save the JSON form from either language and hand the resulting placements to the existing encoder bindings.

This layer backs forge atmos-path and atmos-encode's optional scene argument, the GUI's object-path export, and the station broadcast scene's ten authored objects.

docs.title: The same authoring for AC-4 objects
docs.text: The AC-4 object encoder (AC-4 § Encoding objects) takes each object's PCM and its metadata over time in iclforge::ac4::ObjectProperties, and reads no scene format. The applications feed it the layers on this page and the ADM and IAB bridges: forge atmos-encode, atmos-adm and atmos-iab with codec=ac4, and the Forge GUI's encoder page, turn each object's authored position and gain into one metadata update a frame (apps/shared/media/src/ac4_objects_core.hpp). ObjectScene, motion.hpp and AtmosEncoder know nothing of AC-4.

docs.title: Objects-or-nothing: AtmosConfig::emit_object_metadata
docs.text:
Whether to emit the EMDF object container (OAMD + JOC) at all. On by default: an object-aware decoder gets the objects, and one that ignores the container plays the 5.1 bed underneath it — the design target. Turning it off is the only way to keep the bed playable on a decoder that validates emdf_protection (see Object signing): such a decoder treats the container's sync word as a commitment to object decoding and refuses the whole stream if the tag doesn't check out, rather than falling back. With no container there is no sync word to find, so it decodes the bed as ordinary 5.1. The choice is objects-or-nothing, never both.

iclforge::ac3::oba::AtmosEncoder encoder{{.bitrate_kbps = 448, .emit_object_metadata = false}, kObjects};

Turning it off drops TS 103 420 §8.3.1's addbsi object marker along with the container, so the stream doesn't advertise an object layer either. That marker (flag_ec3_extension_type_a plus §8.3.2.2's complexity_index_type_a) is the only thing a reader has to go on: it is what iclforge::ac3::io::scan reports as ScannedStream::oba_complexity_index, what iclforge::ac3::io::build_codec_config_box turns into the dec3 box's Dolby Atmos extension, what forge fmp4 writes as an HLS CHANNELS="<N>/JOC" attribute, and what FFmpeg keys its "Dolby Digital Plus + Dolby Atmos" profile off. Left in, all four would claim objects that were never encoded — the same empty-promise this mode exists to avoid.

Full program: examples/atmos_fallback.cpp — encodes the same objects both ways and confirms both decode as an ordinary 5.1 bed.

The stream size is unaffected either way — this is CBR, so frmsiz follows bitrate_kbps regardless of what rides in the skip field. What differs is where those bits go: with the container left out, the frame's rate control gives the freed skip-field bytes back to the mantissas, so the two configurations' decoded bed is close but not bit-identical.

See also: Encoding E-AC-3 — Atmos objects ride inside an ordinary E-AC-3 stream; Object signing — what makes a validating decoder accept the container in the first place; A worked scene: the station broadcast — a complete 115-second authored scene built on this API, from synthesis to .ec3; ADM → Atmos bridging — mapping a professional ADM BWF master's beds and objects onto this same ObjectPath/AtmosEncoder surface.

docs.title: A worked scene: the station broadcast
docs.text:
examples/station_broadcast.cpp is the library's fully worked Atmos example: a complete 115-second scene — synthesis, motion, mix, and encode — in one compiled program with no binary assets. Everything the other pages introduce piecemeal appears here doing a job: one ObjectScene holds every ship's automation, ObjectPlacement gains perform the edit, lfe_send opens the wormhole, and the same scene is encoded twice, with the EMDF container and without it.

The premise is borrowed lovingly from the title sequence of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine — and from the fan edit that re-mixed its theme as if the music were coming from the station. Every sound is diegetic: the anthem is a radio broadcast from the station, and everything else that happens in the scene happens to that broadcast.

docs.title: The cue sheet
docs.text:
Times are scene-relative. (Against the reference videos: the original title sequence starts at 0:01, the diegetic fan edit at about 0:14.)

Cue Scene Object work 0:00 A comet drifts across the black, left to right x 0.02 → 0.98 across the front of the room 0:02 The station's broadcast fades up Far front-centre (0.5, 0.04), gain 0.05 — tinny, distant, mono 0:14 The station pans into view Gain steps to 0.30 as the picture finds the source 0:26 Cargo jalopy flypast Two co-moving objects (engine + its own radio) cross from rear-right; at closest approach the radio's 0.75 drowns the station's 0.30 0:38 Cut to a station close-up The broadcast's bandpass opens to nearly clean and its gain doubles — same object, the mix performs the edit 0:52 A runabout undocks and sweeps overhead z reaches 0.65: real height metadata for a renderer with tops; the 5.1 bed folds it onto the ring 1:01 The anthem surges back for the reprise The cue's own measured form: full restatement at 1:01, climax plateau from 1:19 1:12 A second runabout crosses the port side Rear-left to a front-left docking 1:24 A maintenance pod welds on an upper pylon Static object, front-right, raised 1:43 The wormhole opens behind the station A subsonic core almost entirely on lfe_send — the only route to the LFE — plus two shimmer objects that split and wrap up and over the room; the score's final cadence lands on the flash at 1:44, as in the original 1:51 ...and swallows itself Pitch and gains collapse back to front-centre

Ten named objects in one iclforge::objects::oba::ObjectScene, each with its own authored automation, evaluated at the end of each frame — the same convention as forge atmos-path, because both metadata layers interpolate to that point. It is the same type that command reads from a file and the GUI's timeline edits, so this cue sheet could equally have been loaded from JSON rather than written in C++.

docs.title: What it adds beyond atmos_objects.cpp
docs.text:
• Authored motion, not orbits. Every object is a hand-written cue table; distance lives in the authored gains, so the "swamping" of the broadcast by a passing ship is just two gain arcs crossing.
  • Doppler, outside the library. The example derives radial velocity from its own paths and bends its oscillators before the samples ever reach the encoder. The library deliberately has no opinion here: essences are audio, placement is metadata.
  • Both fallback strategies, side by side. The same scene is encoded with objects (out.ec3) and with emit_object_metadata = false (out_bed51.ec3). The 5.1 mix is identical; the second file exists for decoders that validate emdf_protection and refuse the whole stream rather than fall back — see the two limitations.
  • The bed as a deliverable. encoder.bed() — the thing a legacy decoder hears — is captured per frame and written as out_bed.wav, plus an Lo/Ro fold-down out_stereo.wav for headphones.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
station_broadcast                          # smoke test: 0:24–0:34 in memory
station_broadcast out [seconds] [wav]      # full render, writes four files

To listen immediately: out_stereo.wav in any player, or the E-AC-3 through FFmpeg (ffplay out_bed51.ec3). Consumer Dolby hardware should be fed the bed51 variant for the reason above.

The built-in anthem is a synthesizer cover of the Deep Space Nine main title (Dennis McCarthy) — the seasons 1–3 arrangement, made by ear in C major for the example's own voices: the solo horn call over a pad, the solo-trumpet fanfare, and a final open-fifth cadence timed, as in the original, to the wormhole. The middle section has never been transcribed anywhere, so it is recomposed from the theme's own material. Note well: distributing a cover requires the appropriate licence wherever you distribute it — this repository's author has secured their own position, and forks must consider theirs. The third argument replaces the built-in cover with a WAV you have the rights to; it is mixed to mono, resampled, and played from scene time 0:02 through the same transmitter chain, so the 0:38 bandwidth-opening cut still happens to your recording.

See also: Spatial & Atmos objects — the API this scene is built on; Atmos & JOC — what survives of the object layer, and where.

docs.title: TrueHD and MLP: iclforge::truehd
docs.text:
iclforge/truehd/decoder/decoder.hpp, with the bitstream layer under it in iclforge/truehd/core/ and iclforge/truehd/io/, all in the library iclforge::truehd. A reader, a lossless decoder and an encoder for Dolby TrueHD (0xF8726FBA, Blu-ray and HD DVD) and MLP (0xF8726FBB, DVD-Audio) elementary streams, written from the owner's Dolby TrueHD (MLP) Reference Specification, v3.9 ("TH spec" in the code). The library links iclforge::base and nothing else; the Atmos substream and the object metadata are phase T2b (the plan).

The specification contradicts itself and the streams in places and is silent in others. Every such place is an entry of libs/truehd/ERRATA.md, which lists first the questions only the specification's owner can answer. Where a stream forced a reading the specification does not give, the entry says so.

docs.title: What it decodes
docs.text:
The layers a stream has, in the order the reader walks them:

  • the access unit: a four-byte header (a check nibble that makes the nibbles of the header and the substream directory XOR to 0xF, a length in 16-bit words, input_timing), a major sync when the unit has one (28 bytes, CRC-16), the substream directory, the segments, and extra data after them;
  • each segment: blocks, each with an optional restart header (CRC-8) and block header, then the residuals, Huffman-coded with one of the three codebooks or raw, and a parity byte and a CRC-8 after the last block;
  • the reconstruction: the FIR and IIR prediction filters, the quantiser step, the primitive matrices (with LSB bypass), ch_assign and the output shift, and the lossless check of each restart interval, which the next restart header carries.

Substreams 0 to 2 (2, 6 and 8 channels) and the generic 16-channel substream 3 decode the same way, each reading the channels the ones before it produced. Sample rates are 44.1 to 192 kHz in 16 and 24 bits (a decode is always 24 bits wide, in an int32).

docs.title: Decoding
docs.text:
#include "iclforge/truehd/decoder/decoder.hpp"
#include "iclforge/truehd/io/elementary.hpp"

iclforge::truehd::ElementaryReader reader(stream);
iclforge::truehd::Decoder decoder;               // DecoderConfig: presentation, strictness
while (const auto unit = reader.next()) {
    auto result = decoder.decode(*unit);         // std::expected<std::optional<DecodedAccessUnit>, Error>
    if (result && *result) {
        // (*result)->pcm: samples x channels, interleaved; ->layout names the speakers when the major sync does
    }
}

A stream may have bytes in front of its first access unit (the owner's timecode fixtures have a 16 byte packet there). find_stream_start and the reader look for the first offset, at most kMaxLeadingBytes (64 KiB) in, at which a unit reads with a valid major sync CRC and the unit after it reads too (or is cut short by the end of the data with a consistent header). ElementaryReader::leading_bytes() says how many were skipped, forge truehd-decode and forge probe warn with the count (a warning, not an error), and what the bytes hold is not looked into.

Length, timing and seeking. scan_stream() (iclforge/truehd/io/scan.hpp) reads a stream held in memory once and gives a ScannedStream: the sample rate, the samples in a unit, the units and their bytes, the bytes it skipped (those ahead of the first unit counted apart), the padding the last unit's end-of-stream marker counts, and the restarts. A unit holds 40, 80 or 160 samples, the same number for every unit, so a unit's first sample is its number times that and needs no record. A decoder can only join at a unit with a major sync, so those units are the seek granule: the scan keeps their numbers and byte offsets, at least restart_spacing units apart (256 by default, about 0.2 s at 48 kHz; 1 keeps every one, which are also the only places a cut or a join may start). To reach a sample, restart_for_sample() gives the last restart at or before its unit; decode on from there and drop the samples before the one wanted.

const auto scan = iclforge::truehd::scan_stream(stream);          // std::expected<ScannedStream, Error>
if (scan) {
    const double seconds = scan->duration_seconds();               // samples() / sample_rate, padding left out
    const auto from = scan->restart_for_sample(scan->sample_at_seconds(90.0));  // nothing past the end
    // iclforge::truehd::ElementaryReader reader(std::span(stream).subspan(from->offset)); decode from there;
    // its first sample is scan->unit_start_sample(from->unit)
}

Unit numbers count the units that read, so a stream that lost bytes in the middle numbers the units after the loss as if they followed. The padding is read by decoding the last restart interval once, so the scan costs one reading of the stream and one interval's decode. A stream whose last interval does not decode to its end reports no padding. The window the Hearth player plays a stream through keeps its own index of the same shape over a file it reads in windows (apps/hearth/engine/src/truehd_index.hpp); the scan holds the whole stream in memory.

decode() gives no samples and no error for a unit that comes before the first major sync or before a substream's first restart header (a stream joined partway). Presentation picks the substreams read: kBest (0 to 2, the default), k2ch, k6ch, k8ch or kAll (substream 3 too). Strictness::kStrict makes a failed check (check nibble, CRC, parity, lossless check) an error that drops the unit and leaves the substream waiting for its next restart header; kLenient counts it (DecoderCounters) and decodes on. The last unit of a stream that does not end on a unit boundary carries an end-of-stream marker; the decoder removes the padding samples it counts (padding_samples). Decoding does not allocate once a stream is running (the buffers are sized when the decoder is built), apart from a change of major sync and an extra data field longer than 256 bytes. The extra data of a unit is not decoded: extra_data hands back its bytes. read_extra_data and read_evolution (iclforge/truehd/io/evolution.hpp) read them into plain structures, as a reading that waits for the owner: the check nibble (the four nibbles of the header word XOR to 0xF, §16.2; a zero header word is padding), the framing and the parity are reported (not enforced), and the evolution payload is read as the bit-level container of TH spec section 15.4 (version, key id, payloads with their configuration and bytes, and the protection field, which is returned and not verified). EvolutionFrame::oamd() hands out the bytes of payload id 11, the object audio metadata, for a program that links iclforge::objects to parse with iclforge::objects::oba::parse_payload; this library links iclforge::base and nothing else. forge probe prints what it finds. The reading is provisional (libs/truehd/ERRATA.md, questions 22 to 24): the owner's reading is that this container is the outer one and the Thrift content signature is nested in one of its payloads, so every payload is carried as bytes with its id and size and none but the object audio metadata is looked into here.

The syntax is also written: write_restart_header, write_block_header, write_major_sync and write_access_unit_prefix are the readers' inverses, which the encoder is built on.

docs.title: Encoding
docs.text:
iclforge/truehd/encoder/encoder.hpp: Encoder, EncoderConfig, EncodedAccessUnit, EncoderStats. The encoder streams: create() checks the configuration (refusal_reason() gives the same sentence without building one), encode() takes interleaved PCM and returns the access units that are complete, and flush() codes what is left, pads the last unit with zero samples and ends the stream with the marker the decoder removes.

#include "iclforge/truehd/encoder/encoder.hpp"

iclforge::truehd::EncoderConfig config;
config.sample_rate = 48000;                       // 44.1, 48, 88.2, 96, 176.4 or 192 kHz
config.channels = 6;                              // 1 to 8
config.bits = 24;                                 // 16, 20 or 24: the width of the PCM given to encode()
auto encoder = iclforge::truehd::Encoder::create(config);   // std::expected<Encoder, EncodeError>
if (!encoder) { /* encoder.error().detail names the rule */ }
for (const auto& chunk : pcm_chunks) {            // interleaved int32
    auto units = encoder->encode(chunk);          // std::expected<std::vector<EncodedAccessUnit>, EncodeError>
    // append each unit's bytes to the .thd file
}
auto tail = encoder->flush();

The encoder holds one restart interval of input before it emits it (128 access units by default, 107 ms at 48 kHz). In each interval it finds the low bits every sample leaves clear and sends them as the output shift and the quantiser step (a 16 bit source in a 24 bit container is shift 7, step 1), decorrelates neighbouring pairs of channels with a primitive matrix where that makes the stream smaller, predicts each channel with a FIR filter of up to order 8 found by windowed autocorrelation and the Levinson-Durbin recursion (order 4 at 176.4 and 192 kHz, the specification's limit), and codes each block's residual with whichever of the three codebooks or raw bits takes the fewest bits, with the offset and raw width to match. Channels are spread over substreams the way FFmpeg's encoder spreads them: two in substream 0, the next four in substream 1 and the last two in substream 2 (stereo and mono are one substream at 176.4 and 192 kHz, and 3 to 6 channels there are two, as FFmpeg writes them although the specification's text says one: ERRATA entry 91, provisional).

DownmixMode::kStandard writes the 2 and 6 channel presentations as downmixes instead: substream 0 holds a stereo mix, the matrices of the later substreams take the folded-in channels out again, and a 7.1 stream folds its rear surrounds into substream 1's 5.1 the same way. The gains are EncoderConfig::downmix_gains; a fold that would leave a presentation outside 24 bits has its gains lowered for that interval and EncoderStats::downmix_reduced_intervals counts it. The full presentation always comes back exactly; the gains and the limiter are the encoder's choice, since the specification gives none (libs/truehd/ERRATA.md, entry 38), and no decoder checks them.

EncoderConfig::channel_meaning writes the channel meaning of TH spec §14.1 into every major sync: for the 2, 6 and 8 channel presentations a dialogue norm, a mix level, a source format (not the 2 channel one) and a control-enabled bit, and the two DRC start-up gains. A field outside its width, or extra_present (the sixteen-channel extension is not written), is EncodeErrorKind::kInvalidConfig with the field's name in the detail (channel_meaning_problem() gives the same sentence); left alone every field is zero, as in FFmpeg's streams, so a configuration that does not set them writes the stream it always wrote. Provisional, no oracle until the DEE set: the units, the presentation that applies when and what a control bit gates are open (libs/truehd/ERRATA.md, questions 51 to 55).

iclforge/truehd/io/metadata_edit.hpp changes the same fields in a finished stream: edit_channel_meaning(stream, edit) takes a ChannelMeaningEdit (each member optional, range-checked by apply_edit()), finds the major syncs as ElementaryReader finds the access units, sets the named fields in every one and re-stamps its CRC-16. No other check covers the major sync, so no other byte changes and a decoder gives the same samples; bytes that are not an access unit, units without a major sync and the 16-channel extension are left as they are. An MLP stream (its bytes at that place are not described), a stream with no major sync and a value outside its field's width are errors, and then nothing is written. forge metadata and forge normalize are the commands over it.

The stream is held to the peak data rate it declares (18 Mbps by default, Blu-ray's) and to the 75 ms latency of the specification's FIFO model: a stream that cannot be sent in time is EncodeErrorKind::kRateExceeded, or with allow_rate_violations is written and counted. verify decodes every unit with this library's decoder as it is produced and compares it with the input. extra_data frames a payload into a unit's extra data and never looks inside it. The restart interval is 1 or at least 8 access units; a longer interval makes a smaller stream and a shorter one a quicker random access.

FFmpeg's strict decode of what it writes is the check, sample for sample (tools/checks/verify_truehd_encode_interop.py, with --forge through forge truehd-encode); the streams are 0.85 to 0.96 times the size of FFmpeg's encoder's at 44.1 to 96 kHz and 1.06 to 1.15 times at 192 kHz, and 0.966 of DEE's on the 5.1 music (the measured table). It writes no noise, no IIR filter and no LSB bypass (nothing outside this library reads them), no MLP, and no block data CRC; the Atmos substream and the evolution payload it only frames, from bytes it is given. libs/truehd/ERRATA.md (entries 30 to 38, questions 12 to 15) records each place the specification and the streams left it a choice. forge truehd-encode is the command; iclforge-truehd-encode-tool (WAV in, .thd out) is the test tool the interoperability checks use.

docs.title: Forge
docs.text:
forge probe stream.thd [json=1]
forge decode stream.thd out.wav [truehd-presentation=best|2ch|6ch|8ch|all] [truehd-check=strict|lenient]
forge truehd-encode in.wav out.thd|out.mkv|out.mp4|out.ts [truehd-downmix=...] [truehd-restart=N] [verify] ...
forge levels|loudness|mkv|mp4|ts|spdif|unspdif|demux|remux  stream.thd ...

The second group reads a TrueHD or MLP stream like the AC-3 family; the command reference has each option, and which commands refuse a TrueHD input.

decode writes a 24-bit PCM WAV with the channels in the order the stream carries them, and a channel mask when that order is the WAV's own (5.1 is). A failed check, or a byte the reader had to skip to find the next unit, stops a strict decode with exit status 2; truehd-check=lenient counts them and goes on. probe describes the stream and checks every unit's header, directory, parity and CRC, and exits 1 if any fails.

docs.title: What it is checked against
docs.text:
Check What it covers Oracle FFmpeg's strict decode (-err_detect crccheck+bitstream+buffer+explode) of the streams its truehd and mlp encoders write 25 fixtures in testdata/truehd/: 1 to 6 channels, 44.1 to 192 kHz, 16, 20 and 24 bits, TrueHD and MLP; 19 more while the decoder was written FFmpeg: sample for sample FFmpeg's strict decode of the streams this library's encoder writes (tools/checks/verify_truehd_encode_interop.py, with --forge it runs forge truehd-encode; the codec matrix's encode legs and the gold-reference gate also run it) 43 cases: 1 to 8 channels, 44.1 to 192 kHz, 16, 20 and 24 bits, real music, speech and 5.1 programme material and synthetic signals chosen to be hard (full-scale squares, impulses, silence, DC, noise, level steps), the downmix presentations, restart intervals of 1, 8 and 128 units, lengths that are not whole units FFmpeg: sample for sample, 43 of 43 tools/ci/fuzz_truehd_encoder_space.py, random legal configurations against adversarial PCM, and the libFuzzer harness fuzz_truehd_encode the encoder's whole configuration space, FFmpeg's strict decode of each stream FFmpeg: sample for sample tools/references/truehd_syntax.py, an independent transcription the same 25, and the hand-built streams none beyond the two readings agreeing Hand-built streams, tools/references/truehd_writer.py (tools/checks/verify_truehd_interop.py --handbuilt) an IIR filter and its new_states, LSB bypass (under either restart sync), noise generators 0 and 1 (at 48, 96 and 192 kHz), a negative output shift and an output shift on a moved channel, a 16 bit MLP stream, terminators of both kinds, several matrices with a permuted ch_assign (also one that changes at each restart), an output shift, the block data check, the end-of-stream marker, extra data, the directory's DRC word, four substreams with a 16-channel one, and one at the limits TH spec v3.6 gives substream 3 (15 matrices, huff_lsbs 31) FFmpeg: the whole signal each was built from, for 19 of the 29; the manifest names what FFmpeg does with the other 10 (it refuses the 16-channel and limit streams and a stream with a terminator, applies no negative output shift, and clears the low bits of a 16 bit MLP stream). None for the extra data's layout, the DRC word's values, the block data CRC and the 16-channel substream DEE's streams of known sources scored on the owner's machine by tools/checks/score_truehd_decode.py, which skips when the set is absent; 13 of them are in testdata/truehd-dee (11 pass, the two at 96 kHz differ from their sources in the encoder, none fail) the sources The owner's Blu-ray (an Atmos 7.1 stream of four substreams), analysed on the owner's machine planning/truehd-disc-findings.md: every lossless-check interval of the 2, 6 and 8 channel presentations, the 8 channel output against FFmpeg's the disc's own lossless checks, and FFmpeg

FFmpeg's encoders do not write an IIR filter, LSB bypass, 7.1, a non-zero noise coefficient or shift, the Atmos substream or extra data. The hand-built streams carry all of them but the Atmos substream, and FFmpeg's decoder reads them to the same samples, except a negative output shift (which it does not apply) and a 16 bit MLP stream with bits below bit 8 (which it clears); 7.1 is checked through this library's encoder. What FFmpeg does not read has no external oracle: the extra data's layout, the DRC word's values, the block data CRC, the 16-channel substream (FFmpeg refuses its restart sync 0x31EC) and the end-of-stream marker in every unit (FFmpeg returns two of the twenty units of the hand-built stream). Validation says what that leaves.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• Several rules the specification states are not checked: saturation in Huffman decoding, coeff_q below 8, the range of filter coefficients and states, output_shift above max_shift, the extra data's length against the unit, the restart-gap rules. The encoder does not model the 30,000-byte FIFO of §18.1 and writes a restart interval of 1 unit throughout when asked, which §7.5 forbids. libs/truehd/ERRATA.md entry 41 lists them.
  • Noise: both generators are decoded. Generator 1 (restart sync 0x31EB) fills a buffer from the 256-entry table of TH spec §17.4 for every access unit and a matrix with a non-zero matrix_noise_shift adds a value of it to its sum (the buffer size, the start index and the stride are measured against FFmpeg and wait for the owner: ERRATA entry 44, question 43). LSB bypass is one explicit bit a sample from the block data under either sync and has nothing to do with the generators (§10.2.1). Generator 0, the default (0x31EA), is decoded from the specification's LFSR: two noise channels follow the matrix channels and enter through ordinary matrix coefficients; shr7 is 16 bits (§17.2). No stream FFmpeg writes uses a non-zero noise coefficient or shift; hand-built streams do, and FFmpeg's strict decode of them equals this library's.
  • Heavy DRC in the restart header (TH spec 12.2): where its bits sit cannot be told from the streams.
  • The block data CRC is not checked, only the length it follows.
  • The evolution frame is read (provisionally) and the object audio metadata in it is handed out as bytes; nothing decodes from either, and the signature and protection bytes are not verified.
  • The encoder does not write an IIR filter, LSB bypass, a negative output shift, heavy DRC, noise or MLP (ExperimentalTools::iir and lsb_bypass are refused with a reason), nor the Atmos substream. Against FFmpeg's encoder the streams are smaller on most material and larger at 192 kHz (the specification's order 4 against FFmpeg's 7), on full-scale square waves, with a restart interval of 1 and with the downmix presentations.
  • The object renderer and the Atmos substream are phase T2b. Python, JavaScript and Rust bindings over the C API (iclforge_truehd_* in the C API) are not written.
  • Content signing: nothing signs or checks a TrueHD stream, and an evolution payload is carried, not read. The owner's specification describes it as the container AC-4's content signature uses; see the seam for other codecs.
  • Protected files: a protected (Common Encryption) mlpa track is refused by the MP4 reader's code for protected audio, which names the scheme; no fixture or test covers an mlpa one.
  • Nothing outside the library uses it but forge (and the C API's callers): the Forge GUI, Hearth and Crucible do not link it, forge cut, cat, transcode, fmp4, monitor and play refuse it by name (the last four read the AC-3 or E-AC-3 track after a TrueHD one in a file that has both), and no device output sends a MAT burst. Development status has each as a row.

CI runs it twice: in the default arithmetic, and in the fixed-point tier (-DICLFORGE_DECODE_SCALAR=fixed, Q7.24 integers under a per-block exponent) which is what a part with no FPU wants and costs 0.37x the default build's instructions on the same leg. docs.title: Reading the evidence
docs.text:
Four strengths of claim appear throughout these tables, and the distance between them matters:

  • Confirmed on hardware. Somebody connected it and it worked: Windows passthrough, the Pi 4B driving an AVR, the Shield playing to a receiver.
  • Built and tested in CI. The code builds and its tests pass on hosted runners. The pull-request gate builds Linux GCC, the merge queue adds Windows MSVC, the run after a merge to main adds the other legs a merge can break, and the nightly run adds the rest (see CI for many agents). This is where macOS sits in full and where every desktop platform sits for anything that does not touch sound hardware. A leg whose failure fails no run is "experimental CI" in the tables.
  • Built, run under emulation. The bare-metal profile decodes correctly on QEMU, and so does the ESP32-S3 build. Correct output; nothing about timing on real silicon, which emulation cannot answer — the ESP32-S3's timing comes from a board, see Timing, and so does the ESP32-C6's, which QEMU does not emulate at all.
  • Written, never exercised. The macOS process tap, and the macOS half of Crucible. The code compiles and one test checks a version gate. Nothing more than that.

A target can sit at different levels for different things, and several do. macOS builds and tests under the second level while its process tap sits at the fourth. Read the platform page before depending on any of it.

For the ESP32 boards, Testing and benchmarking the ESP32 boards says which checks run on the host, under QEMU and in CI, which need a board, and what the boards measured.

docs.title: Codec detail
docs.text: Capabilities and limitations lists every coding mode, layout, sample rate, metadata field and Annex E tool with its spec citation. Desktop and WebAssembly builds expose the full AC-3 and E-AC-3 codec, and the AC-4 decoder and encoder (AC-4 decoding and encoding). Minimum-footprint and fixed-point builds narrow that surface for memory, arithmetic and timing constraints; the variant tables above and the individual bare-metal pages record those limits, and ESP32 memory layout sets the flash and RAM of the three ESP32 kits side by side. The AC-4 decoder is an option of the ESP-IDF component (CONFIG_ICLFORGE_AC4, for parts with an FPU) that has been measured on the ESP32-P4 only. The application coverage matrix shows which broad library capabilities each application exposes.

docs.title: Android (NVIDIA Shield)
docs.text: Android support is a separate, small, Shield-specific demo app, Shield Atmos Demo (apps/demos/android/), that plays an Atmos/JOC stream out through the Shield's HDMI passthrough output to an AV receiver, with a controller or remote moving one of a few objects around the room live. Neither forge nor forge-gui is ported to Android. The app exists to show the encoder's object audio moving in 3D space on consumer hardware, and is not a general-purpose encoding tool. This page covers what is specific to Android; for the core library and the desktop platforms, see Building from source and the other pages in this section.
