docs.title: Toolchains
docs.text:
CI builds with MSVC 14.51 (the Visual Studio 2026 Build Tools) and clang-cl 22.1; the development workstation is Windows 11 (build 26200).

Every Windows preset chainloads a toolchain file that locates cl.exe/clang-cl.exe and link.exe itself (via vswhere and vcvarsall.bat if a Developer PowerShell hasn't already set one up), so configuring works from an ordinary shell — no need to launch a Developer Command Prompt first. clang-cl is MSVC-ABI compatible, so it links the same vcpkg packages and the same prebuilt Qt kit as the MSVC build. See The compiler is pinned, not PATH-found for the mechanics.

docs.title: Audio backend: WASAPI
docs.text:
On Windows, the five pieces that touch sound hardware are all implemented over WASAPI:

  • iclforge::audio — live input/loopback capture through a lock-free SPSC ring.
  • iclforge::containers::iec61937::PassthroughDetector — recognising, from that same capture, that the endpoint is handing over IEC 61937 bursts (AC-3, E-AC-3 or AC-4) rather than PCM.
  • iclforge::audio::PassthroughSink — exclusive-mode/direct bitstream output, for both AC-3 and E-AC-3 burst framing (IEC 61937). AC-4 (IEC 61937-14) is refused here with kUnsupportedFormat: WASAPI asks for a compressed format by its KSDATAFORMAT_SUBTYPE_IEC61937_* subformat, and the Windows SDK (ksmedia.h, 10.0.26100) defines none for AC-4.
  • iclforge::audio::MonitorSink — shared-mode PCM playback: a non-bitstreamed preview/monitor path that decodes what is being encoded and plays it back on an ordinary output. It is also where forge monitor and forge play send an AC-4 stream, decoded, and where an AC-4 stream's objects arrive rendered to speakers by the layout renderer.
  • iclforge::audio::SpatialObjectSink — ISpatialAudioObjectRenderStream: decoded Atmos objects go out as dynamic objects at their real OAMD positions, and the bed's LFE (never a JOC output, TS 103 420 §6.3.2.2) as a static one. Behind forge spatial. This is the one path that lets Dolby's own renderer engage with this project's reconstructed objects at all — a licensed decoder otherwise refuses object decoding without a signing key this project doesn't ship (see Object signing) — and needs nothing but a spatial- sound-capable endpoint to do it, no AVR and no key. It takes E-AC-3 only: forge spatial reads no AC-4 stream (on a spatial-enabled endpoint it answers "not a valid E-AC-3 stream", exit code 2).

What each can carry:

Path Carries Does not carry Capture (iclforge::audio) PCM from an input, an endpoint's loopback or one process tree; IEC 61937 bursts that arrive as PCM, which the detector recognises for AC-3, E-AC-3 and AC-4 MonitorSink PCM the library decoded: AC-3, E-AC-3 (an Atmos stream's bed) and AC-4, whose objects the layout renderer puts on speakers A bitstream PassthroughSink IEC 61937 bursts of AC-3 and E-AC-3, the latter with its JOC objects AC-4, refused with kUnsupportedFormat SpatialObjectSink E-AC-3 object streams, as dynamic objects and a static LFE AC-4 objects

These five are not equally verified on hardware, and the project's own documentation is explicit about the difference.

MonitorSink is confirmed on hardware

forge monitor and forge live's monitor leg have played decoded AC-3 and E-AC-3 (including an Atmos stream's 5.1 bed) through a Realtek output in real time, and a live microphone capture→encode→monitor session has run end to end. Building this path on hardware surfaced two bugs that neither unit tests nor silent/synthetic input would have caught — a fixed submit-readiness threshold smaller than one chunk, which let the ring buffer silently perform a partial write while reporting failure, and the live pipeline's Atmos metering step writing past the end of a buffer sized for the object count rather than the bed's fixed six channels. Both are fixed; see libs/audio/src/backend/windows/monitor.cpp and run_live in apps/forge/cli/src/commands/live_audio.cpp.

MonitorSink: a format refusal is told apart from a WASAPI failure, and any rate plays

MonitorSink::start() reports MonitorError::kFormatRejected for AUDCLNT_E_UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT (0x88890008), checked on both the IAudioClient3 low-latency path and the ordinary fallback; every other failure in start() still reports kComFailure. That was added on 2026-09-22, debugging why iclforge-audio-tests "[monitor-unplug]" would not open the "AV Receiver (NVIDIA High Definition Audio)" HDMI endpoint the exclusive-mode passthrough confirmation below used: start() had no way to say why beyond "a Windows audio (WASAPI/COM) call failed", and a standalone WASAPI probe written outside this codebase found the refusal at 48 kHz on an endpoint whose shared-mode engine ran at 192 kHz, its Advanced-tab "Default Format", while the same formats at 192 kHz opened.

On 2026-09-26 Hearth would not play a 44.1 kHz AC-3 file on a machine whose only output, "Speakers (Realtek(R) Audio)", runs its shared-mode engine at 48 kHz: every play ended in kFormatRejected. The earlier reading, that such an endpoint "converts bit depth but not sample rate", was incomplete. That is what WASAPI's shared mode does for a client that asks for nothing more: it takes the mix format's own rate and channel count and refuses any other with AUDCLNT_E_UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT, unless the stream is initialised with AUDCLNT_STREAMFLAGS_AUTOCONVERTPCM, which puts the engine's own resampler and channel matrixer in front of the mix (AUDCLNT_STREAMFLAGS_SRC_DEFAULT_QUALITY picks its better filter). start() set neither flag, so every rate but the endpoint's own was refused, and a caller that opens at each item's own rate - Hearth - could not play a song there at all. A probe of that Realtek endpoint gave 0x88890008 at 44.1 kHz and at 96 kHz without the flag and success at both with it; 48 kHz opened either way. start() now sets both flags on its ordinary shared-mode initialise. The IAudioClient3 low-latency path is unchanged, and still falls back to that initialise when the engine will not run the format at its smallest period, so a format that needs converting plays through the fallback. kFormatRejected stays for what the converter cannot take. "[monitor-live]" opens at 44.1, 48 and 96 kHz on the default output, with silence, and needs each to play; "[hearth-device]" does the same through Hearth's own output sink, which no other test opens on a real device.

Playback position, pause and flush are confirmed; a multichannel patch is not

MonitorSink's playback position, pause()/resume() and flush() have been exercised against the default Realtek endpoint by iclforge-audio-tests "[monitor-live]" — a hidden case, since it needs a sound card and makes a noise: the position advances with the device's own clock, a pause holds it while the queue goes on taking frames, a flush drops both buffers and the count restarts, and playback resumes from the next submit. forge identify walked the tone across that endpoint's own speakers, over a 5.1 layout it can place only two channels of, and with the pair swapped.

What that machine cannot show is a multichannel patch: both its endpoints are stereo, and which speaker an output actually reaches is exactly what a two-channel device cannot disprove. That check needs an 8-channel endpoint — an AVR over HDMI as LPCM — and is forge identify 0 7.1.4 3 heard from the speaker each printed line names, then the same command with a patch that swaps two channels heard to swap those two speakers and nothing else.

SpatialObjectSink is confirmed against a real spatial endpoint

forge spatial has activated ISpatialAudioObjectRenderStream and rendered a real Atmos stream (4 orbiting objects, 8 s, this project's own encoder) against the default Realtek output after Windows Sonic for Headphones was enabled on it — 250 access units, zero underruns, clean shutdown. The kNoSpatialFormat refusal was confirmed the same session against a second endpoint that still had no spatial format enabled, and against the very endpoint used for the successful run, probed before Windows Sonic was turned on (GetMaxDynamicObjectCount read 0 everywhere on this machine at that point). What is not yet checked: a listening pass confirming the rendered audio actually arrives from where the OAMD positions say it should — nobody running this had ears in the loop, only the OS's own accept-and-render behaviour — and the "bed as static objects" branch beyond the LFE, since every stream this project's own encoder produces is dynamic-object-only (oamd.hpp's own documented shape); a third-party bed-plus-objects Annex E stream would be needed to exercise the rest of oba::bed_labels() against a verified coded-channel-order mapping.

Exclusive-mode passthrough bitstreaming is confirmed against a real receiver on Windows

An Onkyo TX-RZ740 was cabled to a Windows workstation via an Nvidia GPU's HDMI audio endpoint ("AV Receiver (NVIDIA High Definition Audio)"). IsFormatSupported answered yes for both KSDATAFORMAT_SUBTYPE_IEC61937_DOLBY_DIGITAL and ..._DOLBY_DIGITAL_PLUS — the first real device this has ever happened on — and forge play through PassthroughSink itself, not the PCM16-WAV workaround, locked the receiver onto AC-3 (Dolby Digital 5.1), then E-AC-3 (Dolby Digital Plus 5.1), then a signed Atmos stream (forge atmos ... sign-objects), which the receiver decoded as Atmos/DD+, 48 kHz in, 5.0.4 out, with the object's motion confirmed audible — the same result the Shield app got on this same receiver (see docs/platforms/android.md). Clean delivery throughout (0 underruns on the confirming Atmos run).

Getting there surfaced two real defects in PassthroughSink, both fixed: a cross-thread WASAPI crash (Activate/Initialize on the caller's thread, Start/GetBuffer on a worker thread — fine for MonitorSink's shared-mode path, fatal deep inside AUDIOSES.DLL for a real exclusive-mode bitstream client) and a stats bug where the per-callback "bursts rendered" counter truncated to zero almost every WASAPI callback, hanging the CLI's drain-wait loop forever after real playback had already finished. See libs/audio/src/backend/windows/passthrough.cpp.

The AC-3 bursts are byte-exact against FFmpeg's spdif muxer, and the E-AC-3 burst framing (data type 0x15, the 24576-byte/4x-carrier-rate burst, multi-syncframe accumulation, Pd in bytes not bits) is independently verified against both FFmpeg's spdif_header_eac3 and Microsoft's own "Representing Formats for IEC 61937 Transmissions" documentation, plus round-trip and real-audio unit tests — all of which held up against the real device too.

An endpoint that goes away mid-stream

Unplugging the cable, switching the receiver off or disabling the endpoint invalidates the stream: WASAPI answers AUDCLNT_E_DEVICE_INVALIDATED to the render thread's next call, and stops signalling the event it waits on, so a wait that times out asks the endpoint for its padding rather than waiting again. Either answer stops the sink — running() turns false, position() reports nothing, submit() refuses — and start() opens again with no stop() first, on the same endpoint once it is back. iclforge-audio-tests "[passthrough-unplug]" and "[monitor-unplug]" are hidden cases that take a person through it.

[passthrough-unplug] is confirmed, against the same AV Receiver endpoint the exclusive- mode validation above used: the cable was pulled mid-stream, and the sink noticed on its own — running() false, position()/can_submit()/submit()/paused() all answering as a stopped sink would, flush() returning at once, pause()/resume() both refusing with kNotRunning — then a second start(), with no stop() in between, reopened the same endpoint and played real frames once the cable went back in. [monitor-unplug] (MonitorSink's shared-mode path) has not yet been reported from this workstation's own receiver — its own hidden case opens the system's current default render endpoint rather than a named one, so what it actually exercises depends on whatever that is at the time.

SpatialObjectSink answers the same way, over its own two calls: BeginUpdatingAudioObjects failing outright, or — a removed endpoint need never signal the render-ready event again either — a wait that times out reading back GetMaxDynamicObjectCount on the ISpatialAudioClient instead of GetCurrentPadding. Not the stream's own GetAvailableDynamicObjectCount: Microsoft's reference for that call says not to use it once streaming has started, since BeginUpdatingAudioObjects already provides the same count from then on - the client-level call carries no such restriction. iclforge-audio-tests "[spatial-unplug]" is its own hidden case, not yet run against real hardware.

No EDID/ELD backend on Windows

forge play asks a chosen sink what it actually accepts before committing to a format — see CLI → Following the sink — and that read (iclforge::audio::sink_capabilities) exists today for ALSA and for PipeWire (see Linux). WASAPI answers "will this endpoint accept this format" (IsFormatSupported, what enumerate_render_devices() already uses) but does not re-expose the sink's own raw EDID-carried Short Audio Descriptors to user-mode code — the driver consumes them internally to decide what to offer and no documented public API was found that hands the source data back. play falls back to the same IsFormatSupported probe here, exactly as it always has.

The one avenue checked and ruled out: WMI's root\wmi monitor provider (WmiMonitorID/WmiMonitorDescriptor) does expose raw EDID bytes on Windows, but it is a display API keyed to the desktop/monitor topology, not an audio one. Tried against the Onkyo TX-RZ740 used for the passthrough confirmation above: Get-CimInstance -Namespace root\wmi -ClassName WmiMonitorID sees only the two actual desktop monitors on this machine (an Acer and a Samsung, both on DisplayPort); the receiver, despite having a live HDMI audio endpoint WASAPI opens and plays through, is not registered as a display Windows extends onto at all, so there is no WMI monitor entry to read its SADs from even if this project wired one up.

docs.title: TrueHD (MAT)
docs.text:
Not run on any platform

TrueHD over HDMI (MAT) has been built, and tested against software devices, and has not been run against a receiver on Windows. Nothing here says a receiver names the stream TrueHD. The code does what the carrier decision of 2026-10-29 says, which is itself provisional (libs/containers/ERRATA.md, question 7): eight channels of 16 bits at 192 kHz for content in the 48 kHz family and 176.4 kHz for the 44.1 kHz family, 3,840 frames to a 61,440-byte burst. The list of what has been run is apps/hearth/engine/src/mat_status.hpp, and the output decision quotes it.

Exclusive mode asks for TrueHD by KSDATAFORMAT_SUBTYPE_IEC61937_DOLBY_MLP ({0000000c-0cea-0010-8000-00aa00389b71}, taken from ksmedia.h in the 10.0.26100 SDK, and compared with the SDK's own initialiser in a test), on eight channels of 16 bits at the link rate, with the 7.1 speaker mask and the encoded fields as the other two families have them (the content rate and eight channels). Those last fields, and the mask, are what Microsoft's description of the MLP format would settle and this project has not seen a driver accept or refuse: it is why the format builders are in their own header (libs/audio/src/backend/windows/iec61937_format.hpp) with a test of every field (test_windows_formats.cpp). enumerate_render_devices asks IsFormatSupported for it and sets supports_mat_passthrough on a yes; nothing has opened it.

docs.title: When a packet was captured, and a requested period
docs.text:
A microphone is only useful to an application that knows when each sample was captured, so that a take or a score can be placed against a playback position. Capture gives that, alongside the samples, and stays what it was for a caller that does not ask:

  • Capture::stamps() is a second lock-free ring, one CaptureStamp per packet: the index of the packet's first frame in the stream the ring carries (silence fill included), and the time it was captured, in nanoseconds on std::chrono::steady_clock's clock. WASAPI's own packet position (GetBuffer's QPC position, in 100 ns) is read from the performance counter, which the MSVC standard library's steady clock counts from the same zero; a test holds the two to that. A packet the driver flags as having a bad time gets no stamp. For a loopback the stamp is when the endpoint will play the packet, a little after it arrives.
  • CaptureTimeline (capture_timeline.hpp) turns the last 64 stamps into the time of any frame, and a frame's index back from a time, by a least-squares line through them: a driver reads its clock when it gets round to it, so the mean of a run of stamps is better than the nearest. It also reports the rate the device actually runs at.
  • Capture::start(device, kind, CaptureOptions) can ask for a packet period in frames. Where the engine has a shared-mode period of that size (IAudioClient3) the stream opens at the nearest it offers; otherwise it opens as before. Capture::timing() says what was given: the period and the endpoint's buffer.

What this does not tell a caller is the delay between a sound and the microphone's stamp: the device and its driver add some. On the development workstation (a webcam's microphone and the motherboard's speakers, Windows 11 build 26200) a click handed to the render stream reached the application through the microphone about 130 ms later, with less than a millisecond of spread, and the engine's smallest shared-mode period (10 ms for both endpoints) bought nothing. A caller that needs the figure for its own equipment has to measure it.

docs.title: Per-process loopback and device notifications
docs.text:
Two more WASAPI paths, added to the shared audio layer for Crucible and available to anything else that links it, both Windows-only in the backend tree:

  • Capture::start_process_loopback(pid, mode, format) — ActivateAudioInterfaceAsync with AUDIOCLIENT_ACTIVATION_TYPE_PROCESS_LOOPBACK, which captures what one process tree renders and nothing else, whichever endpoint it renders to. Needs Windows 10 build 20348 or later; process_loopback_available() asks the kernel (RtlGetVersion, not the manifest-bound GetVersionEx) and audio_backend().process_loopback reports the same answer. A process-loopback client has no GetMixFormat, so the caller states the format and the engine converts — 48 kHz float at two or eight channels is confirmed. The tap is polled and silence-filled exactly like endpoint loopback, because a quiet process delivers no packets. The library refuses a process id nobody owns (kProcessNotFound) because the OS does not: such a tap activates and delivers zeros forever, as does a tap whose process has since exited.
  • DeviceWatcher — IMMNotificationClient registered with the MMDevice enumerator on a worker thread that owns the COM apartment. Default-changed events are delivered for the console role only (the one every sink in this tree opens; the other two roles would report the same change twice more), and property-value changes (a volume nudge, a rename) are dropped as noise. The listener is hand-rolled IUnknown rather than a WRL RuntimeClass, for the same include-order reason capture.cpp spells its GUIDs out by hand.

Both confirmed on the development workstation, 2026-09-03

Through the raw WASAPI spike first (apps/crucible/spikes/README.md, S1: sixteen taps at once, exact separation, the mute and exclusive-mode hazards) and then through these library entry points themselves (s1_library_tap), on Windows 11 build 26200. Not yet exercised on a hosted CI runner beyond the device-free contract in libs/audio/tests/test_audio_backend.cpp, which does start and stop a real watcher wherever the backend exists.

MonitorSink::start also takes a low_latency flag, added for the demo's one-block mode: it asks IAudioClient3::GetSharedModeEnginePeriod for the engine's smallest shared-mode period for the stream's format and opens with InitializeSharedAudioStream at that, falling back to the default period where the interface is missing or the engine refuses the format at that size; the other backends take the flag and ignore it. On the workstation's Realtek endpoint it changes nothing, and the spike's period_probe (apps/crucible/spikes/s5_latency/) says why: the engine answers 480 frames, 10 ms, for the default, fundamental, minimum and maximum period alike, for the demo's float format and for the mix format both. IAudioClient's "minimum 3 ms" device period is the exclusive-mode floor, not a shared-mode offer. A device that offers 2.7 ms will get it; this one does not.

docs.title: Passthrough capture
docs.text:
The reverse direction — a WASAPI endpoint delivering IEC 61937 rather than PCM, which is what an HDMI or S/PDIF capture card gives, and what a render-endpoint loopback gives when the app playing into it is bitstreaming — is the same framing read backwards, and the same facts govern it. The bursts arrive as ordinary PCM16 samples: IAudioClient has no way to say "this is Dolby Digital", and Capture converts them to float by dividing by 32768, which loses nothing.

iclforge::containers::iec61937::PassthroughDetector recognises the framing from those floats — a Pa/Pb preamble at a repetition period with a syncframe behind it (0x0B77 for AC-3 and E-AC-3, the AC-4 sync word for AC-4) — and forge record switches to writing the elementary stream instead of encoding the bursts as audio; forge live stops with an error instead. forge unspdif does the same job on a capture already saved to disk. carrier_from_capture is the conversion back to PCM16 words, exact for all 65536 of them.

Passthrough capture has never been confirmed against a real capture device

No HDMI or S/PDIF capture card, and no loopback of a bitstreaming player, has been available during development — the same gap the passthrough output side has, from the same missing hardware. What is verified: the burst de-framing itself round-trips byte-exactly against both this project's own wrapper and FFmpeg's spdif muxer, for AC-3 and E-AC-3 and for both 16-bit word orders; the float→PCM16 recovery is exact for every int16 value; and the detector reaches "not a bitstream" on real audio and silence alike. What is not: that a real device's samples reach Capture unmodified in the first place. A shared-mode endpoint that resamples or mixes would destroy the bursts before anything here saw them, which shows up as no detection rather than as wrong output.

docs.title: Qt (the windows: GUI, Hearth, Crucible)
docs.text:
forge-gui needs a prebuilt Qt 6.5+ kit, discovered by cmake/FindQt6.cmake — never from vcpkg. Hearth's and Crucible's windows need Qt 6.8 or later; on an older kit each is skipped with a warning and its engine still builds. CI installs Qt 6.10.3. ICLFORGE_BUILD_GUI defaults ON on Windows. FindQt6.cmake widens CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH to the usual install roots (C:/Qt, %USERPROFILE%/Qt, D:/Qt); to point at a specific kit explicitly:

cmake --preset config-windows-msvc-debug -DICLFORGE_QT_ROOT=D:/Qt/6.8.3/msvc2022_64

See Qt for the full discovery order and options.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
cmake --preset config-windows-msvc-debug
cmake --build --preset build-windows-msvc-debug
ctest --preset test-windows-msvc-debug

Drop -debug for a Release build. The window of Hearth builds by default (ICLFORGE_BUILD_HEARTH is on); Crucible is opt-in with -DICLFORGE_BUILD_CRUCIBLE=ON. Swap msvc for llvm throughout to build with clang-cl instead:

cmake --preset config-windows-llvm-debug
cmake --build --preset build-windows-llvm-debug
ctest --preset test-windows-llvm-debug

A vcpkg checkout is needed (ICL_VCPKG_STORE makes one on the first configure, or VCPKG_ROOT names yours; see building.md). It supplies Catch2 and {fmt}, mbedTLS, cpp-httplib, libFLAC, Opus and mdns through the hearth feature the desktop presets select, and Boost and Tracy only if you opt into the adm/profiling features; see building.md. See Presets for the full preset table and the ci-windows-msvc / ci-windows-llvm workflow presets that chain all three steps.

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text:
cpack --preset pack-windows-msvc

Produces a ZIP, plus an NSIS installer on top if makensis is on PATH (CI's windows-msvc leg installs it via Chocolatey automatically and fails the leg if the installer doesn't come out the other end — see releasing.md; locally, install NSIS yourself or cpack falls back to ZIP-only with a message(WARNING ...) explaining why). pack-windows-llvm is the clang-cl equivalent, and pack-windows-msvc-arm64 the ARM64 one (below). windows-msvc is the only leg packaged in ordinary runs — CI packages it in every run that builds it (the run after a merge, the nightly run) and uploads the result as a workflow artifact, a standing smoke test of the packaging path; a tagged release packages every release_package leg (Windows x64 and ARM64, Linux x64 and arm64, macOS). See Packaging.

An x64 installer built from main (iclforge-<version>-win64.exe) carries forge, forge-gui and hearth; the one in v0.10.0-beta.1, the latest release, predates Hearth's packaging and carries the first two. The Start Menu folder has an entry for forge-gui, one for hearth, and a "forge command prompt" with the install's bin on PATH. The ZIP splits by component: the runtime archive, an iclforge-dev-* library archive, an iclforge-hearth-* archive and an iclforge-crucible-* archive, of which the release has the first two. Crucible stays out of the installer while its driver is test-signed (cmake/CPackProjectConfig.cmake).

The NSIS installer also registers .ac3 and .ec3 as IclForge.Stream, pointing shell\open\command at the installed hearth.exe (forge-gui.exe in a build with no Hearth) and nudging Explorer to pick up the change with SHChangeNotify, and reverses both keys on uninstall — CPACK_NSIS_EXTRA_INSTALL_COMMANDS/_UNINSTALL_COMMANDS in cmake/Packaging.cmake. Nothing registers .ac4. The installer and every binary in it are unsigned (Authenticode signing waits on a certificate), so SmartScreen may warn on install. CI builds and verifies the installer itself in every run that packages Windows; running it and double-clicking a .ac3 file to confirm the file association end to end is still a manual, unautomated check.

docs.title: Windows Firewall
docs.text:
hearth and hearth-testsink each open a socket a Windows Firewall rule has to allow: hearth's mDNS browse for _sendspin._tcp players, and hearth-testsink's own Sendspin listener and mDNS advertisement. Rather than leave this to Windows' own "these features have been blocked" prompt, iclforge::sendspin::firewall::ensure_inbound_rule() (libs/sendspin/include/iclforge/sendspin/firewall.hpp) adds the rule itself, through the same INetFwPolicy2 COM policy object the Settings app's firewall page edits, the first time it finds none already there for that executable and port.

Adding a rule needs an elevated token. ensure_inbound_rule() adds it directly when the calling process is already elevated; otherwise, on an interactive desktop session, it relaunches its own executable once with a UAC prompt (--ac3-sendspin-firewall-helper, maybe_run_as_firewall_helper_and_exit() in the same header) to make just that one COM call, then returns to running unelevated. A non-interactive session - a service, a CI runner - is left for Windows' own prompt instead, same as before this existed. Every rule is scoped to the private and domain network profiles only, never public, and to LocalSubnet: this only ever opens LAN discovery/streaming traffic to the executable that is actually listening, never to the internet or to a different program.

A loopback-only bind needs none of this - Windows does not gate loopback traffic - and is skipped before ensure_inbound_rule() is ever called. hearth-testserver's own ServerHost and reference sink are loopback-only today and so never reach it; the Sendspin and Hearth test binaries' own ServerHost fixtures are the same. Linux and macOS build a no-op implementation of the same two functions and never show a prompt of any kind.

docs.title: ARM64
docs.text:
A third Windows leg, windows-msvc-arm64, runs on GitHub's hosted windows-11-vs2026-arm runner, an ARM64 host. It shares every file the two x64 legs above use; only the vcpkg triplet and the resolved MSVC tools directory differ. It is experimental: true (continue-on-error, so a failure fails no run) and belongs to the nightly tier, so it runs in the nightly run and in a release, not after each merge (.github/ci/legs.jsonc). Its packages have shipped since v0.10.0-beta.1.

Toolchain. cmake/vcpkg/triplets/arm64-windows-msvc.cmake sets VCPKG_TARGET_ARCHITECTURE arm64 (same CRT/library linkage policy as x64-windows-msvc.cmake). cmake/toolchains/windows.msvc.toolchain.cmake resolves the target-appropriate MSVC tools subdirectory the same way linux.gcc.toolchain.cmake/macos.llvm.toolchain.cmake already resolve their own arm64 legs — generically, not hardcoded — and, for the arm64 case specifically, tries more than one candidate directory: bin/Hostarm64/arm64 (a native ARM64-hosted toolset) first, falling back to bin/Hostx64/arm64 (the x64-hosted cross toolset, which also produces ARM64 binaries, via x64 tools running under Windows' x64 emulation). cmake/toolchains/windows.msvc.environment.cmake's vcvarsall.bat bootstrap and .github/actions/setup-msvc-env's CI-side environment loader probe the same pair of vcvarsall.bat arguments (arm64 native, then amd64_arm64 cross), since the target architecture's CRT/Windows SDK library directories have to match whichever compiler actually got picked, or linking fails outright with a machine-type mismatch.

On the runner's windows-11-vs2026-arm64 image (version 20260920.164.1) the first candidate wins. The leg's log of 2026-09-28 shows vcvarsall.bat arm64 succeeding and MSVC toolset 14.51.36231 under bin\HostARM64\ARM64, the toolset version the x64 legs report. That run built the CLI and passed all 2,984 ctest cases. The image before it, windows-11-arm, carried MSVC 14.44.35207 (VS2022), which is why the "Report and assert toolchain versions" step in .github/actions/build-leg/action.yml only prints the toolset for this leg instead of asserting the pin the x64 legs share; the exception is still in place.

CLI-only, for now. Unlike every other packageable Windows/Linux/macOS leg, windows-msvc-arm64 does not build forge-gui — ICLFORGE_BUILD_GUI is off in CMakePresets.json's windows-msvc-arm64 preset. Qt's only Windows ARM64 kit for the pinned 6.10.3 (Qt has offered one since 6.8) is win64_msvc2022_arm64_cross_compiled (python -m aqt list-qt windows desktop --arch 6.10.3) — a cross-compile kit that expects a paired win64_msvc2022_64 install to supply its host build tools (moc/uic/rcc), and aqtinstall/jurplel/install-qt-action have a documented CI bug against exactly that combination (qtpaths.bat pointing at the wrong x64 setup). That is complexity a native-ARM64-host build doesn't need for a first pass, so this leg stays CLI-only. Revisiting this is a natural fast-follow once Qt ships a native-hosted ARM64 Windows kit.

Gold-reference gate. choco's ffmpeg package is x64-only, so this leg installs a static win-arm64 FFmpeg build from BtbN/FFmpeg-Builds (a dated autobuild-* release, pinned in the "Install ffmpeg (Windows ARM64)" step of _ci-windows.yml) instead of choco install ffmpeg.

Unsigned binaries. Like every other Windows binary this project ships today, this leg's output is unsigned — Authenticode signing is blocked project-wide on acquiring a certificate, not on code, and that applies here exactly as it does to the x64 legs. It is worth stating plainly for ARM64 specifically: SmartScreen will warn on install, and an ARM64 user has fewer alternative trusted sources to fall back on than an x64 user does.

docs.title: CI
docs.text: windows-msvc and windows-llvm run in the run after a merge to main, and windows-msvc-arm64 in the nightly run; Windows MSVC also builds in the merge queue. The stages are set out in CI for many agents, and the full matrix, including the Linux and macOS legs and the coverage and FFmpeg-validation jobs, is in Verified configuration. CI runs the CLI and GUI on both x64 Windows legs; the ARM64 leg runs the CLI only (see above) and fails no run while it proves itself out. A separate windows-driver job builds Crucible's null-sink driver, test-signed, on GitHub's windows-latest whenever the Windows lane runs, and alone when a ci.yml dispatch names it (-f legs=windows-driver; see the driver page).

docs.title: Bare metal
docs.text:
Five targets, one profile: iclforge::ac3_minimal, the minimum-footprint build of the codec — one static library, no exceptions, no RTTI, decode-only or encode-only, and none of the direct-form transform tables. What differs between the targets is the part and, on parts with no floating-point unit, the arithmetic tier the decoder runs in (the plan).

AC-4 is built from its own libraries (libs/ac4), the decoder only: no bare-metal build has the AC-4 encoder. The Cortex-M3 leg probes it, and the ESP32-P4 decodes it behind CONFIG_ICLFORGE_AC4, to 5.1 in real time. The ESP32-S3 decodes it with its state in PSRAM, under QEMU in CI and on a board, where 2.0 keeps up (phase D14c). The ESP32-C6 and the ESP32-C3 build it in the fixed-point tier (phase D14d of planning/ac4.md); a decode does not fit a C6 beside WiFi, and on a board the play is refused. A Hearth sink built with the decoder takes AC-4 in a Sendspin group on the P4 and the S3 (Hearth); the published P4 and S3 sink images have the decoder, the C6's has it off.

TrueHD and MLP (libs/truehd) are in none of these builds: the component, the probes and the sinks do not compile the library, and nobody has measured what a decoder for its rates (up to 192 kHz) and channel counts (up to 8, or 16 in the Atmos substream) would need from these parts. The variant table has the row, and the roadmap the work.

The variant table keeps codec support, Hearth support, distribution and evidence separate.

docs.title: Bare-metal and ESP32 support by variant
docs.text:

docs.title: Which page
docs.text:
• Building the library itself for a part with no operating system? Start at Cortex-M3 — it's the reference leg CI measures the profile on, and the page that explains what the profile gives up.
  • Have an ESP32-S3 board? ESP32-S3 is real time on real hardware, with two example players (i2s_player, hearth_sink) that drive I2S, and the Sendspin sink. AC-3 and E-AC-3 only.
  • Have an ESP32-C3 (or another part with no FPU)? ESP32-C3 covers the fixed-point tier and what has and hasn't been measured on it. AC-3 and E-AC-3 only.
  • Have an ESP32-C6? ESP32-C6 has the fixed-point and float tiers timed on a board, with and without WiFi and a stream arriving, and which streams fit. AC-3 and E-AC-3 only.
  • Have an ESP32-P4? ESP32-P4 is the "best" tier of the shared sink family. Its probe is real time on every fixture with no network, and hearth_sink plays a paired Sendspin stream over Wi-Fi through the board's onboard ESP32-C6. If the board is pre-production silicon like the one this was measured on, the page also has a chip-revision trap worth reading before flashing anything. It decodes AC-4 behind a switch, from an HTTP source or a Sendspin group: 2.0 and 5.1 in real time, 5.1.4 slower (AC-4).
  • Porting, tuning or debugging memory on an ESP32 board? ESP32 memory layout has the flash map, the internal RAM split, what lives in PSRAM, the heap floors and what each codec costs on the S3, the C6 and the P4, side by side.
  • Building with ESPHome instead of raw ESP-IDF? ESPHome is the external component. It decodes AC-3 only, and it is not a media_player or speaker source.
  • Building hearth_sink for a dev kit, adding a Kconfig key or changing a board's configuration? ESP32 build profiles has the locked configuration of each board, the guard CI holds a build to, the commands to build a board from its profile, and what a change to one has to carry.
  • Changing the ESP32 firmware, or a decoder it links? Testing and benchmarking the boards says what is tested on the host, under QEMU and in CI, what needs a board, and how a board's plays are held to a recorded baseline.

docs.title: Testing and benchmarking the ESP32 boards
docs.text:
How the hearth_sink firmware (firmware/hearth-sink) is held to account on the ESP32-S3, the ESP32-C6 and the ESP32-P4: what is tested with no board, what CI runs and in which lane, and what is played on a board and compared with a recorded baseline. It is for a developer who changes the firmware, a decoder it links, or the tools around it.

Status as of 2026-10-29

Four of the five build profiles that a board can run have a baseline recorded on a board: s3-n16r8 (S3a), c6-16mb, p4-rev1 (P4a) and p4-rev3 (the P4X kit). c6-4mb has none, since no board of that shape has run the suite. The board suite is run by hand: no CI job has a board.

2026-10-29: s3-n16r8-ac4 was folded into s3-n16r8, which took the decoder, the 64 KB data cache and the AC-4 plays' list (it keeps its 4 KB allocation limit), and p4-rev3 took the decoder and the four AC-4 HTTP rows; both were re-recorded on a board (the tables below).

2026-10-29: p4-rev1-ac4 was folded into p4-rev1 (the same fragments and locked values, so the same hash): its baseline is now p4-rev1's, and every p4-rev1-ac4 column and row below is p4-rev1's figures. The old p4-rev1 baseline (without AC-4) is gone.

A profile is one locked build of the firmware for one board (firmware/hearth-sink/profiles.json, read by tools/hearth/sink_profile.py). An image carries its profile's id and a 12-digit hash of the profile's fragments and locked values, and reports both in GET /hardware. The design records for this page are planning/esp32-platform-profiles.md and planning/esp32-board-bench.md.

docs.text: Layer What it holds Where it runs Needs a board Host tests of libs/device The device-side logic that needs no SDK Pull-request gate, Linux GCC build No Tests of the tools The suite, the bench and the flash tool against stand-ins; suite.json and the baselines against the tree Pull-request gate, Static No Profile guard, configure only Every profile configured and held to its locked values Pull-request gate, ESP32 profiles No QEMU, ESP32-S3 The probes, hearth_sink's plays, the release shape, a Sendspin play esp lane, after a merge and nightly No QEMU, ESP32-C3 The fixed-point decoder's PCM, bit for bit esp lane No Builds with no emulator The C6 and P4 images, built and held to their profiles and budgets, never run esp lane No The board suite Plays on the part, with Wi-Fi up: correctness, decode time, stack, heap By hand Yes

docs.title: Host tests
docs.text:
libs/device is the device-side logic written without the ESP-IDF, so that a desktop compiler builds and tests it: the interleave and the slot conversion, the playout and DAC queue models, the sink planner, the block and log rings, the Improv provisioning protocol, the pairing records, the firmware image and trial rules, and the hardware report. Its tests are one Catch2 binary, iclforge-device-tests:

cmake --preset config-linux-gcc && cmake --build --preset build-linux-gcc
ctest --preset test-linux-gcc -L device

The Python tools have tests beside them (tools/hearth/test_*.py, standard library only):

python -m unittest discover --start-directory tools/hearth --pattern 'test_*.py'

tools/hearth/test_board_suite.py runs the board suite against a stand-in board that answers with what the boards printed on 2026-10-12, and holds the files to the tree: every stream of suite.json is in the repository, every AC-4 row names a pin the host holds, every profile has a play list, and a committed baseline holds exactly its profile's rows. tools/hearth/sink_build_fixture.py makes a hearth_sink build directory from nothing (an app image with a valid checksum and SHA-256, a partition table, flash_args) for the packaging, installer and update tests.

docs.title: QEMU: the S3 and the C3
docs.text:
The esp lane runs two parts under QEMU, in Espressif's espressif/idf:v6.1 image.

ESP32-S3 (build-esp32s3, qemu-system-xtensa):

  • the minimum-footprint probe, in its decode, encode and AC-4 builds (tools/checks/run_esp32s3_probe.sh);
  • hearth_sink with a capture sink in place of I2S: the flash-backed FAT source, TDM at 16-bit slots and at sixteen slots, a height-object stream rendered onto 7.1.4, an E-AC-3 stream fetched over QEMU's Ethernet, the device's web page driven by a browser, and a firmware update over the network;
  • the stream set: 38 streams (5 AC-3, 33 E-AC-3) in firmware/hearth-sink/www/ with a manifest, streams.json, that gives each slot's level on a 7.1.4 output. The step "Play the stream set onto 7.1.4 over QEMU's Ethernet" plays every stream not marked as needing PSRAM (two are) through POST /play, and tools/checks/check_stream_set.py holds each play to the manifest: result=pass, no byte skipped for sync, the stream's access units, and every slot within 1% + 20 of the host's level. The plan is planning/esp32-stream-set.md;
  • the release shape: the s3-n16r8 profile's own fragments with one overlay, qemu-net, which changes what QEMU has no hardware for and nothing else. The step "Play the S3 board's release shape over QEMU's Ethernet" holds the build to the profile (sink_profile.py verify --overlay qemu-net), waits for the boot budget: line, reads the profile and its hash from GET /hardware, plays an AC-3 2/0, an E-AC-3 2/0 and a 5.1 with objects to result=pass with every unit, holds the console to the lines that say the rings and stacks are in PSRAM (sink_profile.py expect-console), and checks the console for a panic, a second boot or a failed allocation (tools/checks/check_esp_console.py --min-budget-headroom 4096).

hearth-esp32s3 then plays to the emulated board over Sendspin with the repository's hearth-testserver, holds its levels to a test sink's, and gives a board with no network one over Improv.

ESP32-C3 (build-esp32c3, qemu-system-riscv32): the fixed-point probe (tools/checks/run_esp32c3_probe.sh). The fixed-point tier decodes to the same PCM on every machine, and this leg holds the probe's pcm_hash lines to testdata/fixed-probe-pcm-hashes.json, the values the x86-64 host and the Cortex-M3 leg are held to.

docs.title: What QEMU cannot run
docs.text:
• The ESP32-C6. ESP-IDF v6.1's qemu-system-riscv32 emulates one Espressif machine, esp32c3, and idf.py qemu refuses the C6. CI builds the C6 probe with both of its network loads and the c6-4mb and c6-16mb images, holds each image to its profile and budgets, and runs none of them.
  • The ESP32-P4. There is no emulator for the part. CI builds the P4 probe and the p4-rev1, and p4-rev3 images (the AC-4 decoder is in p4-rev1 since 2026-10-29), held the same way.
  • On the S3: Wi-Fi, I2S, octal PSRAM and the USB console. The qemu-net overlay puts Ethernet, the capture sink, quad PSRAM and UART0 in their place.
  • Speed. QEMU is not cycle-accurate. The probes print us_per_frame under it and no gate reads it.
  • A board's heap. With no Wi-Fi the emulated S3 has 226,679 bytes of internal RAM free at boot and a largest block of 135,168; an S3 board with the network up had 86,231 and 31,744 (2026-10-12). A play that fails on a board for want of a 32 KB block passes under QEMU, so the release-shape step checks where a stack was placed and leaves the heap budget to the board suite.

Every real-time figure, every heap figure with Wi-Fi up, and everything a C6 or a P4 does when it runs comes from a board.

docs.title: What runs in CI, and in which lane
docs.text:
Job Workflow Runs Holds Static pr-gate.yml → _static.yml Every pull request and merge-queue entry The tools' tests (the suite's among them), sink_profile.py check-docs, sink_profile.py check-change Linux GCC build pr-gate.yml A pull request or queue entry that changes code Every ctest case, the device tests among them ESP32 profiles pr-gate.yml → _profiles.yml A pull request or queue entry that changes firmware/hearth-sink/, firmware/esp-idf/ or the profile tools; every push to main All seven profiles configured with idf.py reconfigure and held by sink_profile.py verify: fragments, locked values, watched keys. No compile, so no size budget build-esp32s3, hearth-esp32s3, build-esp32c3, package-esp32-firmware, build-footprint ci.yml → _build.yml, the esp lane A push to main that lights the lane, and the nightly run The QEMU runs above; every profile built and held by verify with its app, bootloader and static-RAM budgets (idf.py size); the published images packaged

The esp lane does not run on a pull request, so a QEMU failure or a broken budget shows red on main after the merge. A branch that wants the lane first asks for it with gh workflow run ci.yml --ref <branch>. The lane's paths and the fan-out rule are on CI lanes, and the gate's stages on the CI pipeline.

Each step after the first probe in build-esp32s3 and build-esp32c3 runs when an earlier step has failed (if: !cancelled(), #1491 and #1499). Before that, a red probe on 2026-10-12 skipped every firmware build and profile guard after it for fourteen hours, and a static-RAM budget that no C6 image met went unreported.

docs.title: The play suite
docs.text:
tools/hearth/board_suite.py plays a profile's fixed list of streams on a board and holds the run to that profile's baseline. The list is firmware/hearth-sink/suite.json:

Key Holds format The file's format number, 1 note What the file is frame_us 32,000: the microseconds an AC-3 or E-AC-3 frame lasts, which decode time is taken over tolerance The suite's margins (below), with the measurements they came from streams Each stream by name: its file in the repository, its codec, its units (access units), and for AC-4 the host pin it is held to profiles Per profile: plays (the rows, in order), its own tolerance over the suite's, and baseline_accepted where a baseline is kept under an older hash

A row names a stream and how it is played. python tools/hearth/board_suite.py plan --profile s3-n16r8 prints a profile's rows. Every profile with a board plays 30 s of AC-3 2.0 at 192 kbit/s and 30 s of E-AC-3 2.0 at 96 kbit/s (938 frames each); every profile but the C6's adds three- and four-frame AC-4 streams whose PCM the host pins.

docs.title: What a run does
docs.text:
python tools/hearth/board_suite.py run --profile s3-n16r8 --board S3a --session <id> \
    --restart --boots 3 --repeat 2 --compare firmware/hearth-sink/baselines/s3-n16r8.json

In this order, stopping at the first refusal:

  1. Booking. It takes the board's lock (below) and releases it at the end if it took it.
  2. Identity. GET /hardware must give the profile's id and the hash of the file's current definition, and GET /status must say stopped. A board running another profile, an older definition or an image built with neither is refused: its figures are another build's.
  3. Boot. With --restart it restarts the board and reads the boot budget: line; --boots N restarts N times and keeps the worst boot.
  4. Plays. It serves the repository's streams from the machine it runs on and plays each row over POST /play, polls GET /status to the play's end, then reads the play's lines from GET /log. --repeat N plays a row N times.
  5. Asserts, per row: the play finished, the verdict line says result=pass, every unit was decoded, no byte was skipped to resynchronise, the sink did not underrun, no allocation failed, the board did not reboot, and for an AC-4 row the PCM hash is the host's.
  6. Figures, per row: the decoder's time per frame, the decode stack's free bytes, the sink queue's least headroom. Over --repeat plays it keeps the median time and the worst of the rest.
  7. The record. It writes board-run.json. --compare FILE holds the run to a baseline; --record writes the profile's baseline from a run with no finding.

The exit code is 0 for a run that holds, 1 for a finding or a regression, and 2 for a refusal.

docs.title: The PCM hash
docs.text:
An AC-4 row's stream has a pin: the name of a hash in testdata/ac4-probe-pcm-hashes.json, which is the host's hash of that stream's decoded PCM, held on the x86-64 host and on the Cortex-M3 under QEMU. The board prints its own hash of the play on the ac4.<label>= line and the suite requires the two to be equal. For the three 2.0 streams they are, on the S3 and on the P4.

  • The hash is on the line only in an image built with the measure overlay (CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_AC4_PCM_HASH=1). The overlay does not change the profile's hash. A row played on an image without it fails with "no PCM hash on the AC-4 line".
  • A hash that differs from the pin means the board decoded other samples than the host does for the same stream. The row fails; nothing is recorded.
  • A stream the sink cannot play in its own layout has no host hash. The 5.1 stream has pin_layout: 5.1. The image's I2S sink has two outputs, so the decoder folds the stream to 2.0, which is other PCM than the pin's. The row is recorded with its layout and its own hash, and compare holds later runs to that hash. Whether the six-output render equals the host's is not tested by this suite; ESP32-P4 → AC-4 has the 5.1 measurements.

AC-3 and E-AC-3 rows carry no PCM hash, and no row played over Sendspin does. Those are held by their unit count, the verdict and the absence of a resynchronised byte.

docs.title: The real-time figure
docs.text:
decoder_permille is the time the decoder takes for one frame, in thousandths of the time that frame's audio lasts. 1000 is real time exactly. 123 is 12.3% of it: about eight frames decoded in the time one plays. How it is taken depends on the row:

Row Taken from Over AC-3 or E-AC-3 over POST /play us_per_frame less render_us_per_frame and sink_us_per_frame, from GET /status 32,000 µs AC-4 over POST /play The decoder_permille of the board's ac4.<label>= line The audio of a frame Any row over Sendspin burst_us of the board's sendspin.stream= line: its mean time for a burst less the sink's write 32,000 µs; for AC-4 the stream's period_us, 42,667

The Sendspin figure includes the renderer, which the /play figure subtracts, so a Sendspin row is compared with its own baseline and not with the /play row of the same stream.

realtime_permille in GET /status is not this figure. On an I2S sink it includes the wait for the DAC, and it read 981 to 992 for every stereo play on an S3 whatever was decoded.

docs.title: The tolerance
docs.text:
compare holds each figure to the baseline's with a margin from suite.json. The suite's margins were measured on an S3 over ten plays a row; a profile whose figures spread wider has its own, each with the spread it was measured from in a note.

Figure A regression when Profiles with their own margin Decoder time per frame Over the baseline by more than the larger of 5% and 5 permille p4-rev1: 12% (its AC-4 rows are three or four frames, and a play varies by about 6%) Decode stack free More than 512 bytes under Sink queue's least headroom More than 2 ms under Boot: largest internal block More than 1,024 bytes under c6-16mb: 12,288; p4-rev1: 8,192 (the block steps by 4 KB from boot to boot) Boot: internal RAM free More than 2,048 bytes under p4-rev1: 4,096 Glitched plays of a Sendspin row More than one over the baseline's count The S3 allows the E-AC-3 row two Least heap during a Sendspin play Held only for a row that names a margin S3: 2,048 for E-AC-3 and AC-4 music; c6-16mb: 3,072 for E-AC-3 State, units, boot verdict, PCM hash Any difference Sink underruns on a /play row Any

Every margin runs one way: a figure better than the baseline never fails a run. A decoder time under the baseline by more than the margin is printed as improved: … re-baseline, and the change that made the speed-up records the new baseline, so the next regression is measured from there.

docs.title: What a mismatch means
docs.text: The run says Meaning What to do the board says it is '…', not <profile>, or carries <profile> at hash … The image is another profile, or was built from another definition of this one Build the profile from the tree under test and put it on the board the board's /status is 'playing' (or flash) The board is in use, or a play was left running Find who is using it before touching it A finding on a row (… units, expected …, sink underrun(s), failed allocation(s), the board rebooted during the play) The play went wrong on this image Read the board's log and play the row again; a finding that repeats is a defect in the image PCM hash … is not the host's … The board's AC-4 PCM differs from the host's Treat it as a decoder defect in that build: the host decodes the same stream to the pin regression: <row>: the decoder takes N permille … Slower than the baseline by more than the margin Find the cause. A baseline changes only in a pull request that changes the profile or the code and carries a board run regression: boot: … Less internal RAM or a smaller largest block at boot than the baseline's worst boot, or another verdict Find what the image now holds at boot; its static RAM (idf.py size) is the first place to look improved: … re-baseline Faster than the baseline by more than the margin Record a new baseline in the PR that made the change note: the baseline was recorded under profile hash … The baseline is kept from an earlier definition (below) Nothing; the figures are compared as recorded

docs.title: Sendspin rows
docs.text:
A row with "via": "sendspin" is played by the repository's hearth-testserver in place of POST /play: the server dials the board, pairs it and sends the stream as bursts, and the suite reads the board's sendspin.stream= line, printed when the stream ends (tools/hearth/suite_sendspin.py). The C6 refuses an HTTP play on purpose, because a play does not fit beside its Sendspin player, so its /play rows expect that refusal (state: failed, why: memory, no reboot) and its audio is held by these rows alone.

These rows need the server on the bench, on the machine the suite runs from. Build it from the tree under test, as CI's hearth-esp32s3 job does (it needs vcpkg):

cmake --preset config-linux-gcc -DVCPKG_MANIFEST_FEATURES=hearth \
    -DICLFORGE_BUILD_HEARTH=ON -DICLFORGE_BUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF
cmake --build --preset build-linux-gcc --target hearth-testserver

and name the binary with --testserver or ICLFORGE_TESTSERVER. Rebuild it when libs/sendspin or the test server changes. A run that has a Sendspin row and no server stops before it books the board.

What such a row records, beside the figures above:

  • plays and glitched_plays. A stream that plays through with late, dropped or invalid chunks, an underrun or a resynchronisation is a glitch and does not fail the row. A board does this now and then: the C6 ran two of thirteen 30 s AC-3 streams dry on 2026-10-12. A recorded zero would fail a later run, so the row holds how many of its plays glitched.
  • units: the bursts accounted for, which are those played, late or dropped. A burst that is none of them is a finding.
  • play_heap_free: the least internal heap while the stream played.
  • late, dropped, invalid, resyncs, stream_underruns, ring_high, worst_error_us: the worst over the plays of the row.

An AC-4 seed is three frames, which is too short to be a stream. A stream entry with sendspin_seconds is played over and over for that long, and the row holds that every burst the server sent is accounted for.

docs.title: Baselines
docs.text:
firmware/hearth-sink/baselines/ holds one file per profile, written by board_suite.py run --record from a run with no finding.

Field Holds profile, profile_hash The profile and the hash of its definition when the baseline was recorded version The image's version: git describe of the tree it was built from chip, board, recorded The chip, the bench's name for the board, and the time in UTC boot The boot budget: line of the worst boot: internal_free, largest, the asks, headroom, verdict, floor boot_samples internal_free and largest of every boot read, so the spread can be seen plays Per row: state, frames, units, decoder_permille and its samples, decode_stack_free, underruns, dry_ms, min_headroom_ms, resync_bytes, a pcm_hash for an AC-4 row, and the Sendspin figures for a Sendspin row findings Empty: a run with a finding is not recorded

docs.title: The boot budget line
docs.text:
The firmware prints one line once the network and the Sendspin player are up (#1412):

budget: when=boot net=1 internal_free=86231 largest=31744 ask_ring=0 ask_decode_stack=0
ask_fetch_stack=8192 ask_total=8192 ask_biggest=8192 headroom=23552 floor=0 verdict=ok

It is one line on the console, wrapped here; this one is an S3 board's on the s3-n16r8 image, 2026-10-12. The asks are the ring and the stacks an HTTP play takes from internal RAM in this build (one that is in PSRAM asks for 0). headroom is the largest free block less the biggest single ask. verdict is ok, short-block (no block that large), short-total (not that much free in all) or below-floor (the build's CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_PLAY_MIN_FREE_BYTES would refuse a play, which is what a C6 reports). The line reports a play's first allocations only: the decoder, the I2S queue and fragmentation come after it, and the play list holds those.

A board's boot figures vary from boot to boot, and boot_samples shows by how much. In the s3-n16r8 baseline, free RAM read 85,667 to 85,899 bytes on seven boots and 102,503 on one: a 16 KiB start-up task stack is freed either side of the line. In the c6-16mb baseline the largest block read 124,928 bytes on four boots, 122,880 on three and 118,784 on one. A baseline is therefore the worst of several boots (the committed ones are the worst of eight), and a run that boots higher is not a regression.

docs.title: A baseline under another hash
docs.text:
A baseline carries the hash of the profile it was recorded under, and the hash moves whenever the profile is edited. The two kinds of edit are treated differently, and the pull request that makes the edit decides which it is (#1500):

  • A locked value changed. A figure can have moved. The baseline is recorded again on a board, in the same pull request.
  • A key was added at the value it already had in effect (a new switch, left off, and locked so that the guard knows it). No figure moves. The baseline is kept, and the pull request accepts it in the profile's entry in suite.json, against the profile's new hash:
"baseline_accepted": {"profile_hash": "156f7310e8d0", "why": "which key was added, and why no figure moved"}

tools/hearth/test_board_suite.py enforces this in the gate's Static job. A baseline whose hash is not the profile's fails unless baseline_accepted names the profile's current hash and gives a reason. The acceptance names one hash, so the next edit of the profile fails again until it is decided again. An acceptance left behind after a baseline has been recorded under the current hash fails too.

compare does not refuse a kept baseline. It compares the figures as recorded and prints a note that says which hash they were recorded under. The suite still refuses an image built under another hash, so a board is only run on the definition the file has now.

On 2026-10-13 two baselines are kept this way, s3-n16r8 and p4-rev1: #1459 added a Sendspin key to every profile at 0.

docs.title: Real-time figures
docs.text:
From the five baseline files as they were on 2026-10-13 (main at 2155abecb). Each figure is the median of five plays, as permille of real time, with the least and the most of the five in brackets. Lower is faster; 1000 is real time.

What the tables do and do not say:

  • Every row decodes inside real time on the board it was recorded on. The S3 takes 50 to 69% of real time for AC-4 at 2.0, and the C6 66 to 76% for AC-3 and E-AC-3 at 2.0.
  • The AC-4 /play rows are three or four frames long. They show that the PCM is the host's and give a decode time that varies by about 6% from play to play. The Sendspin AC-4 rows loop the same frames for 20 s (471 or 472 bursts) and are the steadier figure.
  • The S3's E-AC-3 stream over Sendspin glitched two plays of five in each profile: 11 to 17 late chunks at the start of the stream. The cause has not been investigated.
  • The S3's least internal heap during an E-AC-3 stream over Sendspin was 2,935 and 2,523 bytes in the two profiles.
  • The figures are one board of each chip. The /play rows of both S3 profiles were also run on a second S3 board and agreed within the rows' spread; the P4 and C6 figures have no second board behind them.
  • 5.1 and wider plays, and the release images' behaviour on a P4 of revision v3.x, are not in the suite. The per-chip pages have those measurements: ESP32-S3, ESP32-C6, ESP32-P4.

docs.title: The bench tools
docs.text:
The tools are in tools/hearth/. They find the boards in a bench file, a JSON table of the boards on one desk; tools/hearth/bench.json is the repository owner's. For another desk, write a file of the same shape and name it in ICLFORGE_BENCH.

Key Holds locks The directory of the boards' lock files idf, idf_tools The ESP-IDF checkout and its tools directory builds Where builds go: one directory per build, named <tag>-<profile> wifi_fragment The path of a fragment with the network's SSID and password. No network value is in the bench file boards Per board: chip, host (its address), port (its serial port), lock (its lock file's name), mac_tail (the last three octets of its MAC), and where they apply after_flash, ota, restart_kills_c6_link, log_bytes

A board is addressed by name, so that its address, its port and its lock come from one row.

Command Does Writes the board bench.py boards, bench.py status [--probe] The table; every lock, and with --probe each board's GET /status state No bench.py lock take BOARD, lock show BOARD, lock release BOARD One board's lock No bench.py log BOARD, bench.py snapshot BOARD… The console, and /hardware with /status, with the network's values taken out No bench.py console BOARD [--reset] The serial console, masked (needs pyserial) No bench.py scrub --check FILE…, scrub --mask FILE… Counts, or masks, the network's values in files No bench_flash.py build PROFILE --tag T [--wifi] [--overlay NAME] The profile's build, sized and held to the profile as CI does it No bench_flash.py flash BOARD --build-dir D --session ID esptool over USB, after the lock and a MAC check Yes bench_flash.py ota BOARD --build-dir D --session ID ota.py push to the board's address, after the lock; refused for a board whose row has "ota": false Yes bench_flash.py verify BOARD --build-dir D [--profile P] What the board says against what was built No bench_flash.py reset BOARD --session ID A system reset by esptool's watchdog reset, then waits for the board Resets it board_suite.py run … The play suite Plays

docs.title: One person at a board at a time
docs.text:
A board that one person is flashing, playing or restarting fails for anyone else using it, in ways that look like a defect in their own work. Before using a board, find out whether it is in use:

python tools/hearth/bench.py status --probe

For each board this prints its lock (who holds it, what for and until when, and OVERDUE once past that time) and the state of its GET /status:

State Meaning stopped Idle. The suite starts only on this playing A play is in progress. With no lock on the board, a play someone left behind finished, failed The last play has ended and nobody has stopped it flash A firmware update is in progress

The command cannot see a running idf.py, esptool, ota.py or serial capture on the board's port, or a person at the desk. Check for those, and ask.

Then book the board, use it, put back the image it had, and release it:

python tools/hearth/bench.py lock take S3a --session <id> --purpose "baseline" --minutes 30
python tools/hearth/bench.py lock release S3a --session <id>

The lock is a one-line file made with exclusive create, so two people cannot both take it. release refuses a lock that is not the caller's, and an overdue lock is a reason to ask its holder. bench_flash.py flash, ota and reset refuse a board the caller has not booked; board_suite.py run takes the lock itself, or uses the caller's own.

docs.title: Building, flashing, verifying
docs.text:
python tools/hearth/bench_flash.py build s3-n16r8 --tag mychange --wifi
python tools/hearth/bench_flash.py ota S3a --build-dir <builds>/mychange-s3-n16r8 --session <id>
python tools/hearth/bench_flash.py verify S3a --build-dir <builds>/mychange-s3-n16r8 --profile s3-n16r8
  • build runs the build CI runs for the profile: the fragments from sink_profile.py defaults, the profile's id and hash, idf.py size, then sink_profile.py verify with the size budgets. --wifi appends the network fragment last, with the wifi-credentials overlay, which lets the image differ from the profile in the network keys and no others; the image still carries the profile's id and hash, so the suite accepts it. --overlay measure adds the PCM hash an AC-4 row needs. --configure-only stops after idf.py reconfigure and the guard, in seconds.
  • flash reads the MAC of the chip on the port first and writes nothing unless its last three octets are the row's mac_tail. A port moves to another board when a cable is changed. --app-only writes the app and otadata and leaves the bootloader, the partition table, NVS and storage. --erase also wipes the board's pairing records and stored network.
  • verify compares the project, the version, and with --profile the profile id and hash in GET /hardware with the build.

docs.title: Reading a board without its network values
docs.text:
The SSID and the password are in the network fragment and in every build directory made with it. The tools take them out of everything they print or write:

  • bench.py log masks the values, the access point's address, and drops any line that carries a pairing token or key. It makes one request, so it prints at most the first 4 KB of the log.
  • bench.py snapshot and bench_flash.py redact /hardware, /status, esptool and idf.py output by key and by value.
  • bench.py scrub --check FILE… counts the values in files in their raw, JSON-escaped, percent-escaped and hex forms and prints the count and never a value; --mask rewrites the files.

board_suite.py reads GET /status by field name and never copies its network object.

docs.title: Hazards
docs.text:
Each with where it was learned.

Reading a board

  • GET /log carries the SSID. It is in the connected with line and in network: wifi station on '…'. A script that prints the log raw publishes it; one did on 2026-10-12. Use bench.py log, and run bench.py scrub --check over anything that will be attached to a pull request.
  • GET /log answers 4 KB at a time out of a 16 KB ring; a client follows the X-Log-Next header for the rest. A read that takes the first reply as the whole log misses the boot budget: line on a P4, whose boot prints more than 4 KB before it, and can end a wait on an earlier play's result= line (found recording the P4 baseline, 2026-10-12).
  • A board that has played has rotated its boot line out of the log. A board with no PSRAM keeps 2 KB of log (CONFIG_ICLFORGE_LOG_BYTES), and the line is still in it just after a restart. Boot figures need --restart; --record refuses a run whose log holds no boot line.
  • GET /hardware is built once, when the control surface starts. A fact that becomes true later in the boot is not in it.
  • One boot is not a baseline. The S3's free RAM has two modes 16 KB apart and the C6's largest block varies by 8 KB (the boot budget line). A baseline taken from one boot of the C6 would have failed one run in five (2026-10-12).

Restarting and flashing

  • A P4's restart could leave it with no Wi-Fi. A restart by esp_restart, or the restart that ends a firmware update, left the P4's link to its on-board C6 dead on 8 of 16 trials (2026-10-12). #1434 makes the firmware reset the whole system and cured it (24 of 24 updates clean). The image that is running does the restart, so a board on an image older than #1434 can fault once more. A dead board is brought back over the serial port, with no flash: esptool --before default-reset --after watchdog-reset read-mac, which is what bench_flash.py reset runs. A bench row with restart_kills_c6_link makes board_suite.py run --restart refuse the board unless it is told --reset-by esptool (the watchdog reset) or --accept-restart-fault.
  • esptool exits 1 after a watchdog reset that worked. The P4's USB-Serial/JTAG port re-enumerates at the reset and pySerial reports the lost port. bench_flash.py flash reads a verified write followed by that error as a verified write, and any other exit of 1 as a failure.
  • A board whose hard reset lands in the ROM's download mode (seen on one of two P4 boards) is started with a watchdog reset: "after_flash": "watchdog-reset" in its bench row.
  • flash --otadata-only boots the first app slot. It restores a board only while the image to restore is in ota_0. Another update in between moves it to ota_1; read ota.py status first (2026-10-12).
  • A plain flash writes more than the app. A build's flash_args lists the bootloader, the partition table, the audio sample and the storage image as well. --app-only leaves them.

Building

  • ESP-IDF's export script refuses a Git Bash or MSYS shell ("MSys/Mingw is not supported"). bench_flash.py runs it with the MSYS variables removed, under pwsh where that is installed.
  • A build that never ran can look built. PowerShell's exit of an unset $LASTEXITCODE is 0, and a build whose environment had not exported idf.py was first reported as built. The tool now exits 127 when idf.py is not found after the export, and fails a build that left no project_description.json.
  • idf.py size configures again. It re-runs CMake on the build directory, so run it on a directory that can be rebuilt.

Sendspin rows

  • Keep one state directory. The test server's key and pairing records are in a state directory (--sendspin-state). A fresh directory is a new server to the board and a new pairing record on each run, and a board keeps eight: eight runs once pushed every other server off a C6.
  • The suite forgets its own record, by id. At the end it sends forget <server_id> for the record it made. A bare forget drops every server the board is paired with. --keep-pairing leaves the record.
  • Do not poll a board while it plays. The C6's HTTP server answers from the same internal heap the stream needs. An E-AC-3 stream then left about 3 KB of it free, and a play with /status polled every second rebooted the board (2026-10-12). The harness reads the totals from the log after the stream.
  • A change that gives a C6 memory back changes its refusal. The C6 refuses an HTTP play when free RAM is under CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_PLAY_MIN_FREE_BYTES. When 28 KB of decoder tables left static RAM, the old floor of 134,008 stopped refusing: an AC-3 play started, ran beside failing Wi-Fi buffer allocations, and the suite's refusal rows failed. The floor is 160,796 now. A change to a C6's free RAM is a change to that figure too.
  • Another server is displaced. A Sendspin server that holds the board (Music Assistant, for one) loses it while a row plays, and has to dial the board again afterwards.

docs.title: A new board or profile
docs.text:
A new board of a chip that has a profile is a row in the bench file: its name, chip, address, serial port, lock file and mac_tail. A bench file of your own needs nothing else. The repository's own bench.json is held by tools/hearth/test_bench.py: names, addresses, ports, locks and MAC tails are unique, every board a profile names (boards in profiles.json) is on the bench with the profile's chip, and the number of boards and the table in planning/esp32-board-bench.md match the file, so a board added there changes the test and that table in the same pull request. Run the profile's existing baseline against the new board as a cross-check before recording anything from it.

A new profile needs a play list before it can have a baseline. suite.json must have an entry for every profile of profiles.json, and the list may be empty: p4-rev3 has no rows until a board of that revision runs the image, and c6-4mb has one refusal row and no baseline.

To record a baseline:

  1. Add the rows to the profile's plays in suite.json. A new stream is a file in the repository with its units; an AC-4 stream also needs a pin in testdata/ac4-probe-pcm-hashes.json.
  2. Build the image from the tree under test: bench_flash.py build <profile> --tag T --wifi, with --overlay measure if the list has an AC-4 row.
  3. Book the board, note the image it is running, and put the build on it (ota or flash), then verify.
  4. Measure the spread before choosing a margin: run with --restart --boots 8 --repeat 5 a few times and read decoder_permille_samples and boot_samples in board-run.json. If a figure spreads by more than the suite's margin allows, give the profile its own tolerance with a note that states the measurements.
  5. Record: board_suite.py run --profile <profile> --board <name> --session <id> --restart --boots 8 --repeat 5 --record. Nothing is written if the run has a finding or the log holds no boot line.
  6. Run again with --compare on the new file. It must hold.
  7. Put the board back on the image it had, and release it.
  8. Open one pull request with the rows, the baseline and any tolerance, and say in it which board, which image and how many plays and boots. The gate's Static job checks that the baseline holds exactly the profile's rows, has no finding, and is under the profile's current hash.

A new row on an existing profile follows the same steps and records the whole baseline again, since a baseline must hold exactly its profile's rows.
