docs.title: ESP32 build profiles
docs.text:
hearth_sink, in firmware/hearth-sink, is the firmware an ESP32 dev kit runs as a Hearth sink. Every board it is built for has one build profile: a named ESP-IDF configuration, written down in one file, that CI holds every build of that board to. This page covers what a profile holds, how CI enforces it, how to build a board from its profile, and how to change one.

The other pages of this section use "profile" for the minimum-footprint build of the codec. A build profile is the configuration of one board's firmware image.

docs.title: What a profile is
docs.text:
ESP-IDF configures a build from Kconfig keys (CONFIG_...). A project sets keys in sdkconfig fragment files and gives the build an ordered list of them in SDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS. A key that no fragment sets takes the default its Kconfig file declares. The result is the sdkconfig file in the build directory.

A profile fixes three things for one board:

  • the fragments and their order;
  • the values of the keys that decide where memory goes and what is built in (the locked keys): each task stack and ring buffer with its size and whether it is in internal RAM or PSRAM, the caches, the flash and PSRAM modes, and the features;
  • the budgets the built image is held to.

All profiles are in firmware/hearth-sink/profiles.json. tools/hearth/sink_profile.py is the only reader: CI, the packager, the bench tools and the profile table in the firmware's README all go through it. The file's top-level keys:

Key Holds format The file's format number, 1. The reader refuses any other note What the file is, for someone reading the JSON watch 25 name patterns. A key in a build's configuration that matches one has to be locked or free (below) free Four patterns for keys that match watch and are left to the build, each with its reason overlays Three named additions a build may take over a profile, each with the keys it may move (below) other_stacks Eight fragment lists the tree spells that are no board's image, each with what it is profiles The seven profiles

Each profile has seven fields:

Field Holds target The ESP-IDF target: esp32s3, esp32c6 or esp32p4 board The board, in words fragments The fragments after sdkconfig.defaults, in order, without the sdkconfig. prefix boards The bench boards that run this profile, by name (below) image The release image built from the profile and the rule it is published under (name, flash size, PSRAM, chip revisions), or null when no release publishes it budget Upper limits for the app image, the bootloader and static internal RAM locked The values the build's sdkconfig must have

docs.title: Why there is one per board and codec set
docs.text:
On 2026-10-12 an HTTP play (POST /play) failed on both ESP32-S3 boards and on the ESP32-C6. The boards ran main (v0.10.0-beta.1-4065), and CI was green. Sendspin streams played on the same boards. The S3's console said:

heap: heap_caps_malloc could not allocate 32768 bytes (caps 0x804); internal free ..., largest 31744
player: could not start the decode task

The cause was a Kconfig default. ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_DECODE_STACK_IN_PSRAM places the 32,768-byte stack of the task that decodes an HTTP play. Its default put the stack in PSRAM only on an S3 image that also had the AC-4 decoder. The S3 release image has no AC-4 decoder, so its stack was in internal RAM, where no free block is over 31,744 bytes once Wi-Fi and the Sendspin player are running. No fragment had changed. The C6 has no PSRAM, and its ring and stack did not fit beside Wi-Fi either.

CI did not see it because no job ran the configuration the boards ship. The HTTP play under QEMU used sdkconfig.ci-http, which has a 24,576-byte stack and no PSRAM, and the board images were built and never played.

A profile is per board and per codec set for three reasons:

  • The same fragment list can resolve to different placements when a default depends on another feature. AC-4 builds were profiles of their own where the decoder moved a placement (s3-n16r8-ac4, p4-rev1-ac4); since 2026-10-29 the decoder is in the S3 and both P4 release profiles, its values locked where the AC-4 profiles held them (on the S3 with the release profile's 4 KB allocation limit kept). sdkconfig.ac4 raises both decode stacks to 40,960 bytes, and on the S3 sdkconfig.s3-dcache takes 32 KB of heap for a 64 KB data cache.
  • A board's flash size and partition table cannot change over the network, so a C6 with 4 MB of flash and one with 16 MB are two profiles and two release images.
  • An ESP32-P4 of chip revision v1.x and one of v3.x refuse each other's images at boot, so each revision has a profile.

The S3's default was fixed in #1387, and sdkconfig.psram now sets the key as well. The C6 refuses an HTTP play it has no room for and says memory as the reason (#1395). The profiles came in the pull requests after those: the file, its reader and the guard (#1403), CI building from the file (#1406), the profile id in the image and the boot budget line (#1412) and the v3.x P4 profile (#1452). The design record is planning/esp32-platform-profiles.md (#1369); it also has the board suite and its figures, which this page leaves out.

docs.title: The profiles
docs.text:
Profile Target Board Release image Bench boards s3-n16r8 esp32s3 ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 N16R8: 16 MB of flash, 8 MB of octal PSRAM, with the AC-4 decoder hearth-sink-esp32s3 S3a, S3b c6-16mb esp32c6 An ESP32-C6 with 16 MB of flash, no PSRAM hearth-sink-esp32c6-16mb C6 c6-4mb esp32c6 Any ESP32-C6 module: 4 MB of flash hearth-sink-esp32c6 none p4-rev1 esp32p4 An ESP32-P4 of chip revision v1.x, such as the FireBeetle 2, with the AC-4 decoder hearth-sink-esp32p4-rev1 P4a, P4b p4-rev3 esp32p4 An ESP32-P4 of chip revision v3.x with the lyric screen and the AC-4 decoder: the ESP32-P4X-Function-EV-Board and its 7-inch MIPI DSI panel hearth-sink-esp32p4-rev3 none

There is no AC-4 profile for the C6: the decoder does not fit beside Wi-Fi on that part (An ESP32-C6 sink). Every other release image has the AC-4 decoder (since 2026-10-29); the C6's has it off. p4-rev3 runs on the P4X kit (P4X).

python tools/hearth/sink_profile.py list prints the same list from the file, with each profile's full SDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS string.

What each board plays and how fast is on the board pages: An ESP32-S3 sink, An ESP32-C6 sink and An ESP32-P4 sink for the sink, and ESP32-S3, ESP32-C6 and ESP32-P4 for the measurements. Sink firmware has which release image goes on which board.

docs.title: The boards a profile names
docs.text:
boards lists the dev kits on the project's bench that run the profile, by the names tools/hearth/bench.json gives them: two ESP32-S3 boards (S3a, S3b), one ESP32-C6 (C6) and two ESP32-P4 boards (P4a, P4b). A test holds every name to a row of that file with the profile's chip. One profile names no board: c6-4mb, whose build differs from c6-16mb in the flash size and the partition table alone.

A board runs one profile at a time, and which one is read from the board.

docs.title: The fragments and their order
docs.text:
Every profile starts with sdkconfig.defaults and adds its fragments after it:

Profile Fragments after sdkconfig.defaults, in order s3-n16r8 hw, psram, psram-4k, sendspin, ac4, s3-fast, s3-dcache c6-16mb hw, sendspin, c6, sendspin-c6, flash16mb c6-4mb hw, sendspin, c6, sendspin-c6 p4-rev1 hw, p4, sendspin, ac4 p4-rev3 hw, p4, p4-rev3, sendspin, ac4, panel, panel-dsi

ESP-IDF reads the files left to right, and a later file's value replaces an earlier one's. The order decides values in several places:

  • sdkconfig.sendspin pins the decode task to core 1, and sdkconfig.c6 after it removes the pin, because the C6 has one core.
  • sdkconfig.c6 chooses 4 MB of flash and partitions_c6.csv, and sdkconfig.flash16mb after it chooses 16 MB and partitions.csv.
  • sdkconfig.p4 admits chip revisions v1.x at 360 MHz, and sdkconfig.p4-rev3 after it admits v3.01 to v3.99 at 400 MHz.

The guard compares the list exactly, so a build given the right files in another order fails, whether or not the two files share a key.

Fragment In What it sets sdkconfig.defaults every profile Optimisation for size, an 8,192-byte main task stack, 16 MB of flash, the partitions.csv table with two application slots, bootloader rollback, 240 MHz sdkconfig.hw every profile The console on the chip's USB-Serial-JTAG port sdkconfig.psram S3 Octal PSRAM at 80 MHz, usable by malloc, with allocations of 16 KB and over tried there first; the I2S DMA queue; a 32 KB instruction cache; the HTTP play's decode stack in PSRAM; no core dump sdkconfig.sendspin every profile The Sendspin player, Wi-Fi, the HTTP source and the control surface on port 80, nothing played at boot, 16 sockets, the decode task on core 1 and lwIP on core 0 sdkconfig.s3-fast S3 QIO flash, 64-byte data-cache lines, code and constants run from PSRAM sdkconfig.s3-dcache s3-n16r8 A 64 KB data cache sdkconfig.ac4 the S3 and P4 profiles The AC-4 decoder, both decode stacks at 40,960 bytes, a frame's per-channel stages on both cores sdkconfig.c6 C6 The target, 160 MHz, QIO flash, 4 MB of flash with partitions_c6.csv, no core pinning sdkconfig.sendspin-c6 C6 The player sized for a part with no PSRAM: a 49,152-byte Sendspin ring, 4,096-byte chunks, a 24,576-byte Sendspin decode stack, no lyrics and no delay lines, two coded channels at most, 16-bit I2S slots, the floor under which an HTTP play is refused, Opus, and Wi-Fi's code kept out of IRAM sdkconfig.flash16mb c6-16mb 16 MB of flash with partitions.csv sdkconfig.p4 P4 The target, chip revisions v1.x, 360 MHz, QIO flash, the wide I2S sink and its pins, PSRAM usable by malloc, code run from PSRAM, the hosted Wi-Fi buffers in PSRAM, the low-power SRAM kept out of the heap sdkconfig.p4-rev3 p4-rev3 Chip revisions v3.01 to v3.99, 400 MHz, the bootloader's log level at Warn so that it fits its window sdkconfig.panel p4-rev3 LVGL with its heap in PSRAM, TrueType fonts and their caches, right-to-left text sdkconfig.panel-dsi p4-rev3 The MIPI DSI panel, and a read-back route on port 8081

Each fragment's own header comment has the reason and the measurement behind every line.

docs.title: What locked holds
docs.text:
locked maps a key to the value the build's sdkconfig must have. On 2026-10-13 the profiles lock 95 keys (the two C6 profiles) to 136 (p4-rev3); 80 keys are locked in every profile.

sink_profile.py snapshot writes the map from a configured build. It takes two sets of keys:

  • every key one of the profile's fragments sets, 38 to 50 of them;
  • every key in the resolved configuration that matches a watch pattern and is on or has a value.

So most locked values are ones no fragment sets. They are defaults of ESP-IDF and of the project's own Kconfig, recorded so that a default that changes is seen. That is the case of 2026-10-12.

The classes of key, with examples (names without CONFIG_):

Class Examples Chip, flash and partition table IDF_TARGET, ESPTOOLPY_FLASHSIZE, ESPTOOLPY_FLASHMODE_QIO, PARTITION_TABLE_CUSTOM_FILENAME, ESP_DEFAULT_CPU_FREQ_MHZ_240, ESP32P4_REV_MIN_FULL, BOOTLOADER_APP_ROLLBACK_ENABLE PSRAM and heap policy SPIRAM, SPIRAM_MODE_OCT, SPIRAM_USE_MALLOC, SPIRAM_MALLOC_ALWAYSINTERNAL, SPIRAM_FETCH_INSTRUCTIONS, ESP_SYSTEM_ALLOW_RTC_FAST_MEM_AS_HEAP, ESP_HOSTED_MEMPOOL_PREFER_SPIRAM, ESP_COREDUMP_ENABLE_TO_NONE Caches ESP32S3_DATA_CACHE_SIZE, ESP32S3_DATA_CACHE_LINE_64B, ESP32S3_INSTRUCTION_CACHE_32KB Code kept in IRAM ESP_WIFI_IRAM_OPT, ESP_WIFI_RX_IRAM_OPT, ESP_PHY_IRAM_OPT Task stacks, size and placement ESP_MAIN_TASK_STACK_SIZE, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_DECODE_STACK_BYTES, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_DECODE_STACK_IN_PSRAM, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_SENDSPIN_DECODE_STACK_BYTES, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_SENDSPIN_SERVER_STACK_BYTES, and ESP-IDF's own (ESP_TIMER_TASK_STACK_SIZE, LWIP_TCPIP_TASK_STACK_SIZE, MDNS_TASK_STACK_SIZE) Rings, queues and buffers ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_RING_BYTES, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_RING_IN_PSRAM, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_SENDSPIN_RING_BYTES, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_SENDSPIN_MAX_CHUNK_BYTES, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_I2S_DMA_DESCRIPTORS, LWIP_MAX_SOCKETS Cores ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_DECODE_CORE, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_FETCH_CORE, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_DECODE_LANE, LWIP_TCPIP_TASK_AFFINITY_CPU0 Features ICLFORGE_SENDSPIN, ICLFORGE_AC4, ICLFORGE_SENDSPIN_OPUS, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_SENDSPIN_AC4, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_PLAY_MIN_FREE_BYTES

The keys behind the 2026-10-12 failure, as the file locks them on 2026-10-13 (names after ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_; the file is the authority):

Key s3-n16r8 c6-16mb, c6-4mb p4-rev1 p4-rev3 DECODE_STACK_BYTES 40960 32768 40960 40960 DECODE_STACK_IN_PSRAM 1 0 0 1 SENDSPIN_DECODE_STACK_BYTES 40960 24576 40960 40960 SENDSPIN_DECODE_STACK_IN_PSRAM 1 0 0 0 SENDSPIN_RING_BYTES 262144 49152 262144 262144 PLAY_MIN_FREE_BYTES 0 160796 0 0

Two values need a word:

  • n locks a key off. A key that is missing from the configuration also satisfies it.
  • <absent> means the key must not be in the configuration at all. snapshot writes it when a fragment asks for a key and Kconfig drops it, as p4-rev3 does for ESP32P4_REV_MIN_100: sdkconfig.p4 asks for it and sdkconfig.p4-rev3 chooses another revision.

docs.title: The profile's hash
docs.text:
sink_profile.py identity <profile> prints the id and a 12-digit hash: the first 12 hex digits of a SHA-256 over the profile's fragments and locked. Any edit to either changes it. The budgets, the board names and the image rule are not part of it.

$ python tools/hearth/sink_profile.py identity s3-n16r8
s3-n16r8 156f7310e8d0

With --cmake the command prints -DICLFORGE_PROFILE=<id> -DICLFORGE_PROFILE_HASH=<hash>. A build configured with those two options compiles them into the image, and the board reports them (below).

docs.title: watch and free
docs.text:
watch is a list of shell-style patterns, matched against a key's name without CONFIG_. They name the kinds of key that place or size something:

Kind Patterns Stacks and placement *STACK*, *IN_PSRAM* The player's rings, queues and cores ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_*RING*, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_I2S_DMA_*, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_*_CORE, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_DECODE_LANE, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_HOLD_FIRST_UNIT, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_PLAY_MIN_FREE_BYTES Sendspin and AC-4 ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_SENDSPIN_*, ICLFORGE_SENDSPIN*, ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_AC4_*, ICLFORGE_AC4* PSRAM, caches and IRAM SPIRAM*, ESP32S3_*CACHE*, *IRAM_OPT*, ESP_HOSTED_MEMPOOL_PREFER_SPIRAM, ESP_SYSTEM_ALLOW_RTC_FAST_MEM_AS_HEAP Flash, table and chip ESPTOOLPY_FLASHSIZE*, ESPTOOLPY_FLASHMODE*, PARTITION_TABLE_CUSTOM_FILENAME, ESP32P4_*REV*, ESP_DEFAULT_CPU_FREQ_MHZ_* Bootloader and core dump BOOTLOADER_APP_ROLLBACK_ENABLE, BOOTLOADER_LOG_LEVEL_*, ESP_COREDUMP_ENABLE_TO_*

A key in a build's configuration that matches a pattern, and is on or has a value, has to be in the profile's locked or match a free pattern. Otherwise the guard reports it as [unplaced]. A new stack or buffer option then cannot reach a board without someone deciding its value for that board.

free holds the exceptions, each with its reason in the file:

Pattern Why it is free ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_WIFI_* A board's network is its own and is kept in NVS. A published image has none built in ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_HTTP_URL The stream a build plays at boot: empty on a board, a test server's address in a CI build ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_PANEL_STACK_BYTES The screen task's stack. It is declared for every target and does nothing in a profile with no screen. p4-rev3 locks it by hand LV_SPAN_SNIPPET_STACK_SIZE An LVGL count of text snippets, which matches *STACK* and is no task's stack

A key that is both free and locked is held to the locked value. snapshot skips free keys, so a lock like p4-rev3's is added by hand after a snapshot.

docs.title: Overlays and other fragment lists
docs.text:
An overlay is a declared addition to a profile's build. It lists the key patterns it may move (touches) and may name one more fragment, which goes after the profile's own. A build made with an overlay is verified with the same --overlay name, and the guard then skips the keys the overlay touches.

Overlay Fragment What it is for wifi-credentials a file of the board's network, given last (defaults --wifi FILE) A build for a bench board. The packager refuses to publish an image with a network built in measure sdkconfig.measure Turns on the PCM hash an AC-4 play prints, so a board's output can be compared with the host's panel-capture sdkconfig.panel-capture The P4 profile with a screen, with its read-back and touch server on 8081 (no authentication), for a bench; a release image has it off and the packager refuses one with it on qemu-net sdkconfig.qemu-net The S3 release profile under QEMU: Ethernet for Wi-Fi, the capture sink for I2S, quad PSRAM for octal, the console on UART0

other_stacks lists fragment lists that appear in the documentation and in fragment headers and are no board's image: the bare-metal probes' builds, the lists a fragment's header gives as its own example, and the P4 build that draws the screen into a frame buffer with no panel. sink_profile.py check-docs reads the firmware's README and fragments, the Hearth pages, the ESP32 platform pages and the ESP32 planning notes, and fails on a sdkconfig.defaults;sdkconfig... list that is neither a profile's, nor listed here, nor a CI test configuration (sdkconfig.ci*). The same command with --write regenerates the profile table in the firmware's README.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.text:
budget has three upper limits in bytes. null means the figure is not held.

Profile app_bytes_max bootloader_bytes_max internal_static_bytes_max s3-n16r8 2,750,000 32,768 185,000 c6-16mb 2,000,000 32,768 117,000 c6-4mb 1,966,080 32,768 117,000 p4-rev1 3,400,000 24,576 not held p4-rev3 3,950,000 24,576 175,000
  • The app image is iclforge_hearth_sink.bin in the build directory. c6-4mb's limit is the size of an application slot in partitions_c6.csv.
  • The bootloader is bootloader/bootloader.bin. On the P4 it starts at 0x2000 and the partition table is at 0x8000, which leaves it 24,576 bytes.
  • Static internal RAM is the DIRAM figure of idf.py size --format json2. Every byte of it is a byte the heap does not have at run time, on any board. The guard judges it only when it is given the size report (--size-json).

The budgets need a compiled build. A configured build is checked for everything else.

docs.title: The guard
docs.text:
sink_profile.py verify <profile> --build-dir <dir> holds a build directory to its profile. It works on a directory that has been configured (idf.py reconfigure) or built. Each finding is one line, <profile>: [rule] message, and the command exits 1. With none it prints <profile>: the build holds to its profile and exits 0.

Rule Reported when The message, for example fragments The SDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS in the build's CMakeCache.txt is not the profile's list, in order, with the fragments of the overlays named; or it has a file that no named overlay declares the build was given sdkconfig.defaults;sdkconfig.hw;... and the profile's are ... identity The build carries no profile id, another profile's, or a hash from another definition of this one the build carries hash 9ed6f4eb5c70 and profile s3-n16r8 is 156f7310e8d0: it was configured from another definition locked A locked key has another value in sdkconfig CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_DECODE_STACK_IN_PSRAM is 0, the profile locks 1 unplaced A watched key is on or has a value, and the profile neither locks nor frees it CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_NEW_STACK_BYTES=4096 matches a watch pattern and the profile neither locks nor frees it budget The app image, the bootloader or static internal RAM is over its limit static internal RAM (DIRAM) is 190,112 bytes, over the profile's 185,000

--github prints the findings as GitHub annotations. --warn-only reports them as warnings and exits 0.

docs.title: How CI enforces a profile
docs.text:
Where When What it holds PR Gate, the static checks (_static.yml) Every pull request and merge-queue entry check-docs; the tools' own tests, which hold profiles.json to the workflow's build steps, to the release rules in tools/ci/check_firmware_package.py and to the baselines; and check-change for the Kconfig (below) PR Gate, the ESP32 profiles job (_profiles.yml) A pull request that changes firmware/hearth-sink/, firmware/esp-idf/ or the two profile tools; every merge-queue entry and push to main Every profile configured with idf.py reconfigure in the espressif/idf:v6.1 container and passed to verify: the fragments, the identity, the locked values and the unplaced keys. Nothing is compiled, so no budget is judged The build jobs of _build.yml, called by ci.yml After a merge to main whose changes reach the ESP builds, in the nightly run and in a dispatched run Each profile built, measured with idf.py size and passed to verify with the budgets; the release images packaged

The ESP32 profiles job is where a pull request that changes a fragment's value or the default of a locked key fails before it merges, with the guard's own [locked] or [unplaced] line (#1506). It also checks merge-queue entries, which is where two changes that each pass alone first meet.

docs.title: The build jobs
docs.text:
Each board build in _build.yml is the same five commands with the profile's id:

  1. sink_profile.py defaults <profile> gives the SDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS string.
  2. sink_profile.py identity <profile> --cmake gives the two -D options that put the id and the hash in the image.
  3. idf.py ... build builds into a directory of its own, with its own sdkconfig.
  4. idf.py size --format json2 writes the size report.
  5. sink_profile.py verify <profile> --size-json ... holds the build to the profile, and a finding fails the step.

A profile with a release image then goes to tools/hearth/package_firmware.py package --profile <profile>, which runs the guard again and refuses a build that is not the profile, or a profile whose image has another name.

Profile Job in _build.yml What CI does with it s3-n16r8 build-esp32s3 Built, verified, packaged as hearth-sink-esp32s3. Built a second time with the qemu-net overlay and run under QEMU c6-4mb build-esp32c3 Built, verified, packaged as hearth-sink-esp32c6 c6-16mb build-esp32c3 Built, verified, packaged as hearth-sink-esp32c6-16mb p4-rev1 build-esp32c3 Built, verified, packaged as hearth-sink-esp32p4-rev1 p4-rev3 build-esp32c3 Built, verified, packaged as hearth-sink-esp32p4-rev3 p4-rev1 (again) build-esp32c3 Built with the stage timers on, and verified

The QEMU run of s3-n16r8 is the one place CI plays a board's release configuration. It checks that GET /hardware reports the profile's id and hash, plays an AC-3 and two E-AC-3 streams over POST /play, and looks on the console for the lines that say the rings and stacks are where the profile locks them (sink_profile.py expect-console s3-n16r8 prints those lines). QEMU has no Wi-Fi, so it says nothing about the heap a board has left. The C6 and the P4 have no emulator and are built without being run.

The job package-esp32-firmware then writes the manifest and runs tools/ci/check_firmware_package.py over every image: chip, revisions, flash size, PSRAM and no network built in. A test holds those rules to each profile's image.

Two details of the jobs:

  • Every guard step has if: !cancelled(), so it runs when an earlier step of its job has failed (#1491, #1499). The sink builds share their jobs with the minimum-footprint probes. While a probe was failing on main, the steps after it were skipped, and a wrong static-RAM budget on the C6 went unreported until a run on a board showed it.
  • The repository variable ESP32_PROFILE_GUARD=warn turns the guard's findings into warnings in all of these jobs. It is not set.

docs.title: A new Kconfig key
docs.text:
A pull request that adds a Kconfig key the guard watches has to place it in the profiles in the same pull request (#1504). The static checks run:

python tools/hearth/sink_profile.py check-change --base <base commit>

It needs no ESP-IDF. tools/hearth/kconfig_scan.py reads the two Kconfig files a hearth_sink build configures, firmware/hearth-sink/main/Kconfig.projbuild and firmware/esp-idf/iclforge/Kconfig, at the head and at the base. The command reports two things:

  • A key the change adds that matches a watch pattern, is not free, and is in the configuration of a profile that does not lock it. Whether a key is in a profile's configuration is worked out from its depends on lines and the if blocks around it, against the profile's target and locked values. A bool counts only when it has a plain default y.
  • A lock on a key no Kconfig declares: a CONFIG_ICLFORGE_* key locked to something other than n. That is a key that was removed, or a misspelt lock.

The message names the file, the key and the profiles. For a new int key with a default, on one line:

kconfig: [kconfig] firmware/hearth-sink/main/Kconfig.projbuild: CONFIG_ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_NEW_STACK_BYTES
is new and the guard watches it, and it is in c6-16mb, c6-4mb, p4-rev1, p4-rev3,
s3-n16r8, which neither lock nor free it: lock its value in profiles.json (the hash
moves: baselines are re-recorded or accepted, planning/esp32-platform-profiles.md 'Changing a
profile'), or name it in `free`

The fix is one of two edits to profiles.json: lock the key in every profile named, at the value that profile's build resolves, or add it to free with the reason. Locking a key changes the profile's hash, so the baselines need a decision too (below).

Where the scan cannot tell whether a key is in a profile (a condition on a symbol the profile does not lock), it reports nothing, and the ESP32 profiles job decides from the configured build. check-change --all treats every key as new, which checks the whole tree.

docs.title: Which profile a running board is
docs.text:
GET /hardware answers it:

curl http://<board>/hardware
Field of the reply Holds profile The profile's id, such as s3-n16r8 profile_hash The hash of the definition the image was built from version The image's version: a release's tag, or git describe of the checkout it was built from target, chip, revision, psram_bytes The chip, its revision and its PSRAM

Compare profile and profile_hash with sink_profile.py identity <profile> in your checkout:

/hardware says Meaning The id and the same hash The image was built from the profile as your checkout defines it The id and another hash The image was built from another definition of the profile: an older or a newer profiles.json Two empty strings The image was built without the identity options, for example with the plain idf.py commands on the board pages

Two more places help:

  • The boot line. At boot, once the Sendspin player has started, the board prints one budget: line on its console, which GET /log also returns, and another if a network comes up later. It does not name the profile. It shows what the profile's placement asks of internal RAM on this boot. The line has this form:

    budget: when=boot net=1 internal_free=90931 largest=31744 ask_ring=0 ask_decode_stack=0 ask_fetch_stack=8192 ask_total=8192 ask_biggest=8192 headroom=23552 floor=0 verdict=ok

    ask_ring and ask_decode_stack are 0 when the profile puts the HTTP play's ring and stack in PSRAM. floor is the profile's ICLFORGE_EXAMPLE_PLAY_MIN_FREE_BYTES. verdict is ok, short-block (no free block as large as the biggest ask), short-total (not that much free in all) or below-floor (an HTTP play would be refused, which is what the C6 profiles say). The line is a lower bound: the decoder's own allocations come after it.

  • GET /firmware. It reports the image in each of the two application slots (running and other, each with its version and state), the flash size and the partition table. It has no profile id. It tells a 4 MB C6 from a 16 MB one, and shows which build is in each slot.

docs.title: Building a board from its profile
docs.text:
These are CI's commands. They need ESP-IDF v6.1 and a checkout of the repository. Give each profile its own build directory and its own sdkconfig in it, as below: ESP-IDF otherwise keeps one sdkconfig in the project directory, and a second profile's build inherits the first's. Build one profile at a time from one checkout, because the component manager downloads into the project directory.

The target is the profile's, from the table.

docs.title: In WSL or on Linux
docs.text:
. $IDF_PATH/export.sh
cd firmware/hearth-sink

id=s3-n16r8
target=esp32s3
dir=$HOME/build/hearth-$id

defaults="$(python3 ../../tools/hearth/sink_profile.py defaults $id)"
read -r -a identity <<< "$(python3 ../../tools/hearth/sink_profile.py identity $id --cmake)"

idf.py -B "$dir" -DSDKCONFIG="$dir/sdkconfig" -DIDF_TARGET=$target \
  "-DSDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS=$defaults" "${identity[@]}" build
idf.py -B "$dir" size --format json2 > "$dir/size.json"
python3 ../../tools/hearth/sink_profile.py verify $id --build-dir "$dir" --size-json "$dir/size.json"

docs.title: On Windows
docs.text:
Use PowerShell 7 (pwsh). ESP-IDF refuses Git Bash and other MSYS shells (MSys/Mingw is not supported), and the size report has to be written as UTF-8, which PowerShell 7's > does.

. $env:IDF_PATH\export.ps1
cd firmware\hearth-sink

$id = "s3-n16r8"
$target = "esp32s3"
$dir = "D:\build\hearth-$id"

$defaults = python ..\..\tools\hearth\sink_profile.py defaults $id
$identity = -split (python ..\..\tools\hearth\sink_profile.py identity $id --cmake)

idf.py -B $dir "-DSDKCONFIG=$dir\sdkconfig" "-DIDF_TARGET=$target" "-DSDKCONFIG_DEFAULTS=$defaults" @identity build
idf.py -B $dir size --format json2 > "$dir\size.json"
python ..\..\tools\hearth\sink_profile.py verify $id --build-dir $dir --size-json "$dir\size.json"

docs.title: After the build
docs.text:
verify should print <profile>: the build holds to its profile. To check the configuration without compiling, replace build with reconfigure and run verify without --size-json. That is what the ESP32 profiles job does, and it judges everything but the budgets.

Flash the build with idf.py -B <dir> -p <PORT> flash monitor. The board pages cover the port, the reset after a flash, joining a network and pairing: An ESP32-S3 sink, An ESP32-C6 sink and An ESP32-P4 sink. A profile build has no network built in. A board keeps the network it has stored through a flash, and a new board is given one as those pages describe.

The plain idf.py commands on those pages build from the same fragment lists. The image they make reports no profile, and verify fails it under identity.

python tools/hearth/bench_flash.py build <profile> --tag <tag> runs the same steps and can be started from any shell, Git Bash included. It reads the ESP-IDF location and the build root from tools/hearth/bench.json, which describes the project's own bench; the environment variable ICLFORGE_BENCH names another file of the same form for another machine. Testing and benchmarking the ESP32 boards covers that tool and the rest of the bench.

docs.title: Changing a profile
docs.text:
A change to a profile is one pull request that carries the fragment or Kconfig change and the matching edit to profiles.json. That covers a new value in a fragment, a fragment added to or moved in a list, a new default for a locked key, and a new key.

  1. Make the change and configure each affected profile, with the commands above and reconfigure. A change to sdkconfig.sendspin or to a Kconfig default can reach every profile.

  2. Read what the guard reports. Each line is a decision to make:

    The guard says What changed What to do [locked] CONFIG_X is A, the profile locks B The value a board gets Lock the new value if it is meant; otherwise fix the fragment or the default [unplaced] CONFIG_X=A matches a watch pattern ... A new key that places or sizes something Lock it in the profile, or name it in free with the reason [fragments] the build was given ... and the profile's are ... The list or its order Edit the profile's fragments, and the build step if a file was added [budget] ... over the profile's ... The image grew Reduce it, or raise the budget in the same pull request and say why

  3. Update profiles.json, by hand or with sink_profile.py snapshot <profile> --build-dir <dir> --write, which rewrites that profile's locked from the configured build. It prints a note: for every key a fragment asks for that the build resolved differently. Review the diff: a snapshot drops a hand-made lock on a free key.

  4. Configure again. The hash has changed, so the first build directory now fails under identity. A fresh identity --cmake and reconfigure should hold.
  5. Regenerate the README's table when the fragments, the image or the boards changed: python tools/hearth/sink_profile.py check-docs --write.
  6. Run the tools' tests: python -m unittest discover --start-directory tools/hearth --pattern 'test_*.py'. They hold the file to the workflow, the release rules and the baselines.

docs.title: Baselines
docs.text:
firmware/hearth-sink/baselines/ has one file for each profile a bench board runs: s3-n16r8, c6-16mb, p4-rev1 and p4-rev3. A baseline is a recorded run of the board suite (tools/hearth/board_suite.py): the figures of a fixed list of plays on that profile's image, and the board's boot line. c6-4mb has none, because no bench board runs it. Testing and benchmarking the ESP32 boards describes the suite, its tolerances and how a baseline is recorded.

Each baseline carries the hash of the profile it was recorded under, and an edit to the profile changes the hash. A test fails the pull request until it does one of two things for every baseline whose hash no longer matches:

The edit What the pull request carries A locked value changed The baseline recorded again on a board, from an image built under the new hash (board_suite.py run ... --record) A key was added at the value it already had, so no figure can have moved An entry profiles.<profile>.baseline_accepted in firmware/hearth-sink/suite.json with the profile's new hash and the reason

An acceptance names one hash. The next edit to the profile changes the hash again and the test asks again. When a baseline is later re-recorded, its acceptance is removed; the test fails on one that is left behind.

The suite refuses to run on a board whose /hardware reports another profile or another hash, so a baseline is always recorded from the definition in the checkout.

docs.title: Adding a profile
docs.text: Add the entry with an empty locked, configure it, and run snapshot --write to fill it; verify says locks no key: run snapshot until then. Add its build step to _build.yml in the form of the others, and its id to the list in tools/hearth/test_sink_profile.py that holds the workflow to the file. The ESP32 profiles job picks the new profile up from sink_profile.py list.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• planning/esp32-platform-profiles.md is the design record, with the board suite, its tolerances and each baseline's figures.
  • The firmware's README has the generated profile table and everything else about hearth_sink.
  • Testing and benchmarking the ESP32 boards covers what is tested where, the play suite, the baselines and the bench tools.
  • Sink firmware covers installing a release image and updating a board over its network.
  • Bare metal is the overview of the parts.

docs.title: Bare metal
docs.text:
A board with no operating system, no C++ runtime to speak of, and a few hundred kilobytes of RAM. The library builds for it as iclforge::ac3_minimal: one static archive, no exceptions, no RTTI, and none of the direct-form transform tables.

The reference target is arm-none-eabi cross-compiled for QEMU's mps2-an385 machine — a Cortex-M3 with no floating-point unit, where every floating-point operation is software-emulated. It is the target CI measures the profile on. The ESP32-S3 is the second bare-metal target and the first with hardware floating point.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
AC-3 decode Correct. Mono, stereo and 5.1, and 5.1 folded to Lo/Ro stereo in line mode by the §7.8 output stage, every channel level exact against testdata/baremetal/fixture.hpp E-AC-3 decode Correct. 5.1, 2/0 and 7.1.4 (a bed and two dependent substreams), including AHT, spectral extension and §7.5.4 rematrixing; 5.1 and 7.1.4 folded to Lo/Ro stereo in line mode; and 5.1 in line mode from a stream carrying dynrng words and dialnorm 24 E-AC-3 §E3.5 enhanced coupling Correct, on its own fixture Atmos bed and objects Correct. Objects reconstruct here, and are placed onto 7.1.4 by their positions (eac3_atmos_render, through the block form's object views); the flat newlib heap makes it easier than on the ESP32-S3 Fixed-point decode -DICLFORGE_DECODE_SCALAR=fixed builds every decode row above in Q7.24 integers under a per-block exponent, for a part with no FPU at all - the plan is arithmetic-tiers.md. CI runs the probe twice on this leg, and the fixed build's PCM is identical to the x86 host's and to an ESP32-C3's under qemu-riscv32 - three architectures, one pinned set of hashes (testdata/fixed-probe-pcm-hashes.json). It costs 0.33x the instructions the default build spends on the same frame: eac3.instructions_per_frame=4241000 against 12,942,000, integer arithmetic where that one's is software floating point Encode A separate encode-only profile, ICLFORGE_MINIMAL_ENCODER: six rows (5.1 and 2/0 through each encoder, 2/0 with coupling, spectral extension and AHT, 2/0 §E3.5), each hashed against encode_fixture.hpp with its peak and its time per frame; 226,780-byte image, 158,911 peak, 9.1 M to 48.2 M instructions a frame under --encoder --icount - see Building AC-4 decode A third probe, run_baremetal_probe.sh --ac4, for the AC-4 decoder in float (iclforge::ac4 with its inspector and core, static, without exceptions; the encoder is not built): six committed streams, 2.0 and 5.1 with and without A-CPL, 5.1.4 and 2.0 with companding, each channel's level exact against firmware/baremetal/ac4_fixture.hpp, and the PCM bit-identical to the x86-64 host's (testdata/ac4-probe-pcm-hashes.json). 750,276-byte image (196 KB of it the sample rate converter's tables and 53 KB the inverse transform's), 286 KB to 1.49 MB peak heap by fixture, 48 to 202 allocations a frame, 19.5 KB of stack, 25.2 M to 161.8 M instructions a frame under --ac4 --icount (planning/ac4.md, D14f) - see the AC-4 rows Image size 355,709 bytes — 293,092 .text, 400 .data, 62,217 .bss Peak heap 195,025 bytes, the height-object fixture placed onto 7.1.4 (eac3_atmos_render); 194,655 with Atmos objects reconstructed, 173,794 for the 7.1.4 fixture folded to stereo, 167,386 as coded Retained after teardown 12 bytes, one __cxa_thread_atexit record; the enhanced-coupling scratch (23,552 bytes while §E3.5 is in use) is handed back between fixtures Allocation per frame 1 to 27, by fixture — see the footprint table Audio output None. The probe decodes built-in fixtures and prints levels Real silicon None. Correctness is established under emulation CI build-footprint in .github/workflows/_build.yml, in the esp lane of ci.yml: after a merge to main that changes the ESP32 trees or a tree its component ships (the lane table lists them), and in the nightly run (CI for many agents). A pull request's gate builds none of it

Decode and encode are separate builds, and mutually exclusive: configure fails if both are asked for, because neither fits beside the other in the memory this profile targets.

docs.title: Building and running it
docs.text:
# Cross-compile for arm-none-eabi and run the probe on QEMU
tools/checks/run_baremetal_probe.sh

# The same profile natively, no emulator
tools/checks/run_baremetal_probe.sh --host

# Instructions per frame under QEMU -icount, deterministic and gated
tools/checks/run_baremetal_probe.sh --icount

# The AC-4 decoder's probe, in its own build: the same three ways
tools/checks/run_baremetal_probe.sh --ac4
tools/checks/run_baremetal_probe.sh --ac4 --host
tools/checks/run_baremetal_probe.sh --ac4 --icount

--icount is the one timing figure this leg can give. QEMU is not cycle-accurate and the probe's ordinary clock is semihosting's, which reports the host's time; but under -icount shift=0 the guest's own clock advances one nanosecond per executed instruction, and a build whose clock reads the mps2-an385's 25 MHz timer (ICLFORGE_BAREMETAL_CLOCK=timer, its own preset and build directory) follows it. Every microsecond the probe then prints is a thousand Thumb-2 instructions, identical on every host and every run — eac3.instructions_per_frame=12942000 — gated per fixture with the same headroom rule as the other ceilings, and with --stage-timers counted per stage. It is not cycles on any real part; it is a number that moves when the code does, which the host-time figure never was, and it is what the ESP32-C3 row's speed estimate rests on. That part now runs the fixed tier's probe under qemu-riscv32 for correctness, but its time still comes from here, and instructions are not cycles on either part.

Both drive the presets, which you can also use directly: config-arm-none-eabi-minimal / build-arm-none-eabi-minimal, and config-linux-gcc-minimal or config-linux-llvm-minimal for the host (the runner's --host uses the GCC one). The AC-4 probe's are the same names with -ac4 after minimal, for arm-none-eabi and for GCC on the host; there is no LLVM one. GCC and Clang only.

Building from source covers what the profile changes and the gaps it has not closed. The measured figures are in the footprint table.

docs.title: What you give up
docs.text:
The profile replaces what libs/ac3 builds rather than adding to it, and configure fails with a list if any component needing the full library is still switched on.

Not compiled Consequence Under ICLFORGE_MINIMAL_DECODER: the encoder, container writers, WAV I/O, analysis and QC layers, the object encoder Decode only. libs/ac3/minimal.cmake lists what is compiled, with a line on why each file is reachable from a decode. ICLFORGE_MINIMAL_ENCODER is the same profile pointed the other way. The direct-form transform tables 1,900,544 bytes of .bss absent from the image rather than merely unused. DecoderConfig::fast_imdct = false returns DecodeError::kNoReferenceTransform here instead of being served quietly by the fast path.

docs.title: The probe
docs.text:
firmware/baremetal/probe.cpp links the archive, decodes six frames each of fourteen fixtures, compares every channel's level against testdata/baremetal/fixture.hpp, and prints key=value lines the runner gates on: the levels, image size, peak heap, retained bytes and allocations per frame. encode_probe.cpp is its counterpart, checking a byte count and FNV-1a hash against encode_fixture.hpp, and ac4_probe.cpp the AC-4 decoder's, decoding six streams through Decoder::decode_by_block and reading the stack the decode used by painting a window of it first.

It is not a unit test — the profile requires ICLFORGE_BUILD_TESTS=OFF, since nothing under tests/ builds against this archive — and it answers three questions a test could not: does the archive link with everything else absent, does it produce the right audio on a 32-bit soft-float target, and what did it cost.

Nothing regenerates the fixtures automatically and nothing detects that they have drifted from the encoder: the probe decodes a committed bitstream and compares it against committed levels, so both moving together is invisible to it. Regenerate with python tools/generators/gen_baremetal_fixture.py --forge <path>, and the AC-4 fixtures with python tools/generators/gen_baremetal_ac4_fixture.py --forge <path>.

docs.title: The AC-4 probe
docs.text:
ac4_probe.cpp decodes six committed streams (firmware/baremetal/ac4_fixture.hpp): DEE's 2.0 with A-SPX, a constructed 2.0 in A-CPL, DEE's 5.1, a constructed 5.1 in A-CPL, DEE's 5.1.4 tones and DEE's 2.0 at 48 kbit/s, whose A-SPX runs companding (added by D14a4, the one fixture that reaches float pow and exp2), two to four frames each, all at frame rate index 13 (2,048 samples at 48 kHz). The rows are the build-footprint job's on 2026-09-29, in float, with GCC 14.2.1 under QEMU 10.2.1, -Os, soft float, and the generic SIMD seam, so the QMF banks' vector kernels run through its portable types; the instruction counts, the peak heaps, the allocations and the stack are measured again with D14e on 2026-10-02 (the counts are within 1.1% of D14a4's, the peaks 0.8 to 6.8% lower, and the image 8,448 bytes larger):

Fixture Frames Instructions a frame Peak heap Allocations a frame, steady Stack ac4_20_music, 2.0 3 54,766,000 413,611 56 16,580 ac4_20_acpl, 2.0 A-CPL 4 57,284,000 601,504 50 19,480 ac4_51_music, 5.1 3 116,737,000 946,390 147 19,480 ac4_51_acpl, 5.1 A-CPL 4 122,882,000 1,147,590 84 19,480 ac4_514_tones, 5.1.4 2 206,264,000 1,800,312 203 19,480 ac4_20_companding, 2.0 with companding 3 58,818,000 462,435 73 19,480

These are D14e's figures. D14f lowered the peaks and the instruction counts and raised the image (the performance trend has the table). The runner holds each column to a ceiling about a tenth above the figure (ICOUNT_CEILING_AC4 in tools/checks/run_baremetal_probe.sh; the peaks and the allocations a frame in testdata/ac4-probe-ceilings.json, which the ESP32-S3's QEMU leg reads as well), and the image and the stack have ceilings of their own, set in the runner. Nothing is retained after the decoders are destroyed. The stack is read by painting a window of it below the probe's frame before each fixture and finding how far the decode reached. The PCM of each fixture hashes to the value testdata/ac4-probe-pcm-hashes.json pins, on this leg and on the x86-64 host, and an ESP32-P4 board's hash equals the same six (ESP32-P4). Instructions are not cycles: the P4 page has what the decoder takes on a part with an FPU. In the fixed-point tier (--ac4 --scalar=fixed) the six fixtures take 6.7 M to 43.0 M instructions a frame on this leg, 0.27 to 0.30 of the float tier's (planning/ac4.md, D14f), and hash to the values testdata/ac4-fixed-probe-pcm-hashes.json pins, on this leg, on the x86-64 host and on RV32IMC (the performance trend has the table). No board has run AC-4 in the fixed-point tier.

docs.title: Porting to another part
docs.text:
Two things are target-specific, both under firmware/baremetal/platform/: a thread-pointer stub (baremetal/tls.cpp, whose static block the linker script bounds with two ASSERT()s) and the linker script and startup for the board. Nothing in src/ branches on the target.

Whether a part is viable comes down to floating point. Every operation the decoder does in double is software-emulated without an FPU, and decode_scalar_t is float under this profile precisely because that is what the parts with hardware floating point actually have. The ESP32-C3 page works that argument through one vendor's range.

docs.title: ESP32-C3
docs.text: The fixed-point tier's target: an Espressif ESP32-C3, RISC-V at 160 MHz with no floating-point unit at all. iclforge::ac3_minimal decodes here the same way it does on the Cortex-M3 leg's fixed-point build — -DICLFORGE_DECODE_SCALAR=fixed, Q7.24 integers under a per-block exponent — because that is what a part with no FPU wants (the plan). It shares the same firmware/esp-idf/iclforge/ component and manifest as ESP32-S3; only the target and the arithmetic tier differ.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Decode Correct, and that is all this row claims. firmware/baremetal/platform/esp32c3/ is a probe target CI runs under qemu-riscv32: twelve of the fourteen fixtures decode, every one producing PCM identical to the x86 host's and the Cortex-M3 leg's — three architectures, three compilers, one pinned set of hashes (testdata/fixed-probe-pcm-hashes.json) Memory Peaks at 195,505 bytes of heap across the twelve fixtures that run (eac3_atmos_render). The part reports 246,332 bytes free before a decode in a heap whose largest block is 114,688, so the total is not a budget. The probe skips the two 7.1.4 rows on a budget of 230,000 bytes, against 238,094 and 244,502 recorded for them when the decoder used more memory; the Cortex-M3 leg's fixed tier now peaks at 174,850 and 181,258 bytes on them, and this leg still skips them, so whether they fit here now has not been run Speed Unmeasured. QEMU is not cycle-accurate and no C3 board has run this. On the Cortex-M3 leg an E-AC-3 5.1 frame is 4.2 M integer instructions against 12.9 M soft-float, AC-3 5.1 3.7 M, AC-3 2/0 1.2 M and mono 0.61 M — against 5.12 M cycles per frame at 160 MHz, but instructions are not cycles and no leg models this part's 16 KB flash cache. The ESP32-C6, a 160 MHz RISC-V core with no FPU in the same tier, has been timed on a board: AC-3 5.1 at 0.64x a frame, E-AC-3 5.1 at 0.75x, stereo 0.20x and 0.32x, with no network Encode Not validated here at all: both encoders are floating-point, which on a part with no FPU means software floating point AC-4 Builds in the fixed-point tier (CONFIG_ICLFORGE_AC4; an image of the decoder alone is 1,158,768 bytes) and does not fit the part: the decoder peaks at 286,365 bytes at 2.0, where the probe reports 249,180 bytes free. For the same reason this part's QEMU leg cannot run the AC-4 probe; its instruction set, RV32IMC, gave the fixed tier's pinned hashes on QEMU's virt board with the C3's compiler, run by hand (planning/ac4.md, D14d). No ESP32 sink takes AC-4 in a Sendspin group Real silicon None. Correctness is established under qemu-riscv32 emulation CI The esp32c3 fixed-point leg (build-esp32c3, under QEMU) beside build-esp32s3 in .github/workflows/_build.yml, in the esp lane of ci.yml: after a merge to main that changes the ESP32 trees or a tree its component ships (the lane table lists them), and in the nightly run (CI for many agents)

docs.title: Why this part, and not another ESP32 variant
docs.text:
Whether a part is viable comes down to floating point, not RAM. Espressif measure a single-precision cosine at ~2,377 cycles on an ESP32-C3 against 121 on an ESP32-S3 (Floating-Point Units on Espressif SoCs).

Part Usable RAM Clock FPU Vector unit Viable ESP32-S3 341,760 DIRAM 240 MHz single PIE, integer-only; 128-bit float load/store Yes — the primary target ESP32-P4 768 KB L2MEM 400 MHz (360 on pre-production v1.x silicon) single PIE, integer-only; no wide float load Not as S3 replacement — complementary best sink module, real time on every fixture in the probe, Wi-Fi through the board's C6 in hearth_sink, and the only part here that decodes AC-4 (ESP32-P4, sink tiers) ESP32 (LX6) ~320 KB 240 MHz single none Plausible, slower ESP32-S2 320 KB 240 MHz none none No — soft-float everything ESP32-C3/C6/C61 400/512/320+PSRAM KB 160 MHz none none Yes, in the fixed-point tier — this page and ESP32-C6; C61 proposed, no board (sink tiers)

Every part with an FPU has a single-precision one, so double is soft-float across the whole family and decode_scalar_t earns its keep on all of them.

docs.title: Why not the ESP32-P4
docs.text:
Assessed and declined on 2026-09-08 as a replacement for the ESP32-S3 Wi-Fi Sendspin sink. It is dual-core RISC-V at 400 MHz with 768 KB of SRAM, and holds the peak heap without the float32 work — so it reads as the answer if the S3 misses real time. Three things were checked and two settle that closer.

Its vector extension has no floating point. The P4 is RV32IMAFC plus Xhwlp and Xesppie, vendor extensions no other implementation carries — not the ratified RISC-V Vector extension. Across the 360 instructions in ESP-IDF's own decoder test for it, the only data types are s8, s16, s32, u8, u16, u32. No f32 anywhere. Espressif's own code agrees: in esp-dsp every _arp4 file using a PIE instruction sits under fixed/, and the float32 kernels contain exactly one esp. instruction each — esp.lp.setup, the hardware loop — with scalar fmadd.s arithmetic. So an f32x4 has nothing to compile to there either. (The S3 has the same integer-only PIE limit and still decodes in scalar float.)

It has no radio, and the plan it would replace is a Wi-Fi plan. No Wi-Fi and no Bluetooth; it needs a companion ESP32-C6 or -H2 (or Ethernet). That disqualifies it as a drop-in for the S3 node. The S3 probe has since cleared every fixture in real time, so the “rescue the decode” motivation is gone for that product shape.

What the P4 would buy is clock — 12.8 M cycles per frame against the S3's 7.68 M, 1.67×, per-core in both cases — plus wider TDM (up to 16×32-bit on one controller) and more internal SRAM.

Reopened 2026-09-21 as a complementary “best” module, extended 2026-09-23 with a proposed C61 tier, on a shared dual-ES9080 PCB (C6 = OK, 2.0 shipped / durable ceiling, no PSRAM on this die; C61 = good, 5.1 desired / PSRAM-backed, proposed, no board yet; S3 = better ≤7.1.4 without enhanced coupling / both DACs @ 16-bit, shipped; P4 = best ≤9.1.6 with full tools desired / both DACs @ 32-bit). See planning/esp32-sink-tiers.md. Phase P1 of that plan is done: ESP32-P4 is real time on every fixture on a board with no network in the probe, and hearth_sink has since played a paired Sendspin stream on it over Wi-Fi through the onboard C6 — with a chip-revision trap specific to pre-production silicon worth reading before flashing one.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Uses the same firmware/esp-idf/iclforge/ component and EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS setup as ESP32-S3 → The ESP-IDF component. firmware/baremetal/platform/esp32c3/ is the probe target:

. $IDF_PATH/export.sh
python "$IDF_PATH/tools/idf_tools.py" install qemu-riscv32   # once
cd firmware/baremetal/platform/esp32c3
idf.py set-target esp32c3
idf.py build                                  # -DICLFORGE_DECODE_SCALAR=fixed by default
idf.py qemu

tools/checks/run_esp32c3_probe.sh drives that leg. Its distinguishing gate is not a footprint ceiling but the PCM itself: the tier's arithmetic is integer, so the probe's per-fixture hashes are the same on RISC-V as on the x86 host and the Cortex-M3 leg, and the runner holds all three to one pinned set (testdata/fixed-probe-pcm-hashes.json). --scalar=float builds the same part with the S3's tier, which is what the two arithmetics are compared with.

Any other project built for this target against the component gets the fixed-point tier too: when a project leaves ICLFORGE_DECODE_SCALAR unset, the component sets it from the part, and a part with no FPU gets fixed (ESP32-S3 → The ESP-IDF component).

docs.text:

docs.title: ESP32-C6
docs.text:
The minimum-footprint decoder on an Espressif ESP32-C6: one 160 MHz RISC-V core (RV32IMAC) with no floating-point unit, 512 KB of SRAM shared with WiFi 6, Bluetooth LE and 802.15.4, and no external PSRAM, which ESP-IDF does not support on this part. It decodes in the fixed-point tier, as the ESP32-C3 does, from the same firmware/esp-idf/iclforge/ component, whose manifest lists esp32c6 beside esp32s3, esp32c3 and esp32p4.

Every figure on this page was measured on a board on 2026-09-15, with no network and again with WiFi connected and a TCP stream arriving while the decoder ran. The I2S section's sink figures are from 2026-09-16.

The decoder has used less memory since. On the fixed tier the CI probe now reports a peak of 195,505 bytes at most across the fourteen fixtures on the Cortex-M3 leg, the same figures on the ESP32-C3's QEMU leg for the twelve it runs, and 174,850 and 181,258 bytes for the two 7.1.4 fixtures, where the tables below have 227,662 and 234,070. This part has not been measured again, so the memory and fit figures below are those of 2026-09-15.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Decode Correct: all fourteen fixtures, every channel's level within the probe's tolerance, and every fixed-tier PCM hash equal to the values the x86-64 host, the Cortex-M3 leg and the ESP32-C3 leg are held to (testdata/fixed-probe-pcm-hashes.json). Not the folds to stereo (1.03x and 1.62x), E-AC-3 line mode (1.15x), enhanced coupling (1.71x), 7.1.4 (1.88x) or the Atmos objects rows Real time, with WiFi and a stream AC-3 5.1 (0.82x), E-AC-3 5.1 with AHT, spectral extension and coupling (0.96x), the Atmos bed (0.71x), a 192 kbit/s E-AC-3 5.1 stream (0.64x), and stereo and mono (0.17x to 0.41x). Not E-AC-3 7.1 (1.09x), the folds, line mode, enhanced coupling or the Atmos objects rows Memory, no network Every fixture fits: 383,416 bytes free before the decode, largest block 352,256, against a largest peak of 234,070 (7.1.4 folded to stereo) Memory, with WiFi and a stream About 236,000 bytes free before the decode, largest block 217,088 to 221,184. With ESP-IDF's WiFi IRAM options off every fixture fits, 7.1.4 included, and the decode is slower Encode Not measured. The decoder peaks at 286,365 bytes at 2.0, against about 236,000 free with WiFi up in ESP-IDF's default configuration and 285,408 with WiFi's code kept in flash, and 383,416 with no network. docs.title: Measured, on a board
docs.text:
An ESP32-C6 in the QFN40 package, chip revision v0.2, with 16 MB of flash read in DIO mode at 80 MHz, reached over its USB-Serial/JTAG port. ESP-IDF v6.1 and GCC esp-15.2.0_20251204, -Os with the decode-critical sources at -O2 (ICLFORGE_MINIMAL_HOT_O2, the project's default), the task watchdog off, and 160 MHz as the probe measures it against esp_timer.

The probe decodes six frames of each fixture. Its timing is the decoder's own: the level and hash accumulation it runs inside the decoder's block callback is timed and subtracted.

docs.title: Decode time
docs.text:
Microseconds per frame, and that as a fraction of the 32,000 microseconds a frame lasts. With no network, two runs of the fixed-point build agreed within 3 microseconds on every row. With WiFi, three runs of the same build varied by up to 16% on the stereo and mono rows and 12% on the others, and each WiFi cell is the slowest run.
